#3505. 'IT: Welcome to Derry' Quietly Drops an Essential Stephen King Lore Episode

Editor's note: The below contains spoilers for "A Story of Derry."

The irony that fans of Stranger Things, a show heavily inspired by IT, spent months convincing themselves there was a secret episode is somewhat amusing when considering that the prequel series IT: Welcome to Derry managed to drop a surprise episode on Halloween at midnight. Although the first season of It: Welcome to Derry took place in the 1960s, two decades before the events of Stephen King's original novel, Season 2 is expected to go back further in the timeline to the 1930s during the Great Depression. The show's new prequel episode, a standalone installment titled “A Story of Derry,” goes back even further than that into pre-Colonial times, where the Western Wood hasn't yet been founded as Derry.

The most powerful idea in IT: Welcome to Derry is that the ancient evil doesn't take just one form, as it represents a societal danger that reconfigures itself within different generations based on the context of the era. “A Story of Derry” explains how the spirit known as “The Galloo” was first confined to the land that would eventually become Derry, even if its evil had already caused mass destruction. A core tenet of King’s stories is the idea that there will always be a group of brave, often young outsiders who are willing to take a stand against these supernatural forces, and “A Story of Derry” features a compelling ensemble of new protagonists in Necani (Kiawentiio), Maneese (Michael Podemski-Bedard), and Kino (Isabel Deroy-Olson), the warriors from the Shokopiwah tribe who go hunting for the Galloo.

If the Galloo and the Shokopiwah tribe sound familiar, it’s because they were first introduced in the Season 1 episode “The Great Swirling Apparatus of Our Planet's Function,” where Dick Halloran (Chris Chalk) is working under the orders of Lieutenant General Shaw (James Remar) to interrogate the Native American teenager Taniel (Joshua Odjick) to learn about his aunt’s story about how the Galloo first came to Earth and was eventually imprisoned by their people using a fragment from the star. “A Story of Derry” offers more detail to this origin tale by telling it from the right perspective; instead of this critical piece of Native American mythology being coaxed out of a victim through militaristic interrogation, it is shown from the perspective of the young warriors of the Shokopiwah tribe who would go on to pass it along through oral traditions. Colonialism is a component of how The Galloo reconfigures itself, which is hinted at in “A Story of Derry;” not only does it first take the form of white colonizers who have impeded on the land, but it is implied that The Galloo was awakened by the military in an act of appropriating Native American magic for their own gain.

EPs Andy Muschietti and Barbara Muschietti also talk about that gruesome car ride, the movie theater massacre, and holding back on Pennywise.

One of the bigger surprises in “A Story of Derry” is that the episode includes a great performance from Zahn McClarnon as Mativ, a Native American warrior who initially explains the story of the Galloo to Necani and their friends. The revelation that Mativ has been corrupted by the Galloo, which led him to massacre his own tribe, is a reminder of how cursed the land is to experience acts of violence that leave few survivors, allowing the stories to be lost. It’s also a showcase for McClarnon's terrifically unsettling acting, because Mativ is initially presented as being a caring mentor before revealing himself to be compromised. McClarnon does a great job of showing Mativ's complexity as the character struggles to resist the corrupting influence within him.

The most shocking reveal in “A Story of Derry” is that it marks the first on-screen appearance of Maturin, the cosmic turtle with the power to defeat the Galloo. Although the idea of an all-powerful turtle might seem ridiculous to those who aren’t versed in King’s lore, this character is of critical importance within many of the author’s most legendary texts; Maturin is one of the 12 ancient guardians in The Dark Tower universe responsible for holding up the pillars of reality, and in the original IT novel, Bill recites a ritual taught to him by Maturin to expel Pennywise. It’s been suspected that IT: Welcome to Derry might delve into some of the weirder aspects of King’s mythology and potentially incorporate aspects of some of his other novels, and the introduction of Maturin is the first clue.

Your instincts, your strengths, and your particular way of thinking under pressure point to one villain you actually have a fighting chance against. Everyone else — good luck.

Jason is relentless, but he is also predictable — and that is the gap you would exploit.

Michael watches before he moves. He is patient, methodical, and almost impossible to detect — until it's too late for anyone who isn't paying close enough attention.

Freddy wins by getting inside your head — using your own fears, your own memories, your own subconscious as weapons against you. That strategy requires a target who can be destabilised.

Pennywise is ancient, shapeshifting, and feeds on terror — but it has one critical vulnerability: it cannot function against someone who genuinely stops being afraid of it.

Chucky's greatest advantage is that nobody takes him seriously until it's already too late. He exploits the gap between how something looks and what it actually is.

Although it's an important piece of lore that provides necessary context for the series, “A Story of Derry” is also a thrilling standalone installment that revamps the story from a fresh perspective. IT: Welcome to Derry is at its best when it moves beyond ties to the original novel and goes deep into Derry's history, and hopefully more episodes like this one will take similar risks.

#3504. Why Harry Bosch's New Series Is Releasing On MGM+ After Prime Video's Spinoff Clarified By Michael Connelly

Harry Bosch creator and author Michael Connelly has cleared up why the character’s newest TV show is coming to MGM+ rather than Prime Video.

While Bosch as a literary character has been investigating crimes going back to 1992’s The Black Echo, he made his TV debut in 2014 with Prime Video’s Bosch, starring Titus Welliver in the titular role. Following that show wrapping up in 2021 after seven seasons, Welliver went on to reprise the character in a leading capacity for Bosch: Legacy, and as a guest star on Ballard. Now, Gotham and Shameless’ Cameron Monaghan is stepping in to play a younger Bosch in Bosch: Start of Watch, but unlike its predecessors, this prequel will stream on MGM+.

When asked by a fan on Threads why Start of Watch is airing on MGM+, Connelly answered, “That’s the studio that wanted the show. Others passed.” This won’t be the first time that a show set in the Bosch franchise has been presented on a platform other than Prime Video, as Bosch: Legacy aired on the now-defunct Amazon Freevee. That said, MGM+ is now run as a companion streaming service to Prime Video following Amazon's acquisition of MGM in 2021, so Start of Watch is being kept within the corporate family.

It’s unclear if Bosch: Start of Watch episodes will later become available to watch on Prime Video, or if they’ll remain solely confined to MGM+. Earlier this year, Spider-Noir released its entire season on MGM+ first, and then it was delivered to Prime Video two days later. Other currently-airing MGM+-exclusive original programming include Godfather of Harlem (which is concluding with a two-hour series finale), From, The Institute, Robin Hood, The Westies, and American Hostage.

The 1992-set Bosch: Start of Watch follows Monaghan’s 26-year-old Harry Bosch coming back to the United States after serving in the Persian Gulf War, and joining the Los Angeles Police Department ahead of the city’s riots in response to the Rodney King beating. Although this is the first Bosch TV show not to adapt any of Connelly’s existing work, Welliver’s son Eamonn did portray a younger Bosch as an LAPD officer in Bosch: Legacy flashbacks. Before that, Welliver’s other son, Quinn, played the character as an adolescent in Bosch.

Monaghan is joined in Bosch: Start of Watch by Omari Hardwick as his LAPD training officer Eli Bridges, Ariana Guerra as fellow LAPD officer and romantic interest Rosa, and J.D. Pardo as Cory, Bosch’s criminal foster brother. Connelly has also confirmed that Welliver will not reprise Bosch in any present-day flash-forwards on Start of Watch. Tom Bernardo and Brian Anthony created the prequel and executive produce it, with Bernardo also serving as showrunner.

The first two episodes of Bosch: Start of Watch will be released on Sunday, January 10 on MGM+. New episodes will follow weekly until February 21. Meanwhile, Ballard is returning for season 2, and the latest Harry Bosch book, The Hollow, was released earlier this year.

#3503. The First Time Producers Had to Find a New James Bond, the Result Was the Best 007 Movie Ever

When long-time producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael Wilson stepped away from the James Bond franchise last year and Daniel Craig made it clear that he was finished playing agent 007, new producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman were faced with an unenviable task: finding a new actor to step into one of the most iconic roles in all of cinema. In the last few weeks, it’s been reported that Pascal, Heyman, and new Bond director Denis Villeneuve have zeroed in on a few final contenders including Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor.

Whoever the filmmakers choose, it’s likely to be controversial; Bond fans are very loyal to their particular favorites, and have been ever since Sean Connery was first replaced in the role back in 1969. The general consensus seems to be that Connery was the best Bond (though Craig runs a close second in most polls), but often one’s preference depends on which Bond was one’s first; as someone who grew up with Roger Moore, he’s always been my favorite, and I argued for his supremacy in an earlier IndieWire piece. Related Stories ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Is Lured Into Lily James’ Cult in a Gut-Wrenching Drama ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Review: The King of the Monsters Returns with a Direct Sequel That’s One Better Than the Last Movie in Almost Every Way

The casting of a new James Bond has always set off a media furor, even in the days long before social media and Letterboxd. When Connery decided he had had enough as 007 after shooting the fifth James Bond movie, “You Only Live Twice,” the press followed producers Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and Harry Saltzman’s talent search with bated breath. Once the role was cast, they scrutinized the choice with an intensity that no actor could have survived — certainly not a male model whose only screen credit was a series of chocolate commercials.

After Connery quit, Broccoli, Saltzman, and director Peter Hunt spent over a year interviewing, auditioning, and screen testing hundreds of actors — including a young Shakespearean thespian named Timothy Dalton, who would go on to play Bond nearly 20 years later — to play Bond in “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service.” Anthony Rogers (“Camelot”), John Richardson (“Black Sunday”), and stage actor Roy Marsden were considered before the filmmakers landed on George Lazenby, whose previous acting experience was limited to those chocolate commercials.

Lazenby lied at his initial meeting and said he had been acting in movies in Germany and Hong Kong, figuring the producers wouldn’t be able to check, but came clean to Hunt the next day. Hunt and the producers were concerned about Lazenby’s chops but loved his look, so they took a chance on the newcomer and put him through hours of voice coaching (to lose his Australian accent) and stunt training before deciding to pull the trigger a few weeks before production was scheduled to begin.

The question then became how to frame Lazenby’s onscreen introduction to make the transition as seamless as possible for audiences. One of screenwriter Richard Maibaum’s drafts began with Bond surviving an explosion that required him to undergo reconstructive surgery, but this was scrapped in favor of a more conventional prologue involving Bond encountering love interest Diana Rigg and fighting foes on the beach and in the water. When Rigg leaves Bond behind instead of making love to him as was customary for Bond’s leading ladies, Lazenby looks in the camera and says, “This never happened to the other fellow.”

It’s a very funny and very efficient way of acknowledging the change in personnel and then moving on, and the opening credit sequence further eases the transition by utilizing clips from earlier Bond movies. It also helps that the creative team on the movie consisted of Bond veterans including Maibaum, production designer Syd Cain, composer John Barry, and Hunt, who made his directorial debut with “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” but had been an editor and second unit director on earlier Bond films.

As a result, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” still looks and sounds so much like a Bond film that the introduction of Lazenby is less jarring than it might have been, though what’s interesting about the movie is how much better it is in just about every way than the previous Connery pictures. One can argue about the relative merits of Connery vs. Lazenby, but there’s no debating the visual elegance of “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” which eschews the somewhat bland high-key lighting of the earlier Bond films in favor of something more atmospheric and glamorous.

Audiences at the time might not have appreciated Hunt and cinematographer Michael Reed’s efforts, being distracted by debates over Lazenby, but contemporary directors like Steven Soderbergh and Christopher Nolan have referenced “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” as an influence and made a case for it as the best of all James Bond movies. On his website, Soderbergh wrote that “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was cinematically “the best Bond film and the only one worth watching repeatedly for reasons other than pure entertainment (certainly it’s the only Bond film I look at and think: I’m stealing that shit).”

Aside from containing several of the series’ best set pieces (including some awe-inspiring ski chases that inspired Nolan when he made “Inception”), “On Her Majesty’s Service” is also the most emotionally resonant Bond film to be made before the Daniel Craig era, with a genuinely moving love story between Lazenby and Rigg. Although composer John Barry scored a lot of 007 movies, his talents were never put to better use than in this film, which fully took advantage of Barry’s skill for sweeping, romantic themes that would later win him an Oscar for “Out of Africa.”

Lazenby gets some of the credit here too; he may lack Connery’s icy charm, but he’s a more human Bond. Displaying a slightly goofier sense of humor than Connery, he’s a transitional figure between the original 007 and the more overtly comic one Roger Moore would introduce in “Live and Let Die” four years later. According to Lazenby, he could have expressed even more emotion had Peter Hunt allowed it; when the actor played one particularly devastating scene with tears in his eyes, Hunt ordered a second take, arguing that Bond shouldn’t cry.

As good as he is in the part, Lazenby’s experience shooting “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” doesn’t seem to have been pleasurable, though whether or not the blame rests on his shoulders depends on who’s telling the story. According to Lazenby, Hunt went cold toward him early in shooting over a misunderstanding and was too preoccupied with the technical side of things to give him much attention; Cubby Broccoli, on the other hand, said Lazenby was spoiled and entitled and alienated many of his colleagues.

Although Broccoli was ultimately happy with Lazenby’s performance, by the time the movie opened, there were a lot of lingering hard feelings — a situation that wasn’t helped by the fairly lukewarm reviews Lazenby received, or by one of his representatives making a statement that Lazenby would not be returning to the role of James Bond. This was the first Broccoli or Harry Saltzman heard of any plans for Lazenby to abandon the part, and they quickly announced that Lazenby had been fired to make it seem as though his departure was their decision, not his.

Although Lazenby later stressed that he wasn’t the one who made the announcement he was quitting, he also clearly didn’t have any great desire to stay on as Bond. His contract was for seven years and had multiple clauses that he felt would restrict his career and lifestyle, and he still hadn’t signed it when “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” wrapped. Lazenby figured he could make more money doing one film in Italy than he could in five years on his Bond contract; he also, in one of the great errors in judgment in movie history, assumed that the James Bond franchise was dying in the era of “Easy Rider” and wouldn’t last much longer anyway.

In fact, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” was a sizable hit, grossing $82 million on a production budget of $8 million. It wasn’t as popular as the last Connery film, however, and the mixed reviews gave it the aura of a failure. Broccoli and Saltzman began another worldwide search for a new Bond, considering American stars like Clint Eastwood, Burt Reynolds, and Adam West before convincing Connery to return. The result, “Diamonds Are Forever,” was a monster hit, and Lazenby went on to scattered work around Europe, acknowledging years later that his decision to quit Bond was a major mistake.

Lazenby didn’t completely leave 007 behind, however. After “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service,” he played a James Bond-esque character in the “Alfred Hitchcock Presents” episode “Diamonds Aren’t Forever” and, in 1983, Lazenby appeared in the TV movie “Return of the Man from U.N.C.L.E.” as a spy with the initials J.B. (who drove an Aston Martin, no less). The actor made a handful of interesting films after he played Bond, most notably Brian Trenchard-Smith’s great action film “The Man from Hong Kong” and Peter Bogdanovich’s exquisite Paul Theroux adaptation “Saint Jack.”

Lazenby was never more memorable than he was as James Bond, however, and it’s a shame he didn’t play the character in more pictures and further develop his variations on the persona. It remains to be seen where Villeneuve’s selection will place in the pantheon of Bonds, but whoever is cast would best be advised to ignore the inevitable social media firestorm that’s coming their way.

Lazenby’s saga proves that no matter how capable an actor is stepping into Bond’s shoes, it takes a while for history to render a fair assessment. 57 years after critics dismissed it, “On Her Majesty’s Secret Service” has stood the test of time — it’s Soderbergh and Nolan’s verdicts, not those of the contemporary press, that have proven correct.

#3502. If You Loved 'Crystal Lake,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Peacock’s Crystal Lake is an unexpected treat in a lot of ways, taking one of horror’s most iconic figures—Jason Voorhees of the Friday the 13th franchise—and digging into the universe’s background by focusing on his mother, Pamela. Famously the actual serial killer in the original film, Pamela’s development into a psychotic killer who inspired her son to become the psychotic killer of all time is the engine that drives Crystal Lake, finding the damaged humanity behind the terror. If you’ve burned through all eight episodes of Crystal Lake’s first season, and you’ve worked through the streamalike series with similar DNA, it’s time to check out some movies—starting with the perfect companion film, 2022’s Pearl.

The second film in Ti West’s X trilogy (starting with X and concluding with 2024’s MaXXXine) is the ideal film to watch after Crystal Lake. Like the series, it explores a female serial killer’s backstory and recontextualizes your understanding of their motives and psychology. It also requires that you be familiar with the original story—while you can certainly watch Crystal Lake or Pearl without having seen the Friday the 13th films or X, you’ll be missing out on a lot if you do.

In X, a group of young people descends on a dilapidated old farm to film an adult movie in Texas in 1979, and by the end of the film most of them are dead, killed by the farm’s elderly couple Howard (Stephen Ure) and Pearl (Mia Goth), with Pearl presented as the most deranged and dangerous of the two. It’s a riveting update to the classic splatter movie template, and Goth nails her dual role as the Final Girl Maxine and the psychotic, murderous Pearl. The prequel, Pearl, jumps back to 1918, when Pearl (Goth again) was a young woman living with her strict mother and paralyzed father. Pearl has big dreams of being an entertainer, but her mother tries to trap her to ensure she’s there to care for her parents and work the farm. Pearl’s lonely unhappiness and frustration (both mental and, er, physical) inspire a slow boil of tension as her grip on sanity frays, and her anger toward her parents curdles into something frightening.

Like Crystal Lake, Pearl takes a killer who seems fairly one-dimensional in their original presentation and gives them a deeper back story and psychological framing. Pamela Voorhees wasn’t just crazy—she was driven to madness by the horrible things that happened to her and her son, and the awful way she’s treated by her fellow humans. Similarly, Pearl is a hopeful and innocent young woman who is slowly molded into a killer by the events of her life. Both the series and the film serve as reminders that monsters are rarely born—they’re made. And it’s usually the casual cruelty of the people around them that does the making. If you loved Crystal Lake’s fresh take on Pamela, Pearl is the perfect choice for a movie night. Stream Pearl on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Need more serial killer movies that hit the Crystal Lake vibe? Never fear—here are some other excellent choices to pair with the series.

If you’ve never actually seen the original Friday the 13th (or if it’s been a while), this is a must-watch for fans of Crystal Lake. Although the series takes some liberties to update the timeline, it’s still intended as a glimpse into the events that shaped both Pamela and Jason Voorhees into inhuman (and somewhat supernatural) monsters. Initially given savagely bad reviews, the film was a surprise blockbuster and is now regarded as a classic of a genre it helped to create in the first place; rewatching it today not only helps contextualize Crystal Lake, it puts the entire slasher genre into perspective. Stream Friday the 13th on Netflix or rent it on Prime Video.

The success of Friday the 13th led to a rush of copycat films, of course. Most of those weren’t particularly good or even interesting, but Sleepaway Camp is an exception (although it was similarly savaged by critics at the time). Now a cult classic, Sleepaway Camp has two things that recommend it to fans of Crystal Lake and Friday the 13th: a weird sensibility that gives it an otherworldly atmosphere that enhances the sense of dread, and what is probably the most unexpected twist ending in the history of slasher films (and it’s probably a Top 10 twist in general). Stream Sleepaway Camp on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

One reason Crystal Lake exists is the enduring power and influence of slasher films in general and Friday the 13th specifically. Few recent films have tapped into that dreamy nightmare feel like Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. As with most of Schoenbrun’s work, the film delves into themes of identity, subverting queer tropes, and the malleable nature of reality itself. If you’re looking for a slasher story that’s less straightforward than Crystal Lake while dealing with some similar themes of transformation and destiny, this is it. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

If you’ve seen all the Friday the 13th movies and want more slasher horror with a bit more edge, check out The Burning. Is it a great film? Not really. Combining the straightforward slasher thrills of Friday with some of the villain motivations of fellow classic franchise A Nightmare on Elm Street, The Burning dials the blood and guts up to 11 (and beyond) and remains notoriously gory even by today’s standards. But if your fave part of Crystal Lake is the frequently over-the-top gore and violence, this is an ideal movie choice. Stream The Burning on The Roku Channel or Kanopy.

Want a slasher film that explores the psyche of a female killer the way Crystal Lake deconstructs Pamela Voorhees? Check out May. A fragile young woman, May struggles to find connection with the people around her, and slowly descends into a fantasy world that inspires her to literally make her own ideal friend. What makes May so interesting is the depth of the exploration of May’s personality that’s similar to how Pamela is handled in Crystal Lake, tracing each step of her stumble into a bloody hell. Stream May on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

Here are my top picks from Netflix’s massive library drop

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Netflix just added 30 movies and shows to kick off November 2026. Like many of the best streaming services, Netflix reliably kicks off a new month with a huge drop of movies and TV shows, and the world's biggest streamer isn't bucking that trend this month.

A major library refresh is always welcome, but it can lead to decision paralysis. After all, with so many options to consider, it would be easy to fall into the trap of spending more time scrolling than streaming.

That’s why I’ve put in the hard work for you and sorted through everything added to Netflix in November 2026, and picked out five movies and shows worthy of your watchlist.

My selections include the hilarious 2010s comedy "Bridesmaids," two movies released just a week apart, the intense war thriller "Fury," and the captivating psychological drama "Whiplash." And for those feeling nostalgia, I've got you; be sure to stream the '80s classic "Stand By Me."

Binge-watchers, I haven't forgotten about you either. "Rectify" seasons 1-4 have just found a new home on Netflix, and this slow-burn drama was critically acclaimed across its whole run for good reason.

Want to know more about my top picks? Let’s jump into the five Netflix movies and shows you need to watch to start your November right.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

What's it about? When the underachieving, thirtysomething Annie Walker (Kristen Wiig) is asked to be maid of honor for her lifelong best friend, Lillian (Maya Rudolph), she struggles with her own messy love life while also wrangling an eccentric group of bridesmaids, which includes Helen (Rose Byrne), who wants the maid of honor gig herself.

Why you should watch it: For starters, “Bridesmaids” is absolutely hilarious, but it was also a trailblazer. Released in the early 2010s, a period when male-led raunchy comedies were particularly popular, this Paul Feig flick proved that women can be just as funny, and also equally inappropriate (I'll warn you, there's potty humor aplenty). Melissa McCarthy even nabbed an Oscar nomination for her supporting role.

What's it about? In 1945, during the Allies' invasion of Germany, Don “Wardaddy” Collier (Brad Pitt) commands a Sherman tank nicknamed Fury. Alongside his crew of five fellow soldiers, they face overwhelming odds against enemies that are better-equipped as they head into Nazi territory and attempt to strike a decisive blow to turn the tide of war.

Why you should watch it: “Fury” is an intense war movie that really brings you into the heat of battle. Its tank-centric action scenes are exhilarating and well crafted. However, it’s the camaraderie and close brotherhood of its cast that stands out the most. This is a great movie to watch on Netflix if you’re a fan of HBO’s acclaimed “Band of Brothers.”

What's it about? Andrew Neiman (Miles Teller) is a student at a prestigious music conservatory, drafted into the institution's top ensemble, conducted by the exacting Terence Fletcher (J.K. Simmons). Under Fletcher’s ruthless direction, Andrew is tormented and reaches a breaking point as his skills are pushed to their absolute limit.

Why you should watch it: Inspired by writer/director Damien Chazelle’s own experience in a competitive high school jazz band, “Whiplash” is a modern masterpiece. It’s an incredibly intense ride that builds to a genuinely note-perfect finale. J.K. Simmons steals every single scene with a memorizing performance that won the Oscar, SAG, Globe, BAFTA and Critics' Choice awards.

What's it about? Daniel Holden (Aden Young) has spent the last 19 years on death row for the murder of his girlfriend. When new evidence sees his conviction overturned, he returns to his hometown in Georgia and attempts to reintegrate into society. But that’s not so easy when there are ghosts around every corner, and many locals remain convinced of his guilt.

Why you should watch it: Critically acclaimed throughout its run, “Rectify” arrives in full on Netflix on November 1. You can binge-watch all four seasons; 30 episodes total. Critics praised the show for its performances, writing, and authentic portrayal of Southern culture. It’s very much a slow-burn drama, but stick with it, and you’ll be richly rewarded.

Stream "Rectify" seasons 1-4 on Netflix now

What's it about? Based on Stephen King’s novella “The Body,” this small-town drama follows a day in the life of four adolescents living in (the fictional) Castle Rock, Oregon. Looking for something to do on a hot summer’s day, they head off into the woods to locate the dead body of a missing boy. This adventure proves to be life-defining for them all.

Why you should watch it: “Stand By Me” is a certified classic from the late, great Rob Reiner, and one of the most beloved coming-of-age movies of all time. With an all-star young cast — Wil Wheaton, River Phoenix, Corey Feldman and Kiefer Sutherland — it’s charming and relatable. And if you were wondering, yes, it does feature the iconic Ben E. #3500. ‘Loser Core,’ ‘EBK,’ and Other Gen Z and Gen Alpha Slang You Might Need Help Decoding

If constantly being mogged by sigmas has you feeling like a fuhuhluhtoogan, and you have no idea what any of that means, you've come to the right place. This glossary aims to define and explain popular slang words and phrases of Generation Z (usually defined as people born between 1997 and 2012) and Generation A (anyone born between 2012 and now) so you'll know what the hell people are talking about.

A word of warning: If you aren't of those generations, and/or you need an online list to know what slang words mean, you should not say them aloud unless you're trying to be embarrassing.

Ballhog: A fashion trend among Gen Z and Gen A characterized by wearing vintage clothes that look normal, even drab, to most, but that people in the know can recognize as interesting or unique retro clothing.

Benny tripping: Intentionally overdosing on Benadryl to experience an (almost always unpleasant) "trip."

Crunged: The past tense of "cringe," "crunged" is often used to describe extreme cringe, like "I cringed so hard I crunged."

EBK: stands for "Extreme Baller Knowledge." It goes beyond the sports reference to apply to to anyone who has deep knowledge of a subject. It's usually used ironically.

GiGis: Good game. Pronounced like the name Gigi. The post game pleasantry "good game" has been a staple in sports since forever. Gamers adopted it and shortened it to "GG" in text. So GiGis is a way of saying "good game."

Glass skin: Describes skin that is so smooth, luminous, and clear, it seems to shine.

Loser core: A youth sub-culture/musical sub-genre categorized by listening to depressing, alternative-inspired music and dressing in drab, oversize clothing.

304: Hoe. (Type "304" on a calculator and turn it upside down.)

4+4: Ate. Four plus four is eight, or "ate." (See "ate.")

6-7 (or 67): This piece of Generation Alpha brainrot slang doesn't mean anything. It's just funny to some people to say "6-7," especially in answer to any question involving numbers. Ex: "Q: What time is it? A: six-seveeen."

6-7 weekend: A weekend in which Saturday falls on the 6th day of the month and Sunday on the 7th.

7x7=49: Often refers to a man who is attractive in a self-evident way. Based on the belief that the equation 7x7=49 makes intuitive sense in a way other equations do not.

80/20 rule: An axiom in online incel spaces, the 80/20 is the idea that 80% of women only date the "top" 20% of men.

Algo speak: Coded language used to bypass online content moderation. Examples: "regarded" used instead of "retarded" and "unalive" instead of "kill."

Alpha male: Taken from animal ethology, an alpha male is the dominant member of a group of males, or just a male who is in charge. (See "beta male" and "sigma male.")

Alpine divorce: An alpine divorce is when a man takes his wife or girlfriend on a hike, usually in the mountains, and then just leaves her there to fend for herself.

ASAP (or A$AP): When a rapper has ASAP or A$AP in front of their name, it indicates affiliation with the ASAP Mob, a New York hip-hop collective.

Ate/eat: Done very well, often regarding clothing. e.g.: "You ate that outfit." See also: "serving."

Aura: Someone who is mysterious and cool is said to "have aura."

Aura battle: Aura is coolness or charisma ("rizz" if you prefer). An "aura battle" is a public contest in which the person with the most aura, as determined by the crowd and/or comment section reaction, wins. (See "Aura")

Aura farming: Depending on the context, “aura farming” can refer to a person who does something cool without trying or someone who is trying too hard to appear cool.

Baby Boo syndrome: A joking reference to people who are very into the Baby Boo memes popular on TikTok.

Baddie: A bad/wild girl. Meant as a compliment.

Baka: Japanese word meaning “crazy" or “foolish.” Used mainly in the anime community.

Bed-rotting: Staying in bed all day. You may know it as “lazing around.” (See "Hurkle-durkle.")

Beez: Popularized in Nicki Minaj's 2012 track "Beez in the Trap," beez means something like "I am always." So "beez in the trap" means "I am always in the trap." (See "Trap.")

Beta male: A beta male, or just "beta," is a weaker, subservient male. (See "alpha male" and "sigma male.")

Boombayah: A euphemism for having sex. It’s used mostly online, often to defeat censorship algorithms.

Bop: A girl who sleeps around. Also: a great song.

Boy aquarium: TikTok slang that describes hockey games.

Boy kibble: The male response to "girl dinner," boy kibble is food boys eat. It usually consists of rice and ground beef, often served without spices or vegetables.

Boysober: Someone who has sworn off sex, relationships, and/or dating.

Brain-rot: A description of the overuse of stupid slang. See also: “Skibidi.” Also used to describe the effects of being overly online.

Brat: The contemporary meaning of "brat" is an adjective describing a person who is edgy, imperfect, and confident. It was coined by pop star Charli XCX who defined it as "that girl who is a little messy and likes to party and maybe says some dumb things sometimes. Who feels herself but maybe also has a breakdown."

Bruzz: Bros. Part of the -uzz family of slang words. See "Huzz" and "-uzz."

Bubba truck: A lifted or otherwise modified pick-up truck.

Catch a fade: To have a fight. (See "fade.")

Chad: An attractive man; an “alpha male.” See "Giga-Chad."

Chat: A reference to streamers addressing their chat windows aloud. Saying “chat” in real life is an ironic joke.

Cheesin': The slang word "cheesin'" refers to smiling, particularly a big, goofy smile. It comes from the common exhortation to "say cheese!" before a photo is taken. The word "cheesing," with a "g" at the end, often means the same thing, but it can also refer to the trend of throwing slices of cheese at cars and/or people.

Chopped: Ugly. Chopped is often applied to someone's face or outfit, but anything that isn't aesthetically pleasing could be called "chopped," as could anything that is generally not good, like an awkward situation.

Choppelganger: A portmanteau of "chopped" and "doppelgänger," a choppelganger is someone who looks like another person, but worse. (See "chopped.")

Chud: A physically unappealing person. Sometimes used for a man who holds right-wing views.

Clanker: A slur aimed at robots and AI agents pretending to be human.

Clock that: "I understand and agree." Not to be confused with older slang, where "clock" meant to see, or even older slang where "clock" meant "to hit or punch."

Corn: “Corn” is algo-speak that means “porn.” Used in online spaces where the word might cause your account to be flagged or banned.

Cortisol-coded: Describes something that's meant to be relaxing but is actually stressful, like watching a video of the 5 a.m. yoga routine of an influencer surrounded by $400 candles.

Coworker-core: A catch-all description for things that are unfunny or uninteresting in a way that appeals to older people.

Cracked: This slang term has two meanings: to have sex, as in "I got cracked last night," and to be really good at something, like "he’s cracked at Fortnite."

Crashout: To have an intense emotional outburst, usually accompanied by impulsive behavior. Crashing out is often due to being overwhelmed or overly frustrated.

D1 Crashout: An epic, elite level, extreme crashout. (See "crashout.)

Dah Bih Gah: "That bitch good," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dah Bih Tah: "That bitch tough," ie: "I like that thing." Usually used to describe food.

Dead: Past tense of having died laughing. If someone responds to a joke with "dead" or a skull emoji, they find it funny.

Deadass: Seriously. Used like, "I am deadass not lying."

Deriod: A combination of "dick" and "period," deriod refers to men seeming to experience the mood swings commonly associated with women's menstrual cycles.

Dih: Algo speak for “dick.” (See "Algo speak.")

Doi doi doi: This piece of brain-rot slang doesn't mean anything. It's correctly pronounced by putting your hand up to your mouth and saying "doi doi doi" in a way that sounds funny.

Doomer: A person who is overly negative and/or cynical.

Dwerking: A male-centric variation of twerking. A sexually suggestive dancing characterized by rapid, repeated hip thrusts and shaking of the dick. Other variants include "pwerking" and "bwerking" where the "p" and "b" stand for pussy and boobs.

Edgar: A variation of the Caesar haircut worn especially among Hispanic males. Also refers to the kind of person who wears the haircut.

Fambushing: A combination of "family" and "ambushing," fambushing refers to young people checking where their parents are on location-sharing apps so they can get free food—if you see mom at Chipotle, you ask for a burrito.

Fanum tax: The theft of food between friends. Named for streamer Fanum, known for “taxing” his friends by taking bites of their meals or stealing fries.

Fax, no printer: Telling the truth. Since "fax" and "facts" are pronounced the same, this is a colorful way of saying "facts, no cap."

Fent-fold: A description of the bent-over posture of people nodding on heavy drugs.

Fuhuhluhtoogan: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. Often paired with "Jittleyang."

Fujoshing: The verb form of the Japanese slang term "fujoshi," fujoshing describes women/girls enjoying media that depicts romantic relationships between men. This word is used almost exclusively in online fandom communities.

Gamer dent: The temporary indentation left on someone’s hair or skin after wearing headphones for too long.

Glaze: To overly praise someone, often insincerely, or with the hope of getting something in return.

Gleek: An older slang term that is gaining prominence lately, gleeking describes squirting saliva from under the tongue.

Glizzy: Hot dog. "Glizzy" was originally slang for Glock or gun, but came to mean hot dog based on the hot dog shape of a Glock's magazine.

Green fn: An interjection one might used when someone does something cool or impressive. Often used ironically.

Goonbait: (See "gooning") Goonbait is, essentially, media that exists to inspiring gooning.

Gooner: A man who goons. (See "gooning.")

Goonette: A woman who goons. (See "gooning.")

Gooning: Extended masturbation without orgasm done for the purpose of entering an altered state of consciousness. (See "gooner," "goonette.")

Gyatt or Gyat: Once an interjection used when seeing someone sexy, like “god-DAMN,” “gyatt” has come to mean “attractive booty.”

Heavy soda: Pop with extra syrup. Some gas station soda machines have settings that control the ratio of syrup to carbonated water. A heavy soda is a soda with the syrup level set very high.

Hewwo: An overly cute way of saying "hello." Usually used online, and often ironically.

HGS: Abbreviation for "home girls" used in comment sections.

Hiplet: Derogatory slang for a woman who has "hip dips," i.e. inward curves on their outer thighs just below the hip bone.

Hozier yell: Named for singer/songwriter Andrew Hozier, a "Hozier yell" refers to the sound one makes when experiencing a peak, climactic, and/or awe-inspiring moment.

HTN: This acronym comes from the online incel community, where fairly good-looking men are described as "high-tier normies" or "HTN." (See "normie.")

Hurkle-durkle: Based on an archaic Scottish word, “hurkle-durkle” means to lounge in bed after it is time to get up. See also: “bed-rotting."

Huzz: -uzz slang for "hoes." See "bruzz" and "-uzz."

"It's giving": Used to convey that something has a specific vibe. Example: "That dude texts you every 10 minutes; it's giving desperate."

"It's so over": The situation is hopeless. The opposite of "we're so back." See also: "Doomer."

IWEL: This comment-section acronym is short for "I wouldn't even lie." Sometimes written as "IWL."

Jelqing: The use of stretching or weights in an attempt to increase penis size.

Jittleyang: Supposedly from Baltimore slang, this is a nonsense word used so people will ask what it means but never receive an answer. See also: "Fuhuhluhtoogan."

JOMO: A play on FOMO (fear of missing out) JOMO is an acronym that stands for “joy of missing out.”

"Learn Chinese": Sports slang directed at failing players. They are in danger of being sent to play in China, so they should "learn Chinese."

Loaded water: Water enhanced with something—a flavor boost, fruit juice, electrolytes, carbonation, and even vitamins or prebiotics. The idea is to increase hydration by making water more palatable.

Looksmaxxing: Maximizing one’s physical attractiveness through personal grooming, working out, and dressing stylishly. See also: “-maxxing.”

🪫 (low battery emoji): The low battery emoji means "I am experiencing emotional depletion, heartbreak, or a general feeling of 'I can't anymore.'"

Lowkenuinely: This mash-up of "low key" and "genuinely" expresses sincerity but in a way that says "let's not make a big deal about it."

Lucky Scoops: Lucky Scoops are a kind of TikTok or Instagram video where buyers purchase a scoop that represents a chance to win merchandise. These videos are very popular with children; critics feel like they are a form of gambling.

Mason (or Mason 6-7 kid): A "Mason 6-7 Kid" or "Mason" is a stereotypical male member of Generation Alpha. Mason kids are known for their love of baseball-inspired fashion (caps and shorts), their "ice cream" haircut, and for repeating brainrot slang like "6-7."

-maxxing: A suffix used with any word to indicate trying to improve. Seeing your friends could be called "friendmaxxing," working out could be called "gymmaxxing," making jokes could be called "jestermaxxing," etc.

Mewing: A facial exercise meant to strengthen the jawline.

Mirror sex: Using a mirror to watch yourself have sex.

Misery girl: A young woman with piercings, a penchant for the darkly dramatic, and highly stylized makeup that makes them appear to have a skinny, pointy nose and huge eyes and lips.

Mog: To be more attractive than someone, usually in an intentional or aggressive way. Example: "I was rizzing up this girl, but he walked in and totally mogged me."

"My 90 in a 30": A song played while driving that inspires speeding.

"My steak is too juicy": The phrase "my steak is too juicy" and other variants like "my lobster is too buttery," are online insults that suggest someone is complaining about something they should be grateful for.

Neurospicy: A different way of saying “neuro-divergent.”

Normie: A person who is considered normal or average. It's sometimes an insult suggesting someone is boring and witless. (see also, "mid.")

NPC: Non-player character. Originally describing video game characters, NPC is now used on the internet to mean people who don't think for themselves.

Opp: Short for "opposition." Someone who is out to get you. An enemy.

Performative male: An insult for young men whose tastes, hobbies, and lifestyle are seen as a performance aimed at obtaining societal approval, especially the approval of young women.

Pheromone maxxing: Trying to influence the behaviors of others through your stink. Supposedly, young men in the "looksmaxxing" community are skipping showers and not washing their clothing in an attempt to make young women like them more. (See "-maxxing").

Phonk: The word phonk can refer to one of two musical sub-genres. It originally referred to throwback '90s hip-hop categorized by slow-tempo "chopped and screwed" production and vintage Memphis rap vocals. It now more commonly describes the heavily distorted, up-tempo EDM used in brainrot videos.

Pink cocaine: Also known as "pink snow," pink cocaine is slang for a powdered drug mixture that usually contains some combination of ketamine, MDMA, meth, opioids, and other substances.

"Press F for respect:" In 2014 video game Call of Duty: Advanced Warfighter, the player attends a funeral and a prompt is given that reads "Press F to pay respects." Now, a singular "F" in a chat window indicates respect. It's usually ironic.

Quiet on the creek: A fishing-inspired way to say "keep it on the down low" or "be cool."

Rawdogging boredom: Rawdogging is "doing something with no safeguards or support," so "rawdogging boredom" is consciously doing nothing.

Regarded: “Regarded” is algo-speak for “retarded."

RegencyCore: A fashion and design aesthetic that springs from the popularity of the fantasy-regency era look of the Netflix show Bridgerton, RegencyCore combines the opulent style of the British Regency era of the early 1800s with fantasy elements like pastel colors and gold accents.

"Reheating your own nachos:" This slang phrase comes from cultural critics in online fandom communities. It refers to performers and/or artists whose new works are seen as trying to recapture what was good about their previous artistic output. It's not always negative; it's possible to successfully reheat your own nachos.

Rizz: As a noun, "rizz" means charisma. As a verb, "rizz" or "rizz up" means attracting someone with your charisma.

Scientology speedrun: Young people running into a Scientology building and acting foolish until they are ejected.

Scorigami: A slang term among football fans for when the final score of an NFL game has never happened before in the league's history. The most recent scorigami was on September 28, 2025, when the Green Bay Packers and Dallas Cowboys tied 40 to 40.

SDIYBT: An acronym for "start digging in your butt, twin," this brainrot phrase doesn't mean anything. Some people just think it's funny to say.

Sendy and “Let’s get sendy": Sendy is an adjective based on the older rock-climbing and extreme sports slang phrase "send it." A shortened version of "ascend it," "send it" is said right before one is about to do something challenging. "Sendy" describes a person who is prone to doing bold things. "Let's get sendy" means something like "Let's get wild." It's been adopted by brainrot fans, so it's often repeated with no meaning meant to be attached.

Serve: Wearing a particularly stylish outfit. See also: "ate."

Serve cunt: To act in a powerfully and unapologetically feminine way; to slay.

Sharking: Looking for people to hook up with.

Side quest: A side quest in a video game is a quest that is not necessary to complete the game's main objective. In slang, a side quest is anything you do in life just for the experience of doing it.

Sigma male: An internet-created male classification, a "sigma male" is as dominant as an alpha male, but is outside the male hierarchy, i.e.: a lone wolf. Originally used seriously, the concept was so widely derided it's now almost always used ironically. (See "Alpha male" and "Beta male.")

Skibidi: Named after “Skibidi Toilet,” a popular series of YouTube videos, “skibidi” itself has no specific meaning, beyond ridiculing the overuse of slang itself. See “brain-rot.”

Skrt: Onomatopoetic word for the sound of tires squealing upon acceleration.

Slopcore: This term describes the countless 100s of millions of cheesy-looking, unsettling, AI-generated images, videos, and songs that have hit the internet since AI was given to the masses a couple of years ago.

Slopper: Insult directed at people who use AI programs too much, people who takes conversations with LLMs too seriously, and people who have basically offloaded their thinking to an algorithm.

Snatched: Very attractive and/or flawlessly styled.

Spawn point: Mother. Based on the spot you start in a video game.

Surf Dracula: A hyper-specific phrase that describes "prestige" television series. The joke is that if there were an older TV show called "Surf Dracula," Dracula would be surfing in every episode, but modern shows would make the whole first season about how Dracula got his surfboard.

Sweat: A person who tries too hard, usually used in reference to video games. The adjective form is "sweaty."

SYBAU: An online acronym that stands for “shut your bitch ass up.”

That's AI: "I don't believe you" or "I doubt it," even when not connected to artificial intelligence.

TLPUR: This supposed acronym section has no meaning. The joke is to tell people it means something like "True Love Pills Until Rope" or "Too Late for Puberty."

Tradwife: Believer in traditional married gender roles.

Trap: Once used to refer to a house where drugs are sold, trap has come to describe both a form of music and any place where one works or hustles.

Treatler (and Treatlerite): "Treatler" and "Treatlerite" are online insults that combine "treat" and "Hitler" to refer to entitled users of services like Doordash or Uber Eats who regard luxury delivery services as a human right, and don't consider the hardships of the people who do the work that makes "private taxis for burritos" possible.

TS: TS originally was AAVE shorthand for "this shit," but it is often used to just mean "this."

Turnt: Excited or intoxicated, or excitedly intoxicated.

Tweaking: In older slang, "tweaking" referred to the nervous and erratic actions of someone on drugs, specifically, speed. Generations A and Z have expanded the definition to refer to any actions that are erratic, or even just mildly energetic, not necessarily related to drug use.

Tylenol baby: After President Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a scientifically dubious link between the active ingredient in Tylenol and autism, kids have been calling each other "Tylenol babies."

Unc: Short for "uncle," used to describe slightly older people. Example: "The class of 2024 are unc-status to the class of 2028." See "yunc."

-uzz: -uzz slang words use "uzz" at the end of any word, so "bros" becomes "bruzz," "hoes" becomes "huzz," "granny" becomes "gruzz," etc.

"We're so back": Opposite of "it's so over."

Venus tummy: When a woman's belly is a little fat, but not too fat, she is said to have a Venus tummy. Named for ancient Greek statues of Venus and Aphrodite who were a little fleshy.

Viking rap: A musical sub-genre consisting of AI-generated Vikings rapping about longboats, raiding, and other Viking things.

Wojack: The name of a style of internet drawings used to quickly stereotype someone. See this post for a full explanation of the Wojak universe.

Yapping: Describes a presentational style often seen on online streams of talking a lot and/or quickly while not saying anything worthwhile.

You the birthday: A phrase that means "you're awesome" or "you're great" in the way a birthday is great: fun, exciting, extra, etc.

Young ho: "Young ho" is both a reclamation of the word "ho" and an expression of youth-based solidarity. Young women are posting videos of themselves defining what makes them "young hos," noting things like "Getting up at 7:50 to be at work at 8," and air-frying chicken nuggets.

Yunc: Yunc is a variation of "unc." In AAVE, a "yn" is a "young n-word." So "yunc" means something like "young uncle," or a person who may be young but has uncle vibes or unc status.

Zoomer Perm: A curly on top, short on the sides haircut popular among young people.

Well, it's official: there are two new kids on the block. The new MacBook Pro M6 and the MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen are finally here. If you've been waiting to upgrade, or are looking to pick up your first-ever MacBook, now's the time to do it. Pre-orders are live, and we've even found a trick to help you save up to $1,400 on the OLED model.

As someone who owns a MacBook and uses one for work, and coincidentally tests the latest and greatest peripherals, I know that your setup isn't complete until you buy the right accessories. I couldn't get on with my work without my trusty mouse, keyboard, monitor, and other gadgets.

Whether you're after a new mechanical keyboard or even a touch-sensitive one whose keycaps double as a trackpad, a pair of earbuds, or need a USB-C dock for more connectivity, I've got you covered. I've rounded up what I believe are the best accessories (and gadgets) to make the most of your new MacBook Pro M6 or OLED.

The MacBook Pro OLED is one of the biggest MacBook releases in recent years. It can be configured with an M5 Pro (from $2,899) or M5 Max (from $4,499) CPU and packs a 14.2-inch PROLED XDR touchscreen display with 3024 x 1986 resolution, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB SSD. You also get three Thunderbolt 5 (USB-C) ports, HDMI port, and an SDXC slot. The laptop will be available on November 6.

Power users looking for a boost in performance should opt for the new 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. This powerful laptop sports Apple's M6 chip for blazing-fast performance at home or on the go.

There's no better monitor for your new MacBook Pro than the first-party Apple Studio Display, thanks to its excellent 12MP ultra-wide camera, fantastic six-speaker setup and gorgeous 27-inch 5K screen. It's bright and delivers accurate (and stunning) colors, too.

Read our full Apple Studio Display review.

If you don't mind a third-party display, I can't recommend the BenQ MA270S enough. It's cheaper than the Apple Studio Display and boasts wide color coverage and excellent accuracy, making it a great choice for creatives, and it comes with an Apple-like app for customization. There’s no shortage of ports, and the Nano Gloss 5K panel is a sight to behold.

If you want more screen real estate, the Alogic Edge 40-inch 5K is an excellent choice. Boasting great color coverage and accuracy, and hosting a plethora of ports for Mac users, this monitor offers everything you could ask for. Available in Silver and Space Gray, it’ll fit right into your existing Mac-first setup, too.

The Clevetura S is an outstanding travel-friendly keyboard with touch-sensitive keycaps that turn it into a highly effective and responsive trackpad with MacBook gestures, negating the need for a separate mouse. Its scissor switches are great to type on, too.

The K10 Max is a fantastic iteration of the tried-and-true Keychron formula, offering additional sound dampening, a refined mounting system, and high-performance Super Switches. A deep, thick sound and responsive keystrokes make this a great gaming option, too. It comes with macOS keycaps, making it a solid choice for Apple users.

Want a keyboard that looks a bit different? The typewriter-like Epomaker Glyph (featuring macOS keycaps) is a wonderful, whimsical addition to any setup. It puts the joy back into typing. The keyboard sports a charming typewriter-like design with dual screens and customizable RGB lighting, and build quality is solid.

There's no better mouse for the MacBook other than the Apple Magic Mouse (as long as you don't mind the very flat design). It features a Multi-Touch surface that allows you to perform gestures, and the mouse can last up to a month between charges. This model features a USB-C port. On the bottom.

If you want an ergonomic mouse with buttons that toggle macOS shortcuts, try the BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01. It features dual scrolling wheels, smooth tracking, and you can assign macOS gestures to its buttons. User-friendly companion software makes customization easy, too.

Read my full BenQ INFTYLAB M Mouse PS01 review.

Given how powerful both the MacBook Pro M6 and OLED sound, I won't be surprised if they're great for gaming. The Corsair M75 (Mac) is a superb gaming mouse designed for macOS. This minimalist-looking mouse features 26,000 DPI sensitivity that you can change on the fly, making it suitable for all kinds of gaming titles. It’s very comfortable to use for long hours.

The UGREEN 8-in-1 Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station is a must-have for those who have a desk setup. It's equipped with three Thunderbolt 4 ports (40Gbps, 15W), three USB-A ports (10Gbps), a gigabit ethernet port, and a 140W DC power port. It's great for creatives and professionals who need high transfer speeds.

I couldn't live without my portable USB-C hub. The Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Hub is ideal for those on the move. It features multiple USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as HDMI 4K/60Hz ports for streaming and mirroring content. #3498. What I Love (and What I Don't) About the New Una Fitness Watch

I’ve reviewed every type of fitness watch and thought I had seen it all, but my first glimpse of an Una watch had my jaw on the floor: There is a USB-C port on the side of the watch. Not a set of pins for a magnetic charger, or a socket that requires a proprietary cable—just a hole you can stick a regular old USB-C cable into. This is what watches have been missing.

The Una watch started popping up on my feed about two years ago, and finally started shipping this summer. I’ve been wearing a review unit for a few weeks. The Una watch is advertised as repairable and upgradable, with open source software. There are little screws that I can see around the watch face, and on the back panel. The Una website sells a replacement battery for $40 and a replacement screen for $50. They also sell the tiny screwdriver that you’ll need to make repairs, but if you’re the kind of person who gets excited about a repairable watch, you may already have your own.

Overall, I like it. The Una watch has an MIP screen (an older tech that is a cult favorite) and an app that's simple but effective. Not everything lived up to my expectations in testing, but no features failed outright. This feels like a solid start to the concept of “one watch for life” and I’m excited to see how the hardware and software offerings evolve over time.

Most wearables these days try to do as many jobs as possible, whether they’re the right tool for those jobs or not. I am honestly fine with a running watch measuring time, distance, and heart rate while I run, and not trying to score my sleep or pretend it can tell how fast I’m aging.

The Una watch app shows my steps, activity, and floors climbed for the day, as well as my average and resting heart rates. When I go for a run, it tracks my pace, distance, and heart rate during the run and gives me a nice page of data afterward. It reliably uploads this data to Strava, and can make little bar graphs of how these numbers vary from day to day.

There is a “store” (everything is free, as far as I can tell) where you can download extra watch faces and features. One I’m trying out is a habit tracker called HabitLab: It asks you every evening whether you had alcohol, cigarettes, a late meal, and so on. Every morning, it asks how you’re feeling. And then, even though the watch doesn’t normally track your sleep, the app takes note of your overnight HRV and resting heart rate. Over time, it will correlate the answers to those questions with the sleep data, to hopefully give results that are similar to Whoop’s journal analysis. (I haven’t been using it long enough to judge how well it works, but stay tuned.)

HabitLab appears in one area of the watch as a standalone app; another, called Gym Sets, gives me a strength training activity type, which the watch did not otherwise have. I just select Gym Sets instead of “Run” or “Workout,” and the app tracks my heart rate while also giving me a set timer.

The store is small, and the apps are simple, without many of the features that you can find on the apps for Apple Watch or other more fully featured devices. But the Una watch has only been out for a few months, so it’s not surprising that users haven’t created a plethora of apps yet. The company’s software development kit, and even its circuit board designs, are free for people to download and develop from.

I was worried that the emphasis on repairability, and the affordable price, meant that the Una watch would be made with components that maybe aren’t fully up to date. Heart rate sensors have been getting better over the years, so Una’s will have to be pretty good if it wants to even sit in the middle of the pack. Garmin, Apple, and now Fitbit have raised the bar quite a bit.

I will say the GPS track was reasonably good; on trail runs and road runs, it accurately followed the path I actually took. (It doesn’t seem to do quite as well as a new Garmin, but it’s still perfectly usable and its distance totals added up to reasonably accurate numbers.)

Heart rate accuracy disappointed me, though. When I first got the watch, the heart rate tracking was abysmal. I sent a few emails to my contact at Una, and almost had to publish this review with very bad news about the watch’s accuracy, but then a firmware update for the Una watch popped up on my phone. I installed it, and then tried another test run or two, and the heart rate accuracy is much better. If you get the watch, make sure it’s updated to at least 1.6.0.

That said, the update brought the heart rate accuracy to a level where I’d say it’s adequate, but it’s not good (and definitely not great). Its graph follows the ups and downs of my heart rate as measured by a chest strap, but sometimes the Una will spike and show a reading that’s significantly higher than my heart is actually beating. In the graph below, note the spike to around 165 when the true value was 155, and then later in the workout the Una watch detects another spike around 160 when my heart rate was actually around 145 and decreasing. (I saw similar anomalies in multiple workouts.)

In my time with the Una watch, many things made me happy. I still love the USB-C charging, and it was a delight to just plug it in to the same nightstand cable I normally use with my phone, no need to go looking for an adapter or dongle.

I like the MIP screen, which was brilliant in the sunlight and had a serviceable backlight for use indoors or in the dark. The small number of workout profiles and the small number of glances and apps is just fine if you’re not asking for much from a watch, and I wasn’t. It’s minimalist, low-distraction, and there isn’t a single AI-based feature anywhere. A true breath of fresh air.

And at $199, you’re not paying extra for these privileges. The price is just a little more than the new Fitbit Edge ($179.99), but less than a Coros Pace 4 ($249) or a Garmin 70 (also $249). The Una watch doesn’t have as many features or activities as these watches, but perhaps those pluses I mentioned make up for it.

The Una watch would be a good pick for someone who is excited about developing apps, wants a repairable watch, always loses charging adapters, or appreciates a minimalist approach. But would I recommend it for the average person who just wants a basic fitness watch? I’m not so sure.

The flaky heart rate sensor disqualifies it for a wearer who wants a more accurate, modern watch. The MIP screen is going to look old and weird to people who have gotten used to brighter, clearer AMOLED screens. The lack of sleep tracking or other convenience metrics may be hard to take when plenty of watches have these features.

So I like this watch today, with reservations, and I have high hopes for the future. If Una lives up to its vision, it’s going to be great to see replaceable components become available—perhaps there will be an option for an AMOLED screen for those who want it, and maybe there’s room for heart rate accuracy improvement in future firmware updates.

But a lot depends on the company itself. “One watch for life” implies that the company stays around long enough to make more than one model. I’m also hopeful that the future offerings will match what people want, and that the watch and app will stay uncluttered and subscription-free. But surely there will be competing interests that the company has to balance as they grow (if they grow), so time will tell whether the reality lives up to the vision. That said, I am liking the vision a lot.

#3497. Guy Ritchie's Robert Downey Jr. Sherlock Replacement Succeeded In An Impossible Task

It’s now even more unlikely that Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes 3 with Robert Downey Jr. will happen, but luckily, Ritchie found a perfect replacement that, surprisingly, succeeded at what seemed like an impossible task. Created by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Sherlock Holmes has been the inspiration of many artists for decades, and has been adapted to all types of media. On film, some of the most notable adaptations are Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes and Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows.

Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes movies starred Robert Downey Jr. as the Great Detective and Jude Law as Dr. John Watson, and brought to life some complex and intriguing cases with a good dose of action in Ritchie’s signature style. Ritchie’s movies were a big hit, with Downey Jr.’s performance being praised by critics and fans of the Great Detective, and it’s now regarded as one of the best Sherlock Holmes performances.

Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows left the audience with a major cliffhanger as Holmes supposedly died, along with Moriarty (Jared Harris), at Reichenbach Falls, only to be revealed right at the end that he’s alive and a lot closer to Watson than the latter could ever imagine. However, a third movie is now more unlikely than ever, but luckily, Ritchie found a perfect replacement in the Prime Video show Young Sherlock, which achieved the impossible: replacing Robert Downey Jr.

Loosely based on Andrew Lane’s book series of the same name, Young Sherlock takes the audience back to the Victorian Era to meet a 19-year-old Sherlock Holmes (Hero Fiennes Tiffin). Fresh out of prison for pickpocketing, Holmes starts working at Oxford University as a scout, but he’s framed for the murder of a teacher on campus. With the help of his new and brilliant friend, James Moriarty (Dónal Finn), Holmes sets out to find the real murderer and clear his name.

However, what none of them could have predicted was that their journey would also lead them to uncover a global-level conspiracy and the darkest secrets of the Holmes family. Young Sherlock stays true to the Victorian-era setting of Conan Doyle’s stories, but with some interesting additions to Holmes’ backstory, through which it has already answered some of the biggest mysteries about Holmes’ past and family.

Thanks to its time setting and Ritchie’s involvement, it was speculated before its release whether Young Sherlock was a prequel of sorts to Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes movies, and while it isn't, it's a perfect complement to them. However, its most impressive achievement is that Fiennes successfully replaced Downey Jr. as Ritchie’s Victorian-era Holmes, and his future is a lot brighter than that of Downey Jr.’s version.

A third Sherlock Holmes movie by Ritchie has been in limbo for years, with various updates through the years that either gave hope for its development or crushed it. At the time of writing, it doesn’t seem likely anymore that Sherlock Holmes 3 will happen, but Young Sherlock has successfully filled that void despite not being a movie or being in the same continuity.

Young Sherlock has opened up a bunch of new opportunities for the world of Sherlock Holmes by exploring the younger years of the detective, how he became the famous detective everyone now knows, how he and Moriarty met, how they became enemies, and the dynamic with his family. This also allows Young Sherlock to go on for a long time, exploring other parts of his past that Conan Doyle didn’t go into in his stories and that most adaptations have left aside.

At the time of writing, Young Sherlock is preparing for its second season, which is expected to continue covering Moriarty’s villainous turn and his friendship with Holmes, along with the latter’s discovery of more of his father’s secrets. There’s no projected release date for Young Sherlock season 2 yet, but it’s already one of Prime Video’s most anticipated upcoming projects.

Your instincts, your strengths, and your particular way of thinking under pressure point to one villain you actually have a fighting chance against. Everyone else — good luck.

Michael watches before he moves. He is patient, methodical, and almost impossible to detect — until it's too late for anyone who isn't paying close enough attention.

If you haven't heard of the upstart tech brand Nothing, it's a UK-based company that aims to make products like cellphones and headphones with innovative features and designs—but at a lower price point than tech giants like Apple and Samsung. Last summer, the company released its newest smartwatch, the CMF Watch 3 Pro, which incorporates AI features powered by ChatGPT, and you can currently pick it up at a major discount.

Originally $99, you can get the CMF Watch 3 Pro for $59 at Amazon. This is the lowest price this smartwatch has been, according to price-tracking tools.

According to Nothing, the CMF Watch 3 Pro is designed for "everyday users and casual fitness explorers." It quickly earned a reputation as one of the best budget smartwatch/fitness trackers of 2025. If you have a Nothing phone, the most noteworthy feature is its direct ChatGPT integration: You can use voice prompts to ask the chatbot questions or set reminders, among other things. Another neat feature, regardless of whether you have a Nothing phone or not, is its ability to record voices and auto-transcribe conversations or notes with the Nothing X app, which is great for work meetings or class.

If you've used the CMF Watch 2 Pro, you'll already be familiar with the design, which hasn't changed much. It still has a round display with a rotating crown on the top right, though the display is a bit bigger—1.43 inches compared to the Watch 2 Pro's 1.32 inches. Nothing has also kept the auto brightness adjustment, which is determined by a built-in sensor, and dual-band GPS support with access to five satellite systems, providing greater accuracy when tracking your outdoor activities.

The real upgrades come mainly from the software: The Watch 3 Pro has over 130 sport modes, compared to 120 on the older model. There's also AI tracking with personalized workout recommendations in real time. The battery now lasts 13 days on a single charge, which is two days longer than before. It's certainly in the running for the best sub-$100 fitness watch you can buy right now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're struggling with your pots and plants heading into fall, or, specifically, you keep finding yourself staring at your once-gorgeous chrysanthemum and wondering where its luscious blooms went, I can help.

Mums are wonderful fall flowers, giving us one last burst of color before the grays of winter set in. As with any plant, mums require some care, and there are steps that you can take right now to help your plant before it's too late.

Here’s three things you can do to salvage what you have left of this gorgeous autumnal plant.

Yes, I'm talking about wilted stems, dried-out ones, and even browning blooms. They all need chopping off! Grab some pruning shears and trim to the point where you can see a green stem — if it’s not salvageable, then chop as close to the root as possible.

As always, you want to do this with sharp pruning shears for the best chop. This promotes strong roots, ready for the next blooming season, and obviously, it helps make your plant look lovely and tidy.

Next, give it a good drink. If your plant is potted, then it’d be smart to fill either a bucket or your sink (if the plant is easy to carry inside) with water and place the plant in it. This way, you’re properly watering the roots, which will probably be very dry.

Leave your plant to sit in this water for around 30-45 minutes. The soil should be damp but never wet, as this will encourage mold.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The next step is to repot it. This is important for encouraging growth, so you need to find a new vessel, one that's around 1-2 inches larger than its old home. You need a well-draining, standard potting mix, much like what you used the first time around.

The ideal soil for your plant, this is Amazon's Choice and it will provide natural fertilizer for up to 2 months for your plant. At an affordable price for the amount, it's even made using responsibly sourced peat.

Think about your plant's positionOnce repotted, you may be tempted to pop it back in its usual spot. But it's worth switching things up — clearly, this wasn't working before. It needs direct sunlight for around 6 hours a day to encourage new buds to bloom. So a sunny windowsill works great if you’re keeping it inside.

If inside, keep this plant away from heat sources. You don't want to dry it out or warm up the soil. Saying that, though, these plants do like cool fall afternoon temperatures.

Going outside? You still need to put it in a sunny spot, ideally where the sun hits first thing in the morning. A plant stand or wooden deck is the best home for an outdoor mum plant, rather than concrete.

Make sure to avoid high-wind spots, and don’t assume that hiding your plant underneath shelter is doing it good — it's actually preventing it from soaking in the sunlight that it desperately needs. Positioning is arguably one of the most important factors in growing a healthy chrysanthemum.

If your mum plant is potted in the ground, then the rules are slightly different: you do need to water it, but this can be done using just your hose. Turn it on and run it over the soil bed for around 10-15 minutes for a good drink.

You still need to prune it back, as you would if it were potted, but it might also help to prune back any nearby plants to avoid overcrowding. This will also ensure your mum plant gets all the sunlight, instead of being hidden in the shadows of other stems.

Another step that might help is adding mulch to the mix. You only need a layer around 1 inch tall, but mulch keeps the roots cool in the fall and protects them from frost in the winter. Better yet, it can help retain moisture, so you won't need to water as often.

On sale today, this mulch can be used for lots of gardening jobs, indoors and out, especially at this time of year. Apart from adding an attractive look to your beds, it can help to suppress weeds and keep in moisture.

Marshall’s Monitor III ANC headphones have the kind of design that makes you want to show them off. The textured earcups and gold logo lean fully into the amp-inspired look, and at $199.99 (down from $379.99 at launch), they’re finally priced in a way that feels competitive. It's their lowest price ever, according to price trackers.

These are over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, and they’re clearly aimed at people cross-shopping Bose and Sony. The difference is that Marshall is selling a vibe along with the sound. The build feels sturdy, and small details like replaceable ear cushions and a swappable silicone headband strap suggest they’re made to last longer than most. They fold down neatly into a compact hard case (included), but they’re not water-resistant, so they’re better suited for travel and home listening than sweaty workouts.

Living with them day to day is mostly smooth. The small gold joystick handles volume and track controls in a way that feels intuitive after a few minutes. There’s a separate button to toggle noise cancellation and transparency, plus a customizable shortcut button you can set up in the Marshall app. The app itself is simple, with a five-band EQ and a few presets, though it’s not especially deep if you like fine-tuning every frequency. Bluetooth 5.3 keeps connections stable, but you’re limited to AAC and SBC codecs, so there’s no hi-res audio support. You also can’t charge and listen through a traditional 3.5mm cable at the same time, since the single USB-C port handles both charging and wired playback.

Battery life is where these headphones truly stand out. Up to 70 hours with ANC on is more than enough for long trips, and turning ANC off stretches that to an almost excessive 100 hours. As for sound, they deliver strong bass and crisp highs, with enough punch to make hip-hop and electronic tracks feel lively. Noise cancellation reduces plane engine rumble and city noise well, but it does not match leaders like Bose in blocking midrange chatter, notes this PCMag review.
