We put the new Fitbit head-to-head with Apple’s best smartwatch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earlier this week, my colleague Dan walked 6,000 steps with the new Fitbit Edge and the Apple Watch Series 12 to test which was more accurate when it comes to one of the most basic smartwatch requirements: step counting. Dan found that the $179 Fitbit Edge came out on top of the $399 Apple Watch Series 12. Keen to find out more, I strapped both to my wrist and repeated the test.

Sure, both of these trackers will do a lot more than just count your steps. The Apple Watch Series 12 is like having an extension of your iPhone on your wrist, and is the best smartwatch on the market for most people. The Fitbit Edge seems to toe the line between the $99 screenless Fitbit Air and the Google Pixel Watch 5 — a bright screen, built-in GPS, and a continuous heart rate monitor.

Like all these walk tests, I strapped one watch to each wrist and used a $5 clicker tool from Amazon to count my steps as I walked manually. Both trackers count steps using an internal accelerometer, which measures the swing of your arms. Each swing counts for two steps, and it doesn’t matter whether you wear your watch on your dominant or non-dominant hand. It doesn’t matter if you walk with your hands in your pockets or holding a cup of coffee; the accelerometer should still measure your body’s movement.

Read on to find out which came out on top. You can also read our Apple Watch Series 12 review and our Fitbit Edge review here on Tom’s Guide.

As with all of the best Apple Watches, the Apple Watch Series 12 still doesn’t tell you the number of steps you’ve taken during a specific workout; instead, you see an overall number of steps throughout the day, which you can now pin to your home screen. This is probably because steps aren’t actually that useful a metric beyond a certain point, but annoying for me when writing these articles. For this comparison, I downloaded a third-party Pedometer+ app onto my Apple Watch.

I split this walk up into three different walks, manually clicking each time I took a step. When I got home, I downloaded my data.

As you can see from the results, this one is incredibly close. The Apple Watch Series 12 overcounted by 23 steps; the Fitbit Edge missed 71 steps. With only 50 steps between them, it’s a tough one to call, but unlike Dan, I can say the Apple Watch Series 12 was slightly ahead here.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It’s worth noting that 50-70 steps is pretty much spot on. The average person takes 2,000 steps a mile, so an extra 23 steps is nothing.

To really compare these two watches head-to-head, you’d need to look at more than just how well they count steps. Both are designed to be worn 24/7 and help you track more than just walking workouts.

However, there are some big differences: as mentioned above, the Apple Watch Series 12 is designed to be an extension of your iPhone on your wrist, with plenty of apps at your disposal. The Fitbit Edge, on the other hand, is definitely more of a basic fitness tracker than a smartwatch.

We’ll continue to test and compare the two watches, but which would you buy?

#3489. X-Men Debuts Ultimate Version Of Horsemen Of Apocalypse, All Members and Powers

Across X-Men history, there have been many different versions of the Horsemen of Apocalypse - typically a group of four mutants enhanced by the villain's Celestial technology and brainwashed into his service.

Now, 39 years after the team first appeared in Marvel lore, X-Men has assembled the ultimate version of the Horsemen as the guardians of Apocalypse's hi-tech tomb - the repository of all his deepest secrets and most secret technologies.

In the recent Tomb of Apocalypse #3 - from Ashley Allen, Carlos Nieto, Domenico Carbone, Fernando Sifuentes and Joe Sabino - Wolverine, Jubilee, Rictor and Shatterstar encounter a new team of Horsemen made up of Apocalypse's greatest servants from across time and space. Here are the four terrors who make up the new Horsemen of Apocalypse...

Despite being thousands of years old, Death is suave and cultured, priding himself on winning fights thanks to his skill as a warrior. He uses his mask to hold back his mutant power - a gaseous cloud that kills anyone it touches. He tends to only unleash his powers against unworthy enemies.

The oldest son of Apocalypse, Death was raised as a warrior among his siblings, born at some point before 2620 BC. Each sibling is named after an evil that Apocalypse and the mutants of the utopian nation of Okkara intended to erase from the world. Each member of the team is biologically immortal and possesses incredible superhuman strength and reflexes.

Eyes release a lethal gas that disintegrates its target

Apocalypse's eldest son, the first Horseman ever created

Born in the utopian mutant nation of Okkara, they were corrupted by the millennia-long war with the demonic Amenth. Eventually defeated by Storm's Brotherhood in the war for Arakko (aka Mars)

A member of Genesis' Brotherhood, operating in space

Killed by Death after dishonorably attacking Storm.

When the demonic realm of Amenth attacked Earth, Apocalypse was forced to abandon his children and wife Genesis outside reality, setting out on a mission to raise a mutant army powerful enough to one day free them from their eternal war against the demons of Amenth.

Following the events of the 2019-2024 'Krakoan Era,' Apocalypse now lives on Mars in the mutant settlement of Arakko. He has chosen Doug Ramsey, aka Revelation, as his heir on Earth.

As millennia passed, Apocalypse's children were hardened by war, eventually swearing allegiance to Amenth and attacking Earth. Opposed by Apocalypse and Storm's mutant Brotherhood, only Death switched sides and reclaimed his honor, now seemingly studying under his father on Mars..

A mutant from ancient Rome - implied to be the illegitimate son of the real-life Seneca the Younger - Decimus Furius is a minotaur-like mutant forced into gladiatorial combat at a young age. His appearance led to him being associated with the dark god Asterion, leading a cult to spring up around him.

Decimus was chosen by Apocalypse as one of the Final Horsemen - a team chosen from throughout time and held back unless all his other plans failed. The Final Horsemen were activated following the death of Apocalypse and his return as a clone child, clashing with Wolverine's X-Force.

Can consciously spread almost any disease (must be touching specific metals)

The illegitimate son of an ancient Persian king. His powers activated while he was distributing stolen treasure to the populace

Mysteriously resurrected under the codename 'Life' as leader of the Pan-Asian School for the Unusually Gifted

Massive strength, contagious berserker rage

Spreads psionic 'cancer' through drumming

A Confederate spy whose family were murdered by his allies

Contains a gigantic swarm of carnivorous beetles

A failed geisha whose jealousy activated her powers

Conceived the villainous 'Apocalypse Twins' Uriel and Eimin with Warren Worthington III, current whereabouts unknown.

Incredibly physically powerful, Decimus Furius is able to channel rage through his four-bladed axe, infecting anyone he strikes with a violent desire for conflict. He has a powerful healing factor which has resurrected him from death before, and may explain his appearance here, despite being slain by the Apocalypse Twins, Uriel and Eimin.

One of the first Horsemen to appear chronologically in Marvel Comics, Autumn Rolfson came to loathe her parents due to their shame over both her anorexia and mutant status. Apocalypse played on Autumn's dissatisfaction to recruit her, enhancing her ability to disintegrate biological matter.

Autumn was part of multiple versions of the Horsemen, clashing with the X-Men several times. Unlike other iterations of the Horsemen, the 21st Century team didn't automatically consider themselves answerable to Death, and Autumn frequently rebelled and made plays for leadership of the team.

Metallic wings with poison-tipped feathers

Founding X-Men hero brainwashed by Apocalypse

Recovered heroic identity but kept Horseman powers. Recently led his own X-Corps team

Can induce fear in others and track any mutant's psionic trail

Oppressed 'Morlock' - a weakling granted immense physical power by Apocalypse

Currently possesses a leadership role among the Morlocks

Can amplify the force of his own clapping, creating directed explosions

A severely injured veteran physically restored by Apocalypse

A living disease vector that can consciously spread a lethal virus

An underground 'Morlock' saved from the 'Mutant Massacre' by Apocalypse

Killed during a battle with the X-Factor and Power Pack

Autumn eventually became romantically entangled with Apocalypse, raising their son Genocide while hidden away by Apocalypse's Clan Akkaba, coming to hate her former master. When Warren Worthington III's Archangel usurped Apocalypse's role, she opposed him to protect her son and died in the process.

Tomb of Apocalypse reveals that this current team of Horsemen can only exist within the "Temporal Pocket" of his tomb, suggesting Apocalypse plucked them from the timestream, explaining the presence of dead members.

Apocalypse's most mysterious servants, the Horsemen of 1013 were assembled following a deal between their master and the time-traveling Rama-Tut, who advised Apocalypse to target various ancestors of his future foes.

Initially dispatched to kill Folkbern Logan - an ancestor of X-Men's Wolverine - the 11th Century Horsemen had the bad luck to be unleashed on Scandinavia during a period when a young Thor called the country home.

Gaseous, poisonous body which seemingly caused intense waking nightmares

'Red Plague' energy blast which instantly incinerates its target

Wielding the matter-cleaving axe Jarnbjorn, Thor killed the 11th Century Horsemen to a man, though not before Phantom Bats of the Twelve Minds had killed multiple innocents. Appearing in the present, Phantom Bats of the Twelve Minds makes a beeline for Wolverine, declaring his intent to finish the mission that cost him his life.

In a dark twist, Tomb of Apocalypse reveals that while these new Horsemen have been assigned to guard Apocalypse's tomb, they can't leave its interior. Instead, Apocalypse uses them to capture Jubilee, declaring his intent to forge a new team of Horsemen to serve by his side during his exile on Mars.

Apocalypse has assembled the ultimate version of his Horsemen, but with this time-tossed roster trapped within his tomb, it seems Tomb of Apocalypse's mutant heroes - Jubilee, Wolverine, Shatterstar and Rictor - may make up the next Horsemen as this X-Men spin-off continues.

Tomb of Apocalypse #3 is available now from Marvel Comics, with issue #4 coming November 18.

#3488. These Are Lifehacker's First-Ever 'Gift of the Year' Award Winners

Maybe this is the year your spouse finally wants to ditch physical books and embrace the e-reader; or maybe you want to help make your parent's home a little smarter. As the gift-giving season approaches, Lifehacker's staff of tech experts and product reviewers has selected our inaugural Gift of the Year winners across 15 categories. From smartphones, tablets, and e-readers to fitness trackers, gaming equipment, power tools, and more, these are the items we think are the most gift-worthy in 2026.

And while you're shopping, Lifehacker's sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at CNET, PCMag, Mashable, ZDNET, and Popular Science.

If you’re buying a smartphone for someone on your list, you have no shortage of options. But for most giftees out there, the iPhone 17e is the best choice. This isn’t the best iPhone, but that’s the point. For a starting price of $699, you get an iPhone with a high-quality display, a solid single rear camera, and Apple’s A19 chip, the second-best processor the company currently makes. You sacrifice some features here, like a high-refresh-rate display, higher-quality cameras, and a faster USB-C port, but those things won’t matter to most. The majority of us want an iPhone that can take great photos, send iMessages, take FaceTime calls, and run our favorite apps. The 17e can do that, without the exorbitant price tags of Apple’s more premium iPhones. If your giftee needs an Android, that’s a different conversation, but for Apple fans, or the platform-agnostic in your life, the 17e makes a great smartphone gift.

Apple’s best iPad for most people is the one simply called the “iPad.” This tablet, sometimes called the “iPad A16” or “iPad (11th generation),” comes with all the features you’d expect from an Apple tablet. It has a solid 11-inch display, Apple’s A16 chip to run iPadOS 27, a camera on the back for scanning documents and light photography, a camera on the front for video calls, and the option to use an Apple Pencil if you wish. It’s compatible with all of the apps on the App Store, and it can handle almost every iPadOS feature Apple makes—minus Apple Intelligence, but that might be a perk for some. While it’s far from Apple’s best iPad, it’s really the best for most people—that’s why it’s our pick for the best tablet to gift.

Our pick for the year's most desirable gift for readers isn't one of Amazon's slick new Kindles, but a tiny, 4.3-inch Chinese import that can pack hundreds of books into a device not much bigger than your library card. The Xteink X4 Pro may have a funny name and a form factor that suggests an e-reader left too long in the dryer, but it's packed with features, including a touchscreen and a temperature-adjustable front light, that belie its $99 list price ($50 less than the cheapest Kindle). Sure, there's a learning curve involved (the native firmware is merely fine, but easily replaced with a crowdsourced alternative developed by a community of online fans), and it won't work with your existing library of Kindle books. But once you've gotten it set up, you'll realize its biggest benefit: It's small enough to fit into any pocket—or even magnetically attach to the back of your phone—so you can easily carry it with you everywhere, and read instead of doomscrolling. After all, the best e-reader is the one you actually use.

Picking headphones for someone can be tricky. Some people love long battery life; others are just looking for whatever pair offers the most features. At the end of the day, price is what sets the best headphones apart from the rest. However, there is one outlier that offers a great value for the money and does well enough in most categories to make most people feel like they're upgrading: the Sony ULT WEAR headphones. At their new low price, there is no other pair of headphones that offers better quality active noise cancellation, app experience, comfort, battery life, and audio quality with LDAC support for Android devices. Not to mention the ULT button, which has two levels of extra bass that will have heads rattling like they're front row at a concert.

If you’re looking to buy a smartwatch for someone in your life and you know they don’t have any strong preferences going in, the Apple Watch SE is likely the best choice for you. It might not be Apple’s most powerful smartwatch, nor does it have the biggest, brightest display, but it does just about everything you’d expect an Apple Watch to do. It pings you with your iPhone notifications, tracks workouts and sleep, and lets you send and receive texts. It has the previous-generation S10 chip, which is plenty of power for watchOS (including Apple Intelligence), and Apple should support it for years to come. You can spend more to get more features on watches like the Series 12 or Ultra 4, but for most, the SE is all the Apple Watch you’ll ever need. And, if your giftee wants the cellular option, the SE can connect to 5G, just like Apple's more expensive watches.

These relatively inexpensive display-style glasses have that Christmas morning "woah" factor: Once the recipient plugs them into any device with USB-C video, they will instantly see a virtual display that's the equivalent of a 147-inch TV at 1080p. They’re particularly good for frequent travelers and dorm-dwellers who can’t agree on what to watch, but really, they're for anyone on your list who likes to play games, watch movies, or use their computer. (So, basically everyone.)

Buying a smart home gift is a tall order. There are so many different categories to choose from, and, within each, there are many considerations to keep in mind, like platform compatibility, feature set, and price. That’s why I think the Amazon Echo Dot Max is the best smart home gift of 2026. It supports a variety of smart home platforms, including Zigbee, Matter, Thread, and Alexa. That way, your giftee can likely connect the Echo Dot Max to most, if not all, of their existing smart home devices, as well as future devices they may pick up. It’s also one of Amazon’s better smart speakers: It isn’t as small as the Echo Dot, so it’s able to fill your room with sound, but it’s also not as expensive as the Echo Studio. It’s a great balance at this price, considering the versatility it offers as a smart home hub.

No single gift will please every gamer, but the Steam Deck comes close. This device blurs all the lines in gaming: It’s a PC that’s the size of a handheld, and it plugs into your television like a console. Fans of gaming on the go will love the portability and the touchscreen. Console gamers will love the friendly user interface, thumbstick controllers, and finally getting the chance to play “PC exclusive” games. PC gamers will love being able to move away from their desks and play video games on the couch or at a bus stop for a change. The Steam Deck is a win-win-win.

You’re probably not going to buy someone a new TV for the holidays, but you can buy the media-hound on your list a gadget to make the TV they already own even better. Enhancing your watching and gaming is the mission of the Philips Hue Play Sync Box. It’s a middleman between a TV and HDMI gear like consoles or streaming boxes that analyzes video signals in real time and tells the connected smart light strip (as well as other compatible smart lights) to match what's on screen. This is great for making gaming more immersive, and it also improves just watching TV by projecting colors behind the set that complement the visuals. The result is the illusion of a larger screen and a very cool special effect.

If you work out at home, investing in some adjustable dumbbells is a no-brainer, and you'd be hard-pressed to find a "best home dumbbells" list without the PowerBlock Elite Adjustable Dumbbells near the top. The futuristic cubic look is stylish, but more importantly, it's a seriously economical, space-saving design—which is the whole point of going adjustable over a traditional rack of individual weights. The weights have flat edges so you can hold them on end on your lap, and unlike a lot of adjustable models, they're compact enough that they won’t bump into each other on shoulder or chest presses.

Fitness trackers come in many forms, including watches, rings, and smart bands. I have favorites in every category, but when it comes to the overall best fitness tracker for most people, the Fitbit Air is the clear winner. It does all the essentials without a subscription, including step tracking, sleep tracking, and automatic workout detection. Its battery lasts a week, and your giftee will have the option to either use the new Google Health app (which I mostly like) or bypass it and use a third-party app like Bevel. More importantly, it's a fraction of the cost of any other tracker out there, so it's a lot more likely to fit your gifting budget than something like an Oura ring.

If you gift a subscription to Bespoke Post, you’re giving the chance to open a different gift every month, like Christmas is lasting all year. Unlike some hyper-niche gift services, Bespoke Post lets users customize their loot boxes: One month, they can choose an outdoorsy vibe, and the next, go for a high-end coffee collection. They can even skip a month if they don’t like what’s on offer. This is an essential gift subscription for anyone buying a present for a hard-to-shop-for dude.

Makita invented cordless drills in 1978, and it has been known for making quality drills ever since. Its new 18-volt LXT combo set is even better than its predecessors because it has a longer battery life with improvements to motor control, overheating, and dust and particulates. The drill has about 70% more power than previous models, allowing you to drill into tough materials like pressure-treated lumber more easily, and the impact driver has a three-speed control, allowing you to adjust the power to match the material you’re driving fasteners into. Since a drill and driver are the foundation of a cordless tool kit, this set, which offers better battery life and more power, stands out—it comes with two batteries, a charger, and a tool bag.

Buying a kitchen gift can be challenging because our kitchens are so personal—some of us know what a braiser is, and some of us keep shoes in our ovens. No matter who you’re shopping for, the Our Place Wonder Oven is the perfect gift. This countertop appliance combines six functions into one stylish unit with a small footprint. If the recipient has a small kitchen, they will love it for its compact nature and for the way it replaces at least three other countertop appliances (a toaster, an air fryer, and a convection oven), clearing space. If the person on your shopping list is an accomplished cook or always busy feeding a family, they’ll love it because it makes preparing fast, casual, and healthy meals a breeze without having to fire up that six-burner behemoth and use 16 pans. It can air-fry, bake, roast, toast, broil, and reheat with aplomb, and it sports an amazing steam infusion feature that makes everything come out moist—even those undated leftovers you pulled out of the freezer in desperation. It also comes with everything you’ll need to start cooking: a wire rack, air fry basket, bake pan, and crumb tray are all included. Did we mention it just looks cool?

A lot of tech might be expensive these days, but that doesn’t mean all of it is. In fact, there are plenty of excellent gadgets you can buy friends and family for $50 or less. Our favorite option in this category is the JBL Go 4. This portable Bluetooth speaker is small but mighty, able to get quite loud for such a tiny device. You’ll get seven hours of playback on one charge, plus an extra two hours with “Playback Boost” enabled. The Go 4 has an IP67 rating against dust and water, so you can bring the speaker with you outdoors without worrying about ruining it. If your friends have JBL speakers of their own, not just Go 4s, you can connect them all together for a quick multi-speaker setup. It really is a versatile device, especially when you consider both its size and its price. The JBL Go 4 makes for a great stocking stuffer, Yankee Swap contribution, or gift for anyone looking for a portable speaker for home or on-the-go use.

#3486. 'Avengers: Doomsday' Has Reportedly Already Outgrossed 'Supergirl' 6 Weeks Before Release

Marvel and DC have had a rivalry on the page for decades, now, but there's something particularly striking about the fact that one studio's biggest tentpole movie of the year has been defeated by another before it's even hit theaters. After a difficult few years for the superhero genre, audiences have gotten quite picky about what they'll give their money to, but the one-two punch of Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Robert Downey Jr.'s return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe has just proven too much.

Avengers: Doomsday has reportedly accumulated more than $125 million in worldwide advance ticket sales, bringing it within touching distance of the entire theatrical gross of DC Studios' Supergirl. According to Comic Basics, the Marvel blockbuster has reached the extraordinary milestone with approximately six weeks remaining until its December 18 release.

Supergirl, which starred Milly Alcock as Kara Zor-El, wrapped up its disappointing theatrical run with $126.4 million worldwide, which means Doomsday has reportedly generated almost as much in advance ticket revenue as Supergirl did during its entire theatrical run, which is something of a mind-blowing statistic, although the figures are not directly comparable. The numbers have come from third-party tracking but it's a pretty safe bet to say this is going to be the biggest movie of the year.

The demand has already been through the roof for Doomsday since premium format tickets (but not IMAX, crucially) went on sale in July, subsequently grossing $16.5 million during its first 24 hours, and the tracking since then has suggested worldwide presales crossed $100 million on October 6, with demand continuing to build throughout the month.

The cast includes Chris Evans (Captain America: The First Avenger) as Steve Rogers, Chris Hemsworth (Thor) as Thor, Anthony Mackie (The Falcon and the Winter Soldier) as Sam Wilson, Sebastian Stan (The Apprentice) as Bucky Barnes, Paul Rudd (Ant-Man) as Scott Lang, Letitia Wright (Black Panther) as Shuri, Tom Hiddleston (Loki) as Loki, and Pedro Pascal (The Last of Us) as Reed Richards. The movie will also feature returning X-Men stars, including the late Sir Patrick Stewart as Professor Charles Xavier, Sir Ian McKellen as Magneto, James Marsden as Cyclops, and Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler, while it's directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo.

Marvel Studios' Avengers: Doomsday arrives exclusively in theaters on December 18, 2026.

#3485. Google Is Using Data From Gmail and Drive to Target Ads, but You Can Stop It

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

As Android Authority reports, Google typically doesn't personalize ads based on content from Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos by default. However, the policy now makes these data available for that purpose if you've connected these apps to other Google services—like Personal Intelligence—that do support personalized ads. Personal Intelligence is the opt-in Gemini feature launched earlier this year that links with other Google apps to give you more tailored, contextual responses in Gemini and Google Search's AI Mode.

Personal Intelligence is opt-in by default, but as Ars Technica points out, users are presented with opportunities to enable this feature and connect apps to it without realizing it or understanding the potential consequences of doing so.

Free up your iPhone's storage without deleting all your stuff

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Why is it that you seem to run out of iPhone storage at the worst possible moment? The knee-jerk reaction is to start frantically trashing holiday pictures or deleting apps you actually use. But you do not need to butcher your camera roll or pay for more just to claw back a few precious gigabytes.

A couple of clever, built-in settings reclaim space without touching the things you care about. To keep things simple, here are the two best ways to clear that storage warning for good.

High-definition clips and photos are almost always the secret culprits swallowing up your storage. If you shoot video in 4K, just sixty seconds of footage can eat through nearly half a gigabyte of local space.

Instead of manually picking through your photo library to delete memories, you can let your phone handle the heavy lifting automatically. Head over to Settings, Apps, Photos, and make sure iCloud Photos is switched on, and tap Optimize iPhone Storage.

This feature keeps smaller previews on your phone and moves the full-resolution files to iCloud, downloading originals on demand when you view them.

Most of us have a digital graveyard of apps we only open once in a blue moon — think airline boarding passes, occasional parking apps, or mobile games you haven't touched in weeks.

Offloading gives you the perfect middle ground. Navigate to Settings, General, and iPhone Storage, where your device neatly lists your apps from biggest to smallest. Tap on any culprits you don't need and hit Offload App.

This removes the app to free up storage while keeping your personal data, settings, and logins untouched. When you need it again, tap the grey cloud icon on your home screen to instantly reinstall it.

#3481. Goodbye House Of The Dragon, HBO's New 8-Part Series Is The Fantasy Event Of The Year

While House of the Dragon season 3 might have been massive, another upcoming HBO series will still undoubtedly mark the single biggest fantasy TV event of 2026. Fantasy TV has come a long way since Game of Thrones, HBO’s expensive and risky adaptation of author George RR. Martin’s A Song of Ice & Fire saga, first premiered in 2011. When that show started its run, the idea of an expensive, R-rated, mature fantasy TV show was almost unheard of.

In the years since, everything from The Witcher to Outlander, to Interview with the Vampire, to Arcane, to Prime Video’s Critical Role shows The Legend of Vox Machina and The Mighty Nein, has proven that fantasy shows don’t need to be remotely family-friendly to amass a huge audience and justify their big budgets and high production values. Meanwhile, this has allowed fantasy shows that do appeal to all ages to get even more ambitious.

While HBO’s His Dark Materials and Netflix’s Wednesday are also pricey, Prime Video’s Lord of the Ringr prequel The Rings of Power had a colossal budget that made not just Game of Thrones, but also its spinoffs House of the Dragon and A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms, look comparatively modest. Although House of the Dragon broke various budget records with its first season, The Rings of Power was quick to equal and then outspend the HBO show. Now, HB’s upcoming Harry Potter reboot looks set to blow both franchises out of the water.

Announced in 2023, HBO's Harry Potter reboot is the cable network’s biggest project in years. The show’s run will begin with an eight-episode reimagining of the first novel in the series, Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone, in late December 2026. The reboot is set to last seven seasons, with each season covering one of the novels in the original series.

Harry Potter creator J. K. Rowling’s history of outspoken transphobic comments has led to calls to boycott the series, but the making of documentary Finding Harry: The Craft Behind the Magic rose to HBOMax’s number one most-watched spot upon its April release. As Wednesday season 3 moves away from its original magic school setting, it seems plausible that HBO’s show could fill its place in the market and prove a major hit.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling’s public history of transphobia, the Harry Potter franchise remains one of the biggest brands owned by Warner Brothers. While the Game of Thrones shows are massive, they are also squarely aimed at adult audiences alone, which massively limits their potential audience in comparison to the Harry Potter reboot. Meanwhile, the show’s biggest and most expensive competitors in the YA fantasy genre, like Disney’s Percy Jackson & The Olympians, have far less brand recognition than the Harry Potter books.

Thus, it seems entirely possible that HBO will get the historic hit that the cable network hopes for with the arrival of Harry Potter’s reboot. However, it is not necessarily easy to work out what constitutes a success for a series of this scale. Taking a look at HBO’s biggest historic fantasy hits, like Game of Thrones' final seasons and House of the Dragon, it becomes clear that the series will need to perform historically well to be considered a worthwhile investment.

Where Game of Thrones season 8 had a staggering 44-46 million multi-platform viewers per episode, House of the Dragon season 3 came close to replicating this with 34 million global viewers per outing. This might sound extraordinary, but it is worth noting that Netflix’s comparatively family-friendly fantasy series Wednesday season 2 garnered over 50 million views in only five days.

Thus, for Harry Potter’s reboot to be considered a success, the show would not only need over 40 million global viewers within its first week, but also a regular audience of 40-45 million per episode. If Harry Potter’s reboot can maintain over 30 million viewers by its season 1 finale, the show could potentially live up to its hype.

I’m cutting through the clutter to bring you the gems just added to Prime Video

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

One of my favorite streaming traditions is checking out what each platform has added at the start of a new month. The very first day of the month is when the majority of the best streaming services refresh their libraries with major movie drops, and Prime Video is no exception.

In fact, Prime Video typically drops more movies on the first day of a new month than any of its streaming rivals, and on Sunday, November 1, 2026, Prime’s back catalog is getting a major boost with 103 movies arriving.

That’s an overwhelming amount of choice, which is why I’ve combed through the list to pick out the gems you should stream first. Because it’s now November, Prime Video’s latest movie drop is heavy on holidays, and I’ve picked a couple of Christmas classics to get you in the festive mood nice and early. However, I’ve also found some exciting thrillers for those who don’t start celebrating the holidays until December.

So, let’s get into my top picks; these are the five movies just added to Prime Video that should be at the top of your November 2026 watchlist.

Some of my fondest childhood memories of the festive season involve rewatching “Elf” so many times that the DVD was in danger of getting worn out. This 2000s holiday classic has it all: seasonal spirit, charming comedy, lovable characters and a message about the importance of family. Even now as a grown-up on the wrong side of 30, it’s still a holiday movie I watch every single year, and I’ve no plans to stop in 2026.

Will Ferrell plays Buddy, a human raised by Santa’s elves. Due to his human proportions and inability to make toys, he doesn’t quite fit in at the North Pole. So when Santa reveals to him that his father (James Caan), a New York City bigwig, is on the naughty list, Buddy travels to the Big Apple to meet his biological father and find his place in the world. Once in NYC, he discovers that humans are sorely lacking in holiday cheer.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The perfect movie doesn’t exist. Absolute perfection is an impossible goal. Even my favorite films of all time have some minor flaws. However, when it comes to a movie nailing exactly what it's trying to achieve, it’s hard to argue that “Mean Girls” doesn’t get pretty darn close to perfection. This movie is the quintessential teen comedy, packed with quotable lines, iconic outfits and legendary scenes. And yes, we’re talking about the original here, not the musical remake. Though for the record, I’m a defender of that movie; I think it’s very underrated.

Cady Heron (Lindsay Lohan) is a 16-year-old whose family has recently returned to the U.S. after spending 12 years in Africa. Now attending North Shore High School, Cady is introduced to a complex web of unspoken teenage rules and a strict social hierarchy. At the top of the food chain are The Plastics, a trio of ultra-cool mean girls led by queen bee, Regina George (Rachel McAdams). When Cady is invited into their inner circle, she hatches a plan to sabotage them from within.

This year will see the release of yet another big-screen spin on Charles Dickens’ enduring classic, “A Christmas Carol,” in the form of Ti West’s “Ebenezer.” But why trek out to your local theater when you can already enjoy the best movie adaptation of the timeless tale on Prime Video? Okay, so “Scrooged” is the best adaptation of “A Christmas Carol” that doesn’t feature The Muppets. It's still a great watch even if it doesn't include Kermit, Miss Piggy, and the gang. Plus, it stars Bill Murray at his sarcastic best.

You probably know the basic setup, but if you’re somehow unfamiliar with Dickens’ fable, it follows a cynical and selfish TV executive (named Frank Cross here rather than Ebenezer Scrooge), who is visited by three ghosts on Christmas Eve in an effort to convince him to change his self-centered ways. There’s a pleasant meta twist in “Scrooged.” Cross lives in a world where the “A Christmas Carol” story also exists, so when he starts living the tale for real, he’s not too happy about it.

Moving away from holiday classics and teenage comedies, another movie that’s just arrived as part of Prime Video’s huge November 1 drop is “The Manchurian Candidate.” This 1962 political thriller is one that fans of classic cinema definitely shouldn’t skip. It stars Frank Sinatra, Laurence Harvey, and Janet Leigh, alongside Angela Lansbury, Henry Silva, and James Gregory. And it is perhaps one of the sharpest American movies of the Cold War era.

Raymond Shaw (Harvey) is a U.S. soldier fighting in the Korean War, captured by the enemy, but then released three days later. Returned home, he receives the Medal of Honor, and on the surface it looks like a feel-good homecoming story. But Shaw is hiding a dark secret, a shocking memory that even he can’t recall. “The Manchurian Candidate” is a thriller that hasn’t lost its edge over the last 60+ years and has even inspired modern media like Showtime's “Homeland.”

Watch "The Manchurian Candidate" on Prime Video now

Staying on the theme of political thrillers, “WarGames” is an ‘80s techno ride that does feel a little outdated when watched in the 21st century. However, at the time of its release, it was a real cautionary tale about the dangers of technology and its potential uses in global conflict. Heavily influenced by the Cold War period in which it was released, it marked one of the first movie roles for Matthew Broderick, Ferris Bueller himself.

David Lightman (Broderick) is a smart but unmotivated high school slacker in Seattle. A computer whiz, he uses his aptitude for computers for teenage hijinks. But things get serious when he unknowingly accesses a military central computer with the ability to simulate and even launch a devastating nuclear attack against the USSR. He thinks he’s playing a game, but he might have just started World War III…

#3478. 10 Great Books To Read if You Love 'The Lord of the Rings'

The Lord of the Rings is a trilogy of books written by J. R. R. Tolkien, who penned the series as a very small part of his enormous lexicon of histories, sagas, and developments contained in his own personal world, known as Middle-Earth. The series is famous for being adapted into some of the greatest movies ever made in the early 2000s, which posthumously cemented Tolkien's legacy as one of the greatest writers in human history.

The books follow a group of unlikely heroes as they journey across the land to destroy a magical ring, one created by the servant of the universe's ultimate evil, to weaken the shadow and prevent the world's destruction. Though it might seem like a fantastical, whimsical story, much of it is based on Tolkien's personal beliefs, especially his experience in the First World War, his love of his home of England, and how horrified he was at the world's growing industrialization of rural areas. If you've already read the books or have seen the movies and are looking for something to fill the void they left behind, look no further, because Tolkien inspired a whole bunch of authors, and many books with similar themes have come out in the years since.

The Anvil of the World is a seriously underrated entry into the high fantasy genre, written by the late Kage Baker. It is the first in a series known as the Lord Ermenwyr trilogy, but truth be told, it's less of a series and more like three standalone books that take place in the same world and feature a few of the same characters. This ensures that if you don't like the first, there's no need to pursue it any further since it's entirely self-contained.

Regardless, the book plays out like three smaller stories that fit an overarching story, following the journeys of Smith, a smuggler, and Lord Ermenwyr, a young mage. The book includes some steampunk elements and begins with Smith being assigned to take Lord Ermenwyr to a port city via train, and to protect him from the various factions trying to kill him. It sounds grim, but the book has a lot of brilliantly-written humor in it, and feels like a grand adventure through a vast and mysterious world inhabited by many wondrous creatures. It's highly underrated, yet sure to be enjoyed by any Tolkien fan.

A Wizard of Earthsea, along with its five sequels that comprise the series, takes place on an island archipelago called Earthsea. Here, dragons and humans exist, with most, if not all, humans possessing innate magical talents, though some are obviously more skilled than others. Most of the people in the centre of the archipelago are the Hardic, who are dark-skinned and who see magic as a gift and an asset. In the East are the pale-skinned Kargish, who see magic as evil and frequently clash with the Hardics.

Like The Lord of the Rings, Earthsea obviously has some political undertones to it, portraying very real issues, yet painting them as a high fantasy story. It's a story that shows how universal specific problems are, and that takes in a fully-fleshed-out world, much like Tolkien's Middle-Earth, and the way it tackles real-world issues that Tolkien himself was passionate about. To this day, Earthsea is still seen as one of the most important and influential fantasy works ever made.

Children of Blood and Bone is a YA novel and the first of the Legacy of Orïsha trilogy by Tomi Adeyemi. The books take place in the continent of Orïsha, a land resembling West Africa. Here, there exist two distinct types of people: the Divîners, a group of people who can use magic and turn into a more advanced version of themselves known as Maji, and the Kosidán, non-magical folk who have ripped magic out of the world and risen to rule the continent, condemning the Divîners to a life of poverty.

After years of oppression, a Divîner named Zélie, along with the Kosidán princess, Amari, is determined to restore magic to the world, ending the conflict between the two civilizations. Though the setting is wildly different from that of Tolkien, both Adeyemi and Tolkien have included some subtle political themes in their work, disguising real-world issues through the lens of high fantasy. They also have the same love of their ancestral homes, with the difference being that instead of England, Tomi Adeyemi has recreated Nigeria through a magical lens. It's a fantastic adventure story made even more impressive by the fact that it is Adeyemi's debut novel, and has become such a resounding success that a Children of Blood and Bone movie is set to be released in 2027.

Australian author Emily Rodda, real name Jennifer Rowe, writes crime fiction for adults and fantasy for young adults, with a plethora of books at her back. There's her acclaimed DeltoraQuest series, which was adapted into a Japanese anime and became very popular in the 90s and early 00s. Set in the same universe, there's The Golden Door, the first in a trilogy. This trilogy takes place on the island of Dorne, in the hidden city of Weld, which is constantly improving its defenses, thickening and heightening its walls and not letting anybody beyond them.

Every year, the citizens of Weld become subject to attacks from Skimmers, large bat-like creatures that destroy homes and devour the people within. With no way out of the city, Weld's mayor proposes an expedition to the outside world to find the source of the Skimmers and eliminate it. However, the only way out of the city is three magic doors of gold, silver, and wood. The story details the journey of a young boy named Rye, who travels beyond the walls in search of his missing brothers, who vanished during said expedition. The sweeping adventure of the story, combined with its dangerous beasts and its sinister villains, along with its clearly-defined evil at its heart, make it a different, yet remarkable choice for any Tolkien fan.

The Eye of the World is the first entry into the widely popular The Wheel of Time series, which has since been adapted into an Amazon Prime TV series. The first book (and most of the subsequent entries in the 15-novel long series) is written by the late Robert Jordan, whose work immediately drew comparisons to the works of J. R. R. Tolkien. This first novel is especially similar, centering on a magical individual known as an Aes Sedai named Moiraine Damodred, who arrives in the remote region of the Two Rivers, seeking the legendary Dragon Reborn, a chosen individual who is destined to either save the world from the clutches of the Dark One or to destroy it.

Though the series eventually morphs into its own distinct entity, this first book is ideal for Tolkien fans. It's arguably also one of the best in the entire series, as it's mostly about adventure, a distinct dark vs. light narrative, and a magical world. By far the best part about it, though, is that the first novel is fairly self-contained and doesn't really leave any unanswered questions, which means anyone who didn't enjoy it or doesn't have the energy for 14 more books can easily put it down and walk away while still feeling satisfied.

Brandon Sanderson is the author responsible for finishing The Wheel of Time series after Robert Jordan's untimely death. However, he also developed his own wide-reaching fantasy universe known as the Cosmere. Each series takes place on a different planet and has a different magic system at its core. The Way of Kings is the first in The Stormlight Archive series, which is often regarded as Sanderson's finest work. It is set on the planet of Roshar, which is constantly plagued by powerful weather events known as highstorms. As a result, there is little to no flora since it is commonly uprooted by the storms, and any fauna is crustacean in nature so they can take shelter in their shells.

Amidst a war between humans and the crustacean Parshendi, a primitive evil begins to rise, prompting the resurrection of a once-lost order of magical warriors. The Way of Kings is an absolute monster of a novel at over 1200 pages, but it's a thrilling ride from start to finish. Those who are fans of Middle-Earth's deep and extensive lore, epic battles, stories of unlikely heroes, and the endless battle between good and evil will be sure to appreciate The Stormlight Archive. Even if the world is vastly different from Middle-Earth, it has many of the same themes and the same emotional impact that Tolkien put into his writing.

Gardens of the Moon is the very first novel taking place in the enormous universe of Steven Erikson's Malazan series, which eventually grew into numerous series and subseries all set within the same fascinating world. As one can imagine, this series of books has a heavy bit of lore behind it, with histories detailing fallen kingdoms, extensive wars, ancient artifacts and deities, and the nature of magic in the universe.

For those who have fallen in love with Tolkien's life's work, dedicated to creating an entirely new world with a long history, it is very easy to fall in love with Malazan, and especially with the first novel. This thrilling epic fantasy centers on a power struggle against the tyrannical Malazan Empire, and in 2000, it was nominated for a World Fantasy Award, a highly coveted honor. With the series still going strong and new developments in the overarching narrative always on the horizon, Malazan has found a dedicated fanbase and has drawn many comparisons to J. R. R. Tolkien.

For those who like the whole forlorn ranger aspect that is Aragorn II Elessar, there's Rise of the Ranger, the first entry in The Echoes Saga, comprised of nine novels. This series contains a lot of similar themes to Middle-Earth, namely the rivalry between different races. In Middle-Earth, the dwarves and elves are always at each other's throats, whereas in Rise of the Ranger, it's humanity and the elves that have warred in the past, to the point where the elves have gone all but extinct.

And yet, humanity continues to squabble amongst themselves, totally unaware of the evil looming in the distance, with the world's only hope being the eponymous ranger. The inspiration of J. R. R. Tolkien is made clear in this critically acclaimed series, harboring many of the same ideas and aspects of lore, so it's a brilliant, more modern entry into the genre that no Middle-Earth fan is going to want to miss.

For a little bit of a different read, there's Bored of the Rings, a biting parody of J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. This 150-page novel is super short, but covers much of the same bases, only with a much more humorous twist. It pokes fun at overused fantasy tropes, includes intentionally incorrect nomenclature based on real-world brand names, and deliberately makes things as ridiculous as possible for the sole purpose of having a laugh, as well as being a bit of a critique.

Not everyone wants to read something like this, and that's totally okay. However, any die-hard fan of Tolkien should probably give this one a go, because it feels like an alternate version of a familiar story that's laden with absurdist jokes. It's considered one of the most brilliantly-written parodies of high fantasy, though it has, of course, garnered its fair share of haters. Love it or hate it, Bored of the Rings has definitely been an influential work.

If parody and satire isn't your personal cup of tea, try The King of Elfland's Daughter, a fantasy book written before Tolkien ever penned his debut novel. This forgotten fantasy novel is a short read, not requiring a whole lot of energy or commitment, and has served as one of Tolkien's chief inspirations when he penned his vast and expansive Middle-Earth saga. Obviously, anything that inspired Tolkien is something that any die-hard fan of his should most definitely take a look at.

Story-wise, it's about Lirazel, the daughter of the King of Elfland, as the name implies. She becomes the subject of a romantic pursuit on behalf of Alveric, the son of the Lord of the land of Erl. Unfortunately, though their love is strong, the two find themselves unable to assimilate into each other's culture, prompting magical intervention. The King of Elfland's Daughter is considered one of the pioneering members of the high fantasy genre and is one of the most influential fantasy novels ever written, and is an absolute must-read for any fan of Tolkien.

If you've been a dedicated Arc browser user, the time has finally come to say goodbye. The Browser Company paused development of Arc in 2025, continuing only with security updates. As announced late last week, Arc will officially sunset on Dec. 22, 2026, giving users two months to transition their data to an alternative.

One option is to move to the company's new AI-focused Dia browser, though there are other (potentially better) choices depending on what you're looking for. Most data from Arc—including Spaces, Favorites, pinned tabs, and folders as well as passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history—will transition automatically over to Dia, but if you're switching to a different platform entirely, you'll need to take what you can with you before Dec. 22.

Officially, Arc supports exporting Spaces and tabs only, and the resulting Export.md plain-text file is simply a list of links that you can open and bookmark in your new browser. MacOS users can initiate this process via Arc > Settings > Advanced > Export Data and saving the file to a preferred location. On Windows, open the Arc menu, select Settings, and go to Export Spaces and tabs > Export Data.

To simply copy and paste every link from one folder, right-click the folder, select Copy All Links, and paste them wherever you'd like (select Copy All Links as Markdown to keep link titles on macOS). You can also save Easels as images by tapping the share icon > Share Via... and selecting PNG.

There's no formal process to export other Arc data. If you saved logins in Arc, now is a good time to start moving credentials over to a different platform. (Our top picks for password managers aren't tied to a single browser.)

There are a few alternatives to Arc's official export process, which is highly manual and doesn't keep your folder structure intact. There are several third-party scripts available (for free) that can facilitate the transition as well as a paid extension called ArcEscape that can export folders and pinned tabs and import into another browser. The extension is available for Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi, and Firefox. According to Arc's FAQ, all user accounts will be deactivated on Dec. 22, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days of deactivation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mattress mold is a problem that sneaks up on you. A slightly whiffy bed and small stains can quickly turn to itching, sneezing and watery eyes. And right now is primetime for moldy conditions.

A combination of cold, wet weather outside and warm heating inside increases moisture in the air. Your mattress soaks it up like a sponge and, trapped inside your warm bed, that damp helps mold spores to multiply.

Mattress mold doesn't have to spell the end of your bed, but you need to catch it early. We spoke to Dr Gareth Nye, Biomedical Sciences lecturer at the University of Salford working exclusively with M&S, about how to identify early signs of mold — and get rid of it.

Mold can completely ruin a mattress, but before you rush off to browse our best mattress guide for a replacement bed, look out for these early indicators of mold.

You won't necessarily see early signs of mold in your mattress, but you might be able to smell the problem has taken hold.

Dr. Nye describes the smell of mold as "a persistent musty, damp, or earthy odor" and notes that it can linger "even after the bedding has been washed."

If this new smell is accompanied by an uptick in allergy symptoms when you go to bed (itching, sneezing or watery eyes, for example) mold is the likely culprit. Noticed a sweeter musty smell? It might be bed bugs.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Big, dark stains are often a sign that your mattress is past saving. But before you get to that point, Dr. Nye recommends looking for "tiny, clustered pinpoint stains."

These small marks are the signs of an early mold infestation and they can be treated (we'll explore how below). And don't just look on the top surface of the mattress for stains. The underside of the bed as well as the sides can house mold as well.

Signs of mold aren't always visible on the mattress itself. Look in the surrounding area for indicators your bedroom is growing mold.

Dr. Nye describes "spaces up against a wall or behind units" as 'mold magnets' because they prevent airflow. So if your bed frame is pushed against the wall, move it forward when you clean and check for mold.

He also advices looking in any common sites for condensation, including anything pressed to the "external environment" (like radiators against a window).

"The space under the bed is also a prime spot for mold," says Dr. Nye. And if the mold is under the bed, it might not take long for it to move into the bed.

Mold is more than just an unwanted stain. Left to grow, mold in your mattress can have serious negative repercussions on your health.

"Mold reproduces by releasing microscopic spores and mycotoxins into the air, which are easily inhaled during the 7 to 8 hours you spend asleep," explains Dr. Nye. "This triggers an immune response, leading to allergic rhinitis (sneezing, congestion, runny nose, and itchy eyes) and significantly exacerbating symptoms for those with asthma."

And the longer the problem is allowed to grow, the worse the impact it can have on your health.

"Prolonged exposure can result in chronic illnesses," says Dr. Nye. "Mold spores can also severely worsen conditions like eczema and trigger contact dermatitis."

We previously asked the experts how to get rid of mattress mold. They advised spot treating any stains with ingredients you probably have in your kitchen: white vinegar and baking soda.

Begin by mixing equal parts white vinegar and water. Spray the solution lightly on the stain and leave for 20 minutes. Blot dry, then apply a thin layer of baking soda. Leave to sit for several hours and then vacuum thoroughly.

#3467. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3464. 43 Years Later, TV's Most-Watched Finale Of All Time Is Still A Masterpiece

Now that the monoculture has splintered off into a thousand different niches on their own corners of the internet, it’s tough to convey just how big of a cultural phenomenon the final episode of M*A*S*H was. More than 100 million viewers tuned in to see the last hoorah of this seminal sitcom when it aired its finale in 1983.

Until M*A*S*H came along, sitcoms were strictly for laughs; they were all about absurd scenarios and second-hand embarrassment. But M*A*S*H brought an unprecedented level of pathos and emotionality to the sitcom without sacrificing any of the laughs. It wasn’t just mindless entertainment; it used humor as a coping mechanism to get through the fog of war. It’s one of the funniest shows ever put on television, but it had some truly heartbreaking moments, too. The series finale opens with Hawkeye being treated for PTSD.

The final episode of M*A*S*H — season 11, episode 16, “Goodbye, Farewell, and Amen” — is essentially a feature film, with a two-and-a-half-hour runtime. After stretching out the Korean War for more than a decade, the show finally got to the ceasefire, and the 4077th threw a party to celebrate before tearing down the camp one last time. Not only is it still the most-watched series finale of all time; it still holds up.

After all this time, “Goodbye, Farewell, and Amen” remains one of the greatest series finales ever made, and it continues to influence series finales to this day. It gets everything right: it uses the most obvious setup — a party celebrating the ceasefire — to give everyone a proper sendoff. It sets every character up for the next chapter of their lives, and it uses their heartfelt farewells to each other to bid a heartfelt farewell to the audience.

The final shot of M*A*S*H — a “goodbye” message left in rocks, seen from the helicopter by Hawkeye — was the perfect note to end on. It’s a sweet moment between Hawkeye and B.J., but it’s also a sweet moment between the makers of the show and the loyal audience who stuck with them and invited these characters into their homes for the past decade. These simple visual storytelling tricks are timeless; they’ll always work, no matter how short the audience’s attention span gets.

Cheers, Friends, Seinfeld, and The Fugitive have all come close, but M*A*S*H’s final episode remains the highest-rated series finale in television history — it was bigger than Roots and the Super Bowl — and it’s likely to hold that record forevermore, because it’s highly improbable that 100 million people will ever tune in to the same TV show ever again. Thanks to streaming, terrestrial television is a thing of the past, and even the biggest viewing figures in streaming don’t come close to the numbers posted by M*A*S*H and Roots and the Super Bowl.

Now that on-demand services have made everything so convenient, TV is no longer appointment viewing. In the ‘80s, when M*A*S*H ended, audiences were at the mercy of regularly scheduled programming. There were a small handful of networks, and whatever they were showing at a given time, that’s what you had to watch. But in this day and age, there are so many other options. There are hundreds of TV channels and that’s before you take into account all the streaming services.

Even when a water-cooler show hits the zeitgeist, like The Bear or The Last of Us, most audiences just catch it on streaming when they get a chance; a very slim percentage of viewers are actually watching it when it’s on and contributing to the night-of Nielsen ratings. So, it’s more than likely that M*A*S*H’s finale will hold its viewership record in perpetuity.

Recent news urges us all to prepare for sudden power cuts. I assumed I was fine, until an honest look around my house revealed I was woefully unequipped

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time an emergency agency pops up on the news suggesting households keep a 72-hour emergency kit on hand, I do the same thing: nod knowingly, assume they’re talking to someone far less organized than me, and scroll on.

In my head, I’m a reasonably capable adult. The fridge is full, there are batteries rattling around in a drawer somewhere, and I have a phone flashlight. Surely that counts as disaster preparedness.

Curiosity finally won out, so I decided to run an honest, room-by-room audit of what would actually happen if our power lines went dark for three straight days. The verdict was... humbling.

It turns out my master survival plan was heavily reliant on an active Wi-Fi connection, an electric stovetop, and blind optimism. Here's five glaring blind spots I completely overlooked, and what you should do so you don't make the same mistakes.

Opening my junk drawer during the audit revealed two decorative candles, a lighter that took six clicks to spark, and I didn't have a flashlight. My entire plan, it seemed, was an iPhone and an ancient power bank that refused to charge past 12%. Using a phone flashlight burns through battery, leaving you without light, or a lifeline.

Retire your phone as a light source and stash dedicated LED lights or magnetic lanterns where you can grab them in pitch black, like a bedside drawer. Pair them with an inexpensive hand-crank AM/FM emergency radio: it pulls in vital civil broadcasts with zero Wi-Fi, and the built-in dynamo handle doubles as a manual charger as a last resort if your devices die.

I went looking for medical supplies and found a dusty tin with three sports bandages, one pack of ibuprofen, and a pair of blunt tweezers. That was the entirety of my home trauma unit. Navigating in the dark makes minor injuries inevitable, and local clinics won't be running at full capacity during a power cut.

Ditch the half-empty tin and get a proper, sealed multi-day medical kit stocked with sterile dressings, burn gel, antiseptic wash, and heavy-duty elastic wraps. Crucially, audit your prescription medications right now and set a reminder to refill them at least a week before they run dry.

When a storm knocks out power, pharmacies can't access electronic dispensary records, and nobody is handing out prescription pills over a dark counter.

A packed fridge gives you an immediate, unearned hit of confidence. But an unopened fridge only holds safe temperatures for about four hours, and my pantry was full of dry pasta, lentils, and rice — meals that require boiling water and an electric stove. Unless I fancied crunching raw fettuccine in the dark, I had zero edible food past day one.

Do a pantry check for foods that require zero heat and zero added water. Build a reserve of ready-to-eat staples: crackers, canned fish, pull-tab soups, peanut butter, spam, nuts. It won't win culinary awards, but it keeps you fed without burning precious cooking fuel or risking food poisoning on day three.

Municipal water relies on electric booster pumps. If the grid fails, pipe pressure drops fast, or contamination triggers boil-water alerts you can't comply with on a dead stove. My total water reserve was half a fridge filter carafe and a gym bottle on my desk.

Store the emergency baseline: four litres (one gallon) of water per person, per day, split between drinking and basic hygiene. For a 72-hour blackout, keep a minimum of 12 litres per person tucked into a dark cupboard or wardrobe, plus extra if you have pets. It's worth noting that your water heater has around 150-300 liters stored inside it too in case of an emergency.

Digital payments die the instant the power cut hits. Point-of-sale card readers, phone taps, and bank networks go dark, turning plastic and smartwatches into useless props. Checking my own bags, pockets and drawers produced exactly zero physical money.

If you're able, withdraw an emergency cash reserve and stash it. The guidance states between $100 and $500 depending on your family's size, covering essentials if card systems remain offline for several days. If you're like me and withdrawing in one go isn't feasible, simply start tucking away leftover change. Every little helps, and it adds up quickly.

#3461. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next
