This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3459. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3458. James Bond Star Officially Confirms Franchise Exit Ahead of Denis Villeneuve's Reboot

The next James Bond edges ever closer as the minutes, hours, days and weeks go by, which will end up putting an end to one of Hollywood's longest-running guessing games, and while audiences are still waiting to discover who will inherit the famous tuxedo, there are plenty of other questions up in the air. Denis Villeneuve is currently preparing to reinvent 007 for a new generation but will we see a Judi Dench-style scenario where we get a veteran crossing over? Possibly, but one actor has ruled it out.

Ben Whishaw has confirmed that he won't be returning as Q for Villeneuve's upcoming James Bond reboot, bringing his time as MI6's gadget specialist to an end after three appearances opposite Craig. Speaking with The Sunday Times, the actor explained why he believes the franchise needs to change considerably following the conclusion of Craig's era.

The world has changed so much since the last Bond film so you have to find what is relevant about it. I think it needs to be reinvented completely. But it’s not for me to say.

Whishaw first appeared as Q in 2012's Skyfall, before returning for Spectre and No Time to Die. His younger, technologically gifted interpretation of the character became a popular part of Craig's later adventures, replacing the more traditional gadget-master approach associated with Desmond Llewelyn and John Cleese.

The upcoming reboot will be directed by Villeneuve, whose previous credits include Dune and Blade Runner 2049, with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight writing the screenplay. Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce the movie, although Amazon MGM Studios has yet to announce who will play Bond himself. Among the actors reportedly linked to the role are Callum Turner (Masters of the Air), Jack Lowden (Slow Horses), and Josh O'Connor (Challengers), although no casting decision has been officially announced.

Whishaw also reflected on the extraordinary secrecy surrounding the Bond franchise, admitting that the intense speculation surrounding the character is very much part of the experience.

People go crazy about it. It’s all deliberate hype. When you are working on it, it’s incredibly secretive, almost like being a spy. You only get the pages of the script that you are in. It’s a ploy to create suspense and glamour, but it’s kind of fun.

The next James Bond movie is currently in development at Amazon MGM Studios. An official title, lead actor, and release date have not yet been announced.

There are few things I enjoy more than settling in for a good soapy period drama, preferably one involving extravagant gowns, vicious social maneuvering, forbidden romances and people getting spectacularly worked up over who gets invited to dinner. So of course, I'm a big fan of “The Gilded Age.” Four seasons in, I'm still thoroughly invested. I've been looking forward to this new chapter for months, and I'm happy to report that HBO's lavish historical drama has delivered another delicious helping of everything I love about it.

Verdict: “The Gilded Age” season 4 is another lavish, deliciously soapy treat, with juicy new conflicts and a terrific ensemble that makes even the smallest social squabbles entertaining. A few storylines stumble, but I'm still more than happy to spend another season among New York's most extravagantly dressed troublemakers.

Release schedule: Episode 1 on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 9 p.m. ET

The new season picks up several months after the events of season 3, with the usual assortment of New York's elite navigating romance, family squabbles, and the delicate business of maintaining their social standing. Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) and George (Morgan Spector) are facing serious marital difficulties, while their daughter Gladys (Taissa Farmiga) is preparing for motherhood in England.

Across the street, Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) is adjusting to a household where she no longer calls all the shots; Peggy Scott (Denée Benton) is balancing her writing ambitions with her relationship with Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica); and Marian (Louisa Jacobson) and Larry Russell (Harry Richardson) remain frustratingly complicated.

There's plenty happening across these interconnected households, and while some storylines are more compelling than others, season 4 finds the show giving its best characters fresh reasons to scheme, spar, and occasionally make me want to yell at the television. I've seen all eight episodes, but I promise not to reveal too much, as this is a show's plot turns are best enjoyed weekly.

Warning: Light spoilers ahead (not much beyond the trailer)

Kelly most recently reviewed "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

One of the things I've always loved about “The Gilded Age” is its ability to make seemingly trivial matters feel enormously consequential. A dinner invitation can become a declaration of war.

Season 4 also introduces some genuinely compelling stakes, particularly for the Russell family. I've always enjoyed watching Bertha and George operate as an unstoppable power couple, with her social ambition and his business acumen making them practically invincible. So, seeing them at odds is painful. At the same time, I have to admit that their relationship was in danger of becoming a little too perfect. Now, with their marriage under strain, both have to reckon with what happens when their greatest ally becomes their biggest obstacle.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Coon remains an absolute force as Bertha, who is accustomed to getting what she wants and isn't particularly good at taking no for an answer. Spector gets some terrific material, too, as George grapples with the consequences of getting shot and mounting professional pressures. Their chemistry remains one of the show's biggest assets, and I desperately want these two crazy kids to work things out. But I'm also enjoying the fact that the show isn't making it easy for them.

Meanwhile, Agnes has her own ambitions to pursue, setting up a delicious clash of wills as she and Bertha vie for the opportunity to host President Grover Cleveland (guest star Jim Gaffigan). Baranski is always a treat, particularly when Agnes has a reason to be indignant and mouth off. Seeing these two formidable women competing for the same prize is exactly the sort of society skirmish I break out the popcorn for.

One of the best facets of “The Gilded Age” is its exploration of the world of upper-class Black Americans, and season 4 blessedly gives us more of that. Peggy's growing success as a writer brings new complications as she navigates her upcoming marriage to William and the expectations of his family, particularly his mother, Elizabeth Kirkland Phylicia Rashad), who would make everyone in the r/JustNoMIL subreddit quake. Rashad is simply divine in the role, and I relish seeing her face off against both Peggy and Peggy's mother, Dorothy (Audra McDonald).

Then there's Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) and Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran), whose unconventional partnership is quickly becoming a favorite storyline. The two make a formidable team, and I love watching them scheme their way toward greater influence in New York society. They're a bona fide power couple in the making; long may their unholy alliance reign.

The show also continues to get plenty of mileage out of the household dynamics between Agnes and Ada (Cynthia Nixon). Baranski and Nixon are such a wonderfully entertaining pairing that I could watch them bicker over curtains for an entire episode. Even the lighter storylines involving the servants and their increasingly complicated lives add to the show's rich ensemble feel. Not every subplot lands with equal force, but there's rarely a dull moment.

My biggest frustration remains Marian and Larry, whose romantic entanglement continues to test my patience. I understand that a TV romance needs obstacles, but at some point, the writers have to give these two a break. Their continued complications seem so contrived. Come on, already!

Still, I have few complaints about "The Gilded Age" season 4. The production design and costumes are a feast for the eyes. This is the kind of show where I want to pause every few minutes just to admire someone's dress or the sheer extravagance of a dinner table. The performances are equally strong, with Coon, Baranski, Benton and Rashad among the standouts.

What I appreciate most is that “The Gilded Age” knows exactly what it is. It can explore serious subjects like race and women's independence while also giving us extravagant parties, romantic scandals and enough high-society backstabbing to fill several lifetimes. Sometimes I want challenging prestige television; other times, I just want to watch Christine Baranski deliver a devastating put-down in a spectacular hat. There's room for both. So, take a glass of champagne and enjoy.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3454. Frozen 4 Release Window & Story Get Major Update From Disney Exec

Disney is letting go of its original release plan for Frozen 4.

A third and fourth in Disney's hit animated movie franchise have been in the works for several years, with the intention of releasing them in quick succession. In 2023, director and writer Jennifer Lee explained that Frozen 3 and 4 were happening back-to-back because "We're really excited about where they're going, and we just have a lot of story to tell with that direction we're going in. So, I think, in my head, there may be enough for two in that story. But I'm really, really loving working with the team and where they're going."

In an interview with Collider, Disney's Head of Animation, Jared Bush, revealed that the plan is no longer to have a two-part story being released back-to-back. While this was the original intention, he explained that the release plan changed in order for the focus to be on making Frozen 3 the best movie it can be, along with telling a complete and satisfying story on its own. This approach also leaves more storytelling possibilities open for Frozen 4. Check out his comments below:

Looking at Frozen 3 and what a Frozen 4 could look like, I know early on it was, "We're going to put them right together, and they're going to be out in the world. It's going to happen quick." That's not what we're doing, for a lot of reasons. To me, an important one is we want to make sure that Frozen 3 is the best movie it can possibly be, so that when you get to the end of the movie, do you feel like you've watched a complete story? That it feels like something that feels fulfilling. That doesn't always mean that everything is buttoned up, but it does mean that you have to be building to something that feels worthy of the end of a franchise that's that important to people.

But then you also need to think, "Okay, well, if there was a future story, what might that look like?" You have to have a rough sense of that. But I'd say in my personal experience, I try not to go too in the weeds on that because it can lock you into a Frozen 3 that you may want to change or make better. If you're so rigid on what [Frozen] 4 might look like, then it could stifle you, and that's not something that I want to do.

Frozen 3 is scheduled to be released in theaters on November 24, 2027. Frozen 4 never received a set release date, although based on Bush's update, audiences should not expect it to be released the following year in 2028, as Disney will be taking more time to develop the sequel than originally indicated.

Bush is not concerned about Frozen 4 coming out later than anticipated, explaining how "something I noticed, certainly for Disney Animation, is if the future story is great, it doesn't matter how much time has passed. And I'd say that for a musical, even more so. I think a little extra time is not a bad thing because the character is going to need to sing again."

This outlook is likely connected to Zootopia 2, which he wrote and co-directed. Disney's animated sequel was released nine years after its predecessor, but still went on to gross $1.87 billion worldwide, making it the tenth highest grossing film of all-time and second best for animation, only behind Ne Zha 2.

While many of the plot details have remained under wraps, some Frozen 3 footage was shown at this year's D23, including the wedding of Anna (Kristen Bell) and Kristoff (Jonathan Groff), Olaf (Josh Gad) singing a song about Samantha, the wedding being crashed by a butterfly-like creature, and a new villain walking toward Anna and Elsa (Idina Menzel). There were also first looks at life-size versions of the two sisters, Kristoff, Olaf, and Sven.

Frozen 4 will presumably continue to follow these characters, but the story no longer seems as though it will be a direct continuation of the plot in Frozen 3. This would be more similar to the franchise's previous movies, as they follow the journeys of the same characters, but focus on different conflicts.

#3453. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. They're an affordable alternative to the popular Headphone 1 (currently $199), and seamlessly integrate into the Nothing/CMF ecosystem, which includes smartphones, watches, and other audio products. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). On the other side, you'll find an "Energy Slider," which tunes your sound in real-time, instantly adjusting the treble and bass balance.

You'll get an impressive 100 hours of playback on a single charge (reduced to up to 50 hours with ANC turned on) as well as AAC, SBC, and LDAC support. They have an IPX2 rating for resistance against sweat, and there is a 3.5mm audio jack for wired listening.

Nothing is known for its minimalistic design, but these headphones do a bit more by allowing you to mix and match the earcups with different colors (sold separately for $25). These are a good option for those looking for stylish, budget over-ear headphones that have great battery life and excellent audio quality for their price point.

#3451. I tested the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential Mattress and it delivered plenty of cushioning for side sleepers — but here's who should steer clear

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

The CopperFlex Essential is Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable adult mattress, with a 10" model regularly priced under $600 for a queen. I found its pressure relief excellent for side sleeping, with no pressure whatsoever mounting in my shoulders and hips. Stomach sleepers will need something firmer for more back support, and hot sleepers should look elsewhere for effective cooling. However, couples will detect minimal motion transfer from a restless co-sleeper, and strong edges mean you'll sleep securely. Sure, there are much cheaper mattresses out there that offer better value for money, but the CopperFlex Essential is still worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a super-comfortable mid-market bed.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

We conduct seven robust tests in our lab to capture objective data on the four areas of a mattress that most affect your sleep comfort: pressure relief, temperature regulation, motion isolation and edge support. We also sleep on a mattress for at least three weeks before subjectively rating it. This data is fed into a scoring system, along with feedback captured by our testing panel, to create an overall score. Read our full mattress methodology.

When Brooklyn Bedding's most affordable mattress, the Dreamfoam Essential, was discontinued, it was swiftly replaced by the CopperFlex Essential Mattress. While both models sport a navy-and-grey appearance, come in multiple height options, and are marketed as entry-level, affordable beds, there is one key difference: the addition of copper-infused gel.

With the addition of copper-infused memory foam, the CopperFlex Essential dovetails into Brooklyn Bedding's CopperFlex collection, a cooling line-up of beds that includes the CopperFlex Pro Hybrid Mattress (which rivals some of the year's best mattresses thanks to its luxurious comfort). The CopperFlex Essential is also a mid-range bed, but at the lower end of the spectrum, usually sold for under $600 in a queen.

But while the CopperFlex Essential, like the Dreamfoam, is billed as a budget-friendly, no-frills alternative to the brand's more premium beds, its price still isn't low enough to fit into the budget tier.

So, when compared with the best cheap mattresses out there, including the Siena Signature Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Mattress, does the CopperFlex Essential offer good value for money? And does its addition of cooling copper gel mean it's the right fit for hot sleepers?

To find out, we vigorously tested a full-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential Mattress in our sleep lab and slept on it at home for three weeks. Here are our honest thoughts...

It's easy to tell when you're getting a good deal at Brooklyn Bedding, as the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales are split into two discounts: a regular 25% discount and a holiday-related 30% off sale. If you see a 25% discount on the CopperFlex Essential, then you're looking at the standard price (it's never sold at MSRP).

If there's a 30% off sale, however, then that means you're getting a fantastic discount. This 30% discount typically coincides with the biggest holidays and sale events, including the Black Friday mattress sales, the Cyber Monday mattress sales, and the Presidents' Day mattress sales. This is brand's biggest price drop, and the only time it's ever been topped was a 32% discount during the Labor Day mattress sales in fall 2025.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So, how much is the CopperFlex Essential when these discounts are applied? The price of the CopperFlex Essential varies depending on the height you choose. For the 10" model (which is the model I tested for this review), a queen size is $699 at MSRP and $524.25 with the regular 25% off deal. During 30% off sale, a queen-sized 10" CopperFlex Essential drops down to $489.30.

We define a "budget" or "cheap" mattress as one that's regularly under $400 in a queen, which means that the CopperFlex Essential isn't in the budget price tier (despite being marketed as a budget-friendly option). Instead, it sits in the lower mid-range price tier, along with mattresses such as the Nectar Classic and Bear Original.

The CopperFlex Essential is also a cheaper alternative to mattresses found at the more expensive end of the mid-range tier, such as the Nectar Premier and the Leesa Original (both typically $999 for a queen).

That said, there are plenty of mattresses out there with a similar, if not better, construction. The top-rated 10" Siena Signature Memory Foam Mattress, now $329 in a queen at Siena Sleep is a prime example, as is the cooling 12" CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress, which is regularly $399.99 in a queen at SweetNight.

However, one department where the CopperFlex Essential stands out is its generous benefits, including a free shipping, a 365-night sleep trial, and a lifetime warranty. The only downside is that returns come with a fee of $99.

Thanks to a regular 25% off sale, a queen 10" CopperFlex Essential is always under $600. However, 30% discounts during the biggest mattress sales of the year take a queen 10" model down to $489.30. Whether you buy it for 25% off or 30%, you always get generous benefits, including a 365-night sleep trial and a lifetime warranty (shame about the returns fee, though).

The design of the CopperFlex Essential varies (but not hugely) depending on the height option you choose, with the shortest height (6") containing only two layers with the thicker models (12" and 14") contain four layers.

While the 6" and 8" models are the cheapest, they are not thick enough for most adult sleepers and should only be used as a temporary bed (such as for guests, RVs, and growing children). That's why I opted to test the 10" model, as mattress thickness should be at least 10" to support most adults and sleep styles.

However, all height options have a fiberglass-free all-foam build that features a "Nano Stain Terminator Protector" cover (which safeguards against stains and spills) and a top layer of memory foam infused with antimicrobial copper.

The 10" model I tested features a 1" comfort layer of copper-infused memory foam on top and a durable 5" base layer for stabilizing support at the bottom. In between the comfort and base layer, a 4" transition layer acts as a buffer between the softer and firmer materials for balanced support.

For full context, I'm a side and back sleeper weighing under 130lbs, so I need a mattress that's supportive but has enough softness to soothe my side-sleeper pressure points (namely, my hips and shoulders).

The CopperFlex Essential is not the first all-foam mattress I've tested, as I've also written full reviews for the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress and the SweetNight CoolNest Memory Foam Mattress. Both impressed me with their body-contouring comfort and support, but the former did trap some body heat (which is far from atypical for all-foam beds).

So, on the one hand, I was looking forward to testing a memory foam bed, as I know they can make the best mattresses for side sleepers, but I also didn't want to put up with any heat build-up (the testing period coincided with an unseasonably warm fall).

While the CopperFlex Essential didn't deliver the cooling prowess of the SweetNight CoolNest or the universal support of the EGOHOME Black, it still kept this side sleeper comfortable.

Let's see why I recommend the CopperFlex Essential to side sleepers and how it scored in other areas...

Temperature regulation refers to how well a mattress maintains a comfortable sleep temperature and prevents body heat retention. It's a key testing area, as a mattress that doesn't regulate temperature well can lead to night sweats and 3 a.m. wake ups.

While the best cooling mattresses feature top-of-line cooling tech to regulate temperature, most conventional mattresses today feature some degree of thermal regulation.

The CopperFlex Essential is definitely not a dedicated cooling model (and it isn't marketed as one), and the only form of temperature regulation it has is the addition of heat-dispersing copper. That being said, the Siena Signature features very little cooling materials (just a breathable cover) and it performed incredibly well in our temperature tests.

To test how well the CopperFlex Essential regulates temperature, we used a thermal imaging camera to measure how much of my body heat the mattress absorbs and dissipates. To do this I laid on the CopperFlex mattress for 15 minutes while the temperature of the bed was recorded every minute using a thermal imaging camera.

At its hottest point, we observed a maximum temperature increase (MTI) of 11.1°F — that means it was over 11.1°F warmer than before I laid down on the mattress. We generally rate an MTI over 9°F as "poor" and a 1 out of 5. This result was unsurprising, as the CopperFlex Essential isn't a cooling mattress.

That said, the all-foam Siena Signature had an MTI of 9.8°F, despite possessing no specialist cooling materials. Meanwhile, the mid-range all-foam Nectar Premier had an MTI of 8.1 9°F.

I also know from testing the SweetNight CoolNest (which is a dedicated cooling model) that MTI isn't always the best indicator of cooling ability. Despite being a cooling mattress, the CoolNest actually had a much higher MTI of 15.2°F, but redeemed itself through an ultra-fast cooling rate (CR)

The CR refers to how well a mattress dissipates heat during the first five minutes after the MTI. In the CopperFlex's case, the bed shed my body heat at a rate of 1.32°F per minute, a rapid cooling rate considered to "best in class".

The lower the maximum temperature increase (MTI) and the faster the cooling rate, the cooler you'll sleep.

It wasn't the fastest cooling rate displayed by a memory foam mattress (that distinction goes to the SweetNight CoolNest and the Siena Signature, which had a rapid cooling rate of 1.52°F per minute), but it's still relatively fast when you consider that the Nectar Premier dissipated heat at 0.9°F per minute.

15 minutes after I left the mattress, the CopperFlex Essential still hadn't returned to its baseline temperature. However, I should point out that none of its all-foam rivals did either.

In fact, when comparing the way the CopperFlex regulates heat versus its rivals, I was struck by how similarly it performed to the Leesa Original Mattress (usually between $999 and $1,100 for a queen). Both had an MTI of just over 11°F and had an identical rapid cooling rate 1.32°F per minute, which was surprising as Leesa refers to the Original as a "cooling memory foam mattress".

Based on the thermal imaging camera tests alone, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential an objective temperature control score of 3.8 out of 5.

How effectively the CopperFlex Essential absorbed, managed and dissipated heat compared to its closest rivals

In addition to the objective thermal imaging camera tests, we also conduct subjective tests to see how I (and the wider testing panel) perceive the mattress's sleep temperature.

Our subjective feedback was slightly lower than the objective results, with our testing panel awarding a score of 3 out of 5. This score means the mattress offers generally good thermal comfort, but felt mostly neutral with some heat build-up.

I slept on the CopperFlex Essential for three weeks during an unseasonably warm fall in a bedroom with no AC, and while I wouldn't say I overheated or experienced night sweats, I did feel some patches of heat build-up every now and again. I never experienced this while testing the SweetNight CoolNest during the sweltering summer months.

When you're sleeping on a mattress, certain body parts will come into contact with its surface, creating pressure. These body parts are known as pressure points (for example, pressure points when side sleeping include the hips and shoulders), and the way a mattress cushions and supports these pressure points is known as pressure relief.

While each height option comes with a different feel — mattress thickness as a big impact on firmness — Brooklyn Bedding recommends the 10" version I tested to combination back, side, and stomach sleepers.

During our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I agreed that the CopperFlex suits side sleeping the most, as it cushions the hips and shoulders. We also think it could suit some back sleepers, too, even if it doesn't offer the best lumbar support.

I felt I was the ideal candidate to test the mattress, as I'm a combo side and back sleeper. From the first night, I felt ample cushioning when sleeping on my side, especially in the shoulder region. In fact, I found the CopperFlex to be one of the softest mattresses I've ever tested — and I've tested the ultra-plush Helix Sunset Luxe.

Do I think it's one of the best mattresses for back sleepers? No, but I still felt supported when sleeping on my back, and I didn't wake up with lower back pain. Overall, if you're a side sleeper, or predominantly a side sleeper who also sleeps on your back from time to time, then I recommend the CopperFlex Essential.

The deeper the indentation and faster the response time, the better the ability of a mattress to relieve pressure

A mentioned above, Brooklyn Bedding also recommends the CopperFlex Essential to stomach sleepers. For stomach-sleeping tester Ruth Jones, the CopperFlex Essential did cause some lower back strain when lying on her front, and she warned that back sleepers could feel some lower back pressure.

"When back sleeping, I could feel strain on my core," Jones told me.

However, she agreed that its gentle contouring makes the CopperFlex Essential a top pick for side sleepers.

"Side sleeping was far and away the most comfortable position to lie in," she said. "I wasn’t expecting this as the mattress didn’t initially appear to have much contouring but it was soft at the shoulders and hips which meant no pressure build up."

Thanks to its comfort for side sleepers, we awarded the CopperFlex a subjective pressure relief score of 4 out of 5 ("Very Good").

We also performed objective pressure relief tests using a 25kg weight. We placed the weight at the hip and shoulder areas of the mattress, and then measured how deep the weight sank and how quickly the mattress bounced back when the weight was removed.

The CopperFlex had an average Indentation Depth (ID) of 3.6" and Recovery Time (RT), of 2.25 seconds, achieving an objective pressure relief score of 3.4 out of 5, which is a "Good" objective final rating. The weight test results indicate that the CopperFlex is a responsive bed (I agree, as I found it easy to move around on) but I was surprised that the weights didn't sink further on what I perceive as a cushioning bed.

Even more surprising is that Siena Memory Foam had a higher ID of 3.63", despite being a firm bed that is recommended to anyone but side sleepers. The CopperFlex's RT, on the other hand, was one of the quickest. A quick RT is especially important in a memory foam mattress, as they can be notorious for their "quicksand" sinkage.

Combining subjective and objective feedback, we awarded the CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief a score of 3.76 out of 5, indicating a "Strong Performance".

We rate a mattress's firmness on a standardized scale of one to 10, with 10 being the firmest and 1 being the softest. We don't use any objective tests to measure firmness, as this key area is highly subjective and is dependent on body weight, sleep position, and personal preference.

To get a good idea of the CopperFlex's firmness level, I asked each member of our diverse testing panel to rank the firmness of the CoolNest on a scale of one to 10. I then created a collective rating based on everyone's feedback.

The Brooklyn Bedding calls the firmness of the CopperFlex Essential "medium-firm", which indicates a score of 6-7 out of 10 on the standardized scale. As a team, we mostly agreed with the brand's rating, and awarded the CopperFlex Essential a 6 out of 10 on the firmness scale.

Motion isolation refers to a mattress's ability to prevent a co-sleeper's movements from traveling to your side of the bed and waking you up. Its especially important for couples, co-sleeping families, and anyone who shares a bed with their pets.

Memory foam mattresses tend to be better at absorbing motion than other mattress types, such as innerspring and hybrid mattresses, as they contain dense, slow-moving foams and no springs or coils.

To see how well the CopperFlex Essential isolates motion, we conducted an objective slam ball test and a subjective co-sleeper test.

In our subjective tests, my fellow testers and I evaluated the impact of each other's movements by manually performing motions classed as low, moderate and high force to replicate real-life co-sleeping scenarios.

The faster the decay rate, the better the mattress is at reducing motion transfer (which means you'll be disturbed less by a restless co-sleeper)

During the subjective tests, I felt the high-force movements of my fellow tester, but I would not say the high-force movements were as disruptive as they've been on other mattresses I’ve tested.

My fellow testers were also impressed with the perceived motion isolation, with one panelist saying they could hardly feel the low-force movements. "There was some small motion transfer when the tester moved but I would have slept right through it and it wouldn’t have bothered me as I was falling asleep," they said.

Overall, the CopperFlex Essential earned a subjective score of 3.75 out of 5 for motion isolation.

For for our objective lab-based tests, we dropped a 5kg slam ball on one side of the CopperFlex Essential and measured its impact absorption via an accelerometer on the other. The initial impact average (IIA) was 14.569, which is relatively high when compared to Siena's IIA of 5.527 m/s2 and the Nectar Premier's IIA of 7.961.

However, the CopperFlex Essential redeemed itself with a short decay rate (MDS). So, while the IIA was sizeable, its motion transfer only lasted for 1.72 seconds on average. While not as quick as the Leesa Original's 1.116 second MDS, it still shows that the CopperFlex is adept at deadening the slam ball's motion.

Overall, we rate the CopperFlex's motion isolation as "Strong", with an overall motion isolation score of 3.5. This means that, while you'll feel more moderate and high-force movements, they won't last long enough to cause too much disruption.

Edge support refers to how sturdy the edges of your mattress are, with strong edge support indicating that the sides and foot of the bed will make you feel supported when sitting, sleeping, or getting in and out of bed.

To test the CopperFlex's edge support, we placed a 25kg weight 3" away from the edge of the mattress and measured how far it sank.

After five minutes, the average indentation of the weight was 5.25", which we rate as "strong." The sinkage at the foot of the bed was a little deeper than at the sides of the bed, but we should point out that the edge support at the foot of the bed will only affect sitting rather than sleeping.

To measure the available sleep space, we also performed a roll-off test. For this, our reviewer lies near the edge of the bed and another tester records how close they get to the edge before they feel unstable and are going to roll off. The CopperFlex Essential has a roll-off distance (ROD) of 0.5", a measurement which gets a score of 5 out of 5 as it indicates that most of the mattress can be used for sleeping.

Combing the weight and roll-off test scores, the overall edge support score of the CopperFlex Essential is 4 out of 5, which we rate as "Very Good".

Less compression means better support for sleeping close to the edge or climbing in and out of bed

On the brand's website, the CopperFlex Essential has an overall user score of 4.6 out of 5 from over 800 reviews, which is a pretty glowing score.

Five-star reviews praise how comfortable the mattress is, which many customers buying it for their RVs (it's one of the rare mattress that come in a range of RV sizes). As for negative reviews (which are in the minority) customers criticize the mattress for not being as firm as they expected.

In terms of Brooklyn Bedding's trustworthiness, you can look on review platform TrustPilot website for customer feedback. At the time of writing, the brand has an overall "Excellent" rating of 4.6 out of 5 stars from a total of 210 reviews.

Let me start by saying that there are cheaper memory foam mattress out there that offer better value for money than the CopperFlex Essential. That being said, I would definitely recommend this body-contouring mattress to a certain group: side sleepers.

The CopperFlex Essential's pressure relief, is a standout feature that makes this all-foam bed a top pick for anyone who sleeps on their side.

I tend to perceive mattresses as being firmer than my fellow testers do, and I often require good mattress break-in period to feel comfortable. However, I felt well-cushioned from night one on the CopperFlex Essential, and felt zero pressure build up in my shoulders.

Edge support is good, too, and I always felt secure even when sleeping close to the edge. For couples, motion transfer from a restless partner shouldn't be an issue, and the sleep temperature should remain neutral enough for the average person.

That said, hot sleepers will need to look at a model with more cooling ability, such as the SweetNight CoolNest or the Siena Siena Signature, which are both cheaper than the lower mid-range CopperFlex Essential. I wouldn't recommend this soft mattress to stomach sleepers wither, as the lack of firmness won't keep their hips and lower back supported.

However, I do think this is a mid-range mattress worth considering if you're a side sleeper looking for a mid-market bed for your home, guest room, or even your RV.

Like the CopperFlex Essential, the EGOHOME Black 12" Memory Foam Mattress is a conventional all-foam bed designed for medium-firm comfort. However, I found it to be much more supportive than the CopperFlex Essential, and I slept comfortably on it in all sleep positions. Plus, it's always under $400 for a queen.

If you're looking for an affordable memory foam bed, but the CoolNest seems a little too soft for your sleep position, check out the Siena Memory Foam Mattress as a firmer (and cheaper) alternative. It also regulates temperature surprisingly well, but side sleepers will find it way too hard.

If you want something that sleeps cooler than the CopperFlex, check out this cooling model from SweetNight. The SweetNight CoolNest is one of those rare budget mattresses (always under $400 for a queen) equipped with specialist cooling tech.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

#3443. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3441. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3439. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3436. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

#3435. Steel Guitars by the Dozen: A Cultish Concert Pays Tribute to the Most Country Instrument of All

A certain kind of joy permeated the Ryman Auditorium in Nashville last week — a specific, cultish, even nerdy joy — as thousands of steel guitar enthusiasts gathered for a celebration of the instrument dubbed the “Sho-Bud Showcase Live.” (And I, myself a pedal steel player, was one of them.)

Presented by Sho-Bud, the pedal steel manufacturer synonymous with country music and Nashville, the evening assembled expert steel players from across genres to show just what the 10-stringed contraption can do. Now, as the “Mother Church of Country Music,” the Ryman has seen its fair share of pedal-steel guitars in its storied history, but nothing like the galaxy of steels that graced the stage on this night.

But first, a little back story for the uninitiated. Sho-Bud steel guitars were the brainchild of two legends of the instrument, Shot Jackson and Buddy Emmons (see what they did there?), and became the marquee brand during the 1960s and Seventies. In fact, the Sho-Bud shop occupied what is now Robert’s Western World, Nashville’s revered honky-tonk, on Broadway decades ago. But when guitar manufacturer Gretsch acquired the brand in 1979, production trailed off. Enter Dawn and Will Jackson, grandchildren of Shot, who re-acquired Sho-Bud in 2024 and restarted production. A steel guitar comeback was underway.

Which brings us to “Sho-Bud Showcase Live,” a four-hour long representation of the brand’s revival. Billed as a benefit for causes including the Peter Frampton Myotosis Foundation and the Cerebral Palsy Foundation, the event was as shiny with stars as the namesake steel. Guitar heroes like Slash loomed in the wings, Don Felder materialized to play the Eagles’ “Take It Easy,” and Marcus King shredded some bluesy rock solos.

But this was a night for steel players, and that meant headliner Lloyd Green (over 30,000 studio recordings to his credit, including the Byrds’ Sweetheart of the Rodeo) had to be in the house. Junior Brown picked at his Guit-Steel too, and Dan Dugmore (who’s played for Linda Ronstadt and literally everyone) and Grammy winner Robert Randolph also brought the steel power. There were droves of the instrument’s hottest pickers in the audience as well: Travis Toy (Luke Bryan), Mike Daly (Hank Williams Jr.), and Read Connolly (Zach Bryan), just to name a few. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Yet even with dozens of steel guitars inside the Ryman, the sound didn’t remain the same — steel guitar is not a one-note instrument. Green and Andrea Whitt especially proved that by delivering a beautiful instrumental performance of Elliott Smith’s “Waltz #2.” King highlighted the steel’s use in Southern rock, and his own pedal steel prowess, by re-creating Marshall Tucker Band’s “Fire on the Mountain.” And Randolph, introduced as “The Jimi Hendrix of Pedal Steel,” showed off the steel’s rock edge, roaring through a wah-wah-heavy ”Voodoo Chile” that included his signature stage move: tilting the steel on its side. Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Marty Erlichman, Barbra Streisand’s Manager Since the 1960s, Dead at 97 Martha Stewart ‘Distressed’ by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume

But the night belonged to Green — or perhaps should have. The 89-year-old “Mr. Nashville Sound” appeared onstage and took a seat behind the very first Lloyd Green model Sho-Bud. Opposite him was Slash, sitting behind the very first new Lloyd Green model. The Guns N’ Roses guitarist picked out the intro to that old steel guitar chestnut, “Sweet Child O’ Mine,” and the audience dutifully began filming the moment on their phones. Green added his own parts here and there, but both he and Slash were in danger of being drowned out by the backing band’s rhythm guitar.

It was a metaphor: The pedal steel has often taken a backseat to the electric guitar. But at least on this evening, Sho-Bud gave the most country instrument of all its due.
