#3434. Antonin Baudry & Simon Abkarian Talk French Box Office Hit ‘De Gaulle’: “The National Icon Did Not Exist In 1940”

Charles de Gaulle is arguably one of the most iconic figures in French history but for filmmaker Antonin Baudry, the story of how the wartime leader came to embody the French Resistance during World War II had largely been overlooked by filmmakers. With De Gaulle: Resistance and Liberty, an ambitious two-part historical epic, Baudry looked to revisit the extraordinary journey of a relatively obscure general who refused to accept France’s surrender to Nazi Germany in 1940.

The films will screen at The American French Film Festival in L.A. this year, where both instalments will be presented back-to-back on November 7 at the DGA Theater Complex. It will mark the U.S. premiere of the second part of the film, De Gaulle: Liberty, which will then be followed by a conversation with Baudry and actor Simon Abkarian who stars as De Gaulle in the film. Samuel Goldwyn Films is releasing the title in North America. Related Stories Festivals The American French Film Festival At 30: Building Bridges Between French Cinema & Hollywood Festivals 'Fjord', 'All Of A Sudden', 'Minotaur' & 'Coward' Among Titles Set For 30th Edition Of The American French Film Festival In L.A.

The $84M Pathé production, which was more than five years in the making, grossed more than $50M in France since its summer release, making it one of the year’s biggest box office hits in the country. The story opens in June 1940, as France collapses and signs the armistice and De Gaulle, a then little-known general, flees to London with one irrational conviction that the battle for France is neither over nor lost. Watch on Deadline

“The almost unbelievable story of the Free French, spanning from London to Africa to occupied France to the U.S., had never been shown in a film,” Baudry tells Deadline. “This story is epic, chivalric, tragic – and tragically comical. And, unlike Churchill, De Gaulle was almost a perfect unknown in film theaters.”

Baudry, a former French diplomat who made his directorial debut with submarine thriller Wolf’s Call, tapped into his past profession for the script, which he co-wrote with Bérénice Vila.

“The film actually doesn’t respect the codes of a biopic,” he says. “It all takes place in 1940 to 1942 – no flashbacks. There are three predominant characters: de Gaulle, [Winston] Churchill and Fernand [Bonnier de la Chapelle]. It goes from small bathtubs to epic battles, with Volker Bertelmann’s elegant, powerful music. We are very far from a biopic.”

His ambition, he adds, was straightforward: “I wanted to make a film I would love to see at any stage of my life.”

Baudry was keen to capture de Gaulle as the isolated and “bizarre” individual rather than the polished national icon from the history books. “The national icon did not exist in 1940,” he says. “Therefore, it shouldn’t exist in the film: that was simple. We remained loyal to the descriptions made by the people who met him in 1940 and to what they wrote in their journals. All of them were stunned by how bizarre the man was, whether they agreed with him or not.”

Baudry points out that at this point in history, de Gaulle was almost entirely alone in his conviction of refusing to surrender and this quality of isolation was something that Abkarian found fascinating when deciding to take on the lead role.

“I didn’t know how alone he was,” says Abkarian. “France had capitulated in front of the Nazi German army, and I didn’t know how isolated he was. I didn’t know he was condemned to death by the French Vichy army, and his nationality was taken away from him.”

He was equally struck by de Gaulle’s command of language and intellectual ambition, describing the general as a deeply educated man whose words were inseparable from his political vision.

“He spent his life eating paper and drinking ink,” says Abkarian. “His language was very clear, just like Churchill was at the time. They were educated and the language they had was the messenger for their vision.”

When researching his character, Abkarian admits that his main tool beyond the script was his own imagination. While he had read letters about people who had met de Gaulle and had described him as someone who is “very strange”, Abkarian built on that.

“He had his own theatrics in life, so the goal was not naturalism or realism,” he says. “He was building his own persona, so I had to play someone who plays that.”

In advance of the film’s U.S. bow on November 6 (the second instalment will launch December 4), Abkarian is hopeful that it will resonate with American audiences in that it’s a film that explores the moral choices made by individuals at moments when the odds appear overwhelming. He sees it as a story that explores the values of “courage, honor and resistance.”

“I think we have lost our moral compass, and this kind of film reestablishes the compass of morality, courage and honor,” he says. “People don’t pay attention to honor anymore and we desperately need that now.”

When pressed about what he hopes American audiences will take away from De Gaulle, Baudry is more straightforward: “Hope.”

The American French Film Festival in L.A. takes place November 3-8, 2026.

#3433. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to yesterday's Wordle.

#3431. You Can Preorder XReal's First Wired XR Glasses

The VR headset may be becoming a thing of the past. At Google's Android Developer Summit this morning, XReal officially debuted XReal Aura XR glasses, smart glasses with full XR capability. They're powered by Android XR and run on a Snapdragon Reality Elite-powered puck, with Xreal's X1S Chip in the glasses themselves. The result: Aura packs a 70° field of view in a pair of glasses that weigh less than 95 grams.

Customers in the United States, Canada, Japan, and South Korea can order XReal Aura on XReal's site starting today, and they're expected to begin shipping in mid-November. The limited-time launch price is $1,099 for the 12GB + 256GB configuration and $1,299 for the 16GB + 512GB configuration, $180 and $200 less, respectively, than XReal announced earlier this month. The lower prices will be available until the end of the year.

If the claim of mixed reality in a pair of sunglasses seems dubious, I tried them out a few months ago, and they are exactly that.

Instead of an enclosed headset, XReal Aura projects digital content on transparent lenses so you can be present in the real world while also in the digital world. Unlike "traditional" virtual reality headsets, the Aura's batteries and main compute are in a wired puck/controller you can slip into your pocket. That keeps the weight down and makes them comfortable enough to wear for longer periods. Because it's built on Android XR, users will have access to millions of 2D and 3D Android apps right out of the box.

If you want to go beyond Android, you can plug a USB-C-compatible computer or gaming console into Aura, and use that device in the same virtual space as native Android XR apps.

XReal Aura is launching with a library of over 150 "made for XR" apps as well, including games like Nevatars, designed by Andy Serkis, Fallout: Factions, a dice-based head-to-head game in the Fallout universe, and Landing Party, "the world's first outdoor roleplaying video game." There will also be companion apps for the NBA, NASCAR, and the San Francisco Ballet Company’s The Nutcracker. In terms of productivity, ShapexXR, a platform for software developer collaboration, is making its debut on Android XR, and you'll be able to use apps like Frontline.io for job training and assistance, and Plynk Spatial for stock research and trading.

If you want to get down to the nitty-gritty, here are the Aura's specs:

Split-compute architecture with compact compute puck

Wired Mirroring for laptops and compatible handheld gaming devices

USB-C connectivity using a standard connection

Electrochromic dimming for more immersive viewing

Support for voice, hand, keyboard, trackpad, and game controller input

#3430. Zoe Kazan’s ‘East Of Eden’ Adaptation Manifests Audience Growth Comparable To ‘Adolescence’ — Here’s How It Happened

EXCLUSIVE: Zoe Kazan‘s adaptation of John Steinbeck’s classic American novel East of Eden is slowly but surely staking its claim on Netflix.

The series has now amassed 4.4x its debut-week views, Deadline can reveal exclusively, growing from 6.5 million views in Week 1 to a cumulative 28.9 million views in Week 4.

Per Netflix, only Adolescence has a higher 4-week multiple (4.7x) among the 11 limited series since 2025 that charted in the English-language Top 10 all four weeks. This includes comparable limited series and adaptation titles such as His & Hers, Lord of the Flies, I Will Find You, Vladimir, and Death by Lightning. Related Stories Acquisitions Netflix Acquires Worldwide On Joel Coen's 'Jack Of Spades' For Fall 2027 Theatrical Release News Druski Strikes Deal With Netflix Ahead Of 'Collect & Praise' Launch

“I think we have this collective misconception that ‘great books’ are boring and dusty, like eating our spinach. But most books that we consider to be classics have stood the test of time for a reason–because they are gripping, emotional, and full of the wild drama of being human. One of my aims in making this show was to lower the barrier to entry a little, to allow more people to feel that East of Eden could hold something powerful specifically for them,” Kazan tells Deadline. Watch on Deadline

That said, she acknowledges that regardless of the care that went into crafting the series, “there’s no guarantee that people will actually watch.”

East of Eden debuted on October 1 and found its way to the top of the English-language charts that week with just four days of availability. It was a promising if soft start for the series, given that its 6.5 million views made it the lowest No. 1 opening since the end of March. That said, it has steadily continued to pique curiosity, hitting the Top 10 in 86 countries. As of Week 4, it holds onto the No. 6 spot on the Top 10 with 3.6 million views.

That is not too shabby for a period drama adapted from a 74-year-old novel. Speaking of, the Netflix adaptation has also fueled interest in Steinbeck’s original work. Per Penguin Classics, book sales jumped nearly 200% across all formats, and the publisher went back to press 25 times this year to keep up with the physical demand.

The book reached No. 1 on Amazon’s Best Sellers list and No. 21 on USA Today’s Best Sellers list, and Spotify first-time audiobook listens are up 156%.

“Given how beloved and timeless these classics are, the bar is high when considering an adaptation. For me, it starts with a creator who has a singular point of view and a genuine, personal connection to the material,” says Jinny Howe, head of UCAN scripted series at the streamer. “For East of Eden, that creator is Zoe.”

Kazan is considered an emerging voice, but this isn’t her first rodeo. Prior to East of Eden, she wrote two films that were independently produced, Wildlife and Ruby Sparks, and four plays. Still, it’s somewhat of a risk to hand the reins on an adaptation of this magnitude over to someone with less experience.

Adds Howe: “Zoe has lived with this novel her whole life, and she came in with a clear, unapologetic point of view on what the story needed to be today. She’s always envisioned Cathy at the center of this in a way that readers and viewers of the film haven’t been able to access and experience before, and that made this classic all of a sudden feel thrilling and revelatory. She was so clear-eyed and passionate about expanding upon Lee’s story in the series, and it’s been incredible to see how Hoon Lee’s powerful performance as the moral compass of the family has been embraced by audiences around the world.”

Netflix continues to bet on Kazan, who is now adapting Larry McMurtry’s classic Lonesome Dove novel as a series along with Jeb Stuart, her co-showrunner on East of Eden.

In explaining her philosophy for adapting such classic literature, particularly in this day and age as attention spans are waning and short-form content is all the rage, Kazan says she holds onto a piece of advice given to her by Wildlife author Richard Ford while she and her partner Paul Dano were adapting that novel.

“[He] told us, ‘My book is my book, and your movie will be your movie.’ I think he was giving us permission to follow our creative impulses, wherever they might take us. The book exists, and therefore doesn’t need to be duplicated; it can’t be, really, since the story is being expressed through a completely different medium,” she explains, citing some of her favorite adaptations that she thinks successfully thread the needle of loyalty to the source material and creative freedom like The Ice Storm, The English Patient, Romeo + Juliet, Clueless, Wonder Boys, Howards End, Ghost World, The Sweet Hereafter.

“And that’s just, like, some of the best of the 1990s/2000s,” she says. “I could go on. I love the experience of encountering material I’ve read before, through someone else’s lens, and seeing something new in it.”

East of Eden has so far been praised by critics and audiences, and even the chronically online crowd is taking note. Several social trends have taken hold, including audiences recreating their favorite Cathy Ames looks for Halloween on TikTok and the series audio trending on Instagram Reels.

As for what to expect from Netflix in light of this momentum, Howe says not much has changed.

“What I can tell you is that our philosophy remains the same. We’ll continue to back distinctive storytellers with a compelling vision and something to say, whether the source material is a novel published last year or one written a century ago,” she tells Deadline. “You’ll see that reflected in Pride and Prejudice this December and The Age of Innocence next year, each with its own distinct voice and interpretation of stories we all know and love. While we can’t predict how any of these projects will resonate with audiences, we’re proud of the approach and the creative ambition behind it.”

#3428. As Roku’s Merger With Fox Clears More Hurdles, Streaming Provider Delivers Strong Q3 Results

As its pending $22 billion merger with Fox Corp. inches continues to wind its way through the regulatory process, Roku delivered strong third-quarter results Monday.

Total revenue in the July-to-September period surged 24% from the prior-year period to hit $1.5 billion, with earnings per share zooming to $1.20 from 16 cents in the same frame of 2025. Both metrics were substantially better than Wall Street analysts’ consensus forecast.

When Fox reported its results earlier in the day, CEO Lachlan Murdoch said the merger has cleared all major regulatory hurdles outside the U.S. and also has received shareholder approval. The Department of Justice’s antitrust division is currently reviewing the transaction, which is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch said on the Fox earnings call, adding that the company’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Watch on Deadline

Streaming hours on Roku TVs and connected devices climbed 9% to 39.9 billion, while advertising, subscription and platform revenue all jumped more than 20%. Ad revenue increased 23% to $727.4 million.

“Similar to Q2, political advertising on the Roku platform in Q3 exceeded the comparable quarter from the 2024 U.S. presidential election cycle,” the company wrote in its shareholder letter. “The Media & Entertainment vertical also continued to strengthen, and Q3 was the highest YoY revenue growth in four years as media companies invested on the Roku platform to promote their content and services.”

About 80% of all ads during the quarter were sold via programmatic systems, which involve an automated process rather than traditional campaign planning, the letter also noted.

While devices generate only a minority share of total revenue (up 33% in the quarter to $194 million), the makeup of the segment has shifted a bit. Three years into its effort to make its own TV sets as opposed to purely licensing its user interface to third parties, Roku said its own TVs now account for nearly 8% of all U.S. TV sales by volume.

Vizio, a smart-TV maker and longtime Roku rival, is now owned by Walmart and has sought to leverage its advantage at retail with its streaming advertisers.

#3426. Your Discord Messages Will Soon Be Discoverable on Google Search, but You Can Opt Out

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are a member of a large public Discord, your posts may soon be visible in Google Search—even to those without a Discord account. Starting in November, Discord's Discoverable Servers will have server web pages that show up in web search results, including summaries and messages from public channels. While messages won't be tied to your username or avatar, you may still want to opt out.

This change applies to Discoverable Servers on Discord, which are public spaces that have at least 1,000 members. There's no invite link, so anyone can find and join them as long as they have a Discord account. (Other servers on Discord are either invite-only Community Servers for larger groups or Friend Servers, which are small, private spaces.)

On Nov. 16, Discord is launching server web pages for Discoverable Servers, which will display discussion summaries from public channels as well as some individual messages. By mid-December, these pages may appear in search results. While these servers have always been fairly easy to access since they are public, this removes the requirement to sign up for Discord and join servers in order to view them.

In its announcement detailing the change, Discord notes that private servers and DMs will remain private. Plus, server admins can choose which channels are included in web search or opt them out entirely.

Messages you send before mid-December won't be included in search regardless of your setting preferences. However, if you leave this enabled and decide to turn it off later, anything you send between mid-December and disabling the setting will stay up unless you delete the message from Discord entirely.

#3424. Dane Cook’s Brother Robbed Him Blind. Now He’s Rebuilding His Life — And Gunning for a Comeback

Comedian Dane Cook’s house sits perched above Hollywood like a fortress, or a prison. A $7 million modernist hillside oasis with a baby-blue pool and a view stretching halfway across the Pacific, the house is Cook’s prized possession. He bought it back in 2008, in the boom years, when he was at the height of his career: selling out arenas, breaking chart records — and still a few months away from learning that his brother had stolen nearly every cent he’d earned. But we’ll get to that.

If “Dane Cook” is a name you haven’t thought about for a couple of decades, you wouldn’t be alone. For a period in the mid-2000s, Cook was the pinnacle of the comedy world. His résumé is like an aughts time capsule: one of the first comics to predict the power of social media, who harnessed millions of fans via MySpace; headliner of big Hollywood comedies opposite Jessicas Alba and Simpson; star of an HBO documentary series that aired after Entourage. In one 18-month stretch, Cook released an HBO special, dropped the highest-charting comedy album in 28 years (which eventually went double-platinum), hosted Saturday Night Live — twice — and sold out two shows at Madison Square Garden on the same night. “I had a great run,” he says with a grin.

Yet even at his apex, Cook was often the punch line — his very name a synonym for “overrated douchebag hack.” Other comics couldn’t stand him — partly for artistic reasons, and partly because they were jealous of his success. As a performer, he was always more energy than craft — cannonballing around the stage with his spiky hair and pre-distressed jeans, consonants popping like they were on creatine, sprinkling his Seinfeld-style observational bits on parking garages and mini golf with punchlines about blowjobs and tits. (Sample joke: “When you’re with somebody awful — I call that a relationshit!”) And no one could touch him.

Comedian Nikki Glaser was a huge Cook fan who once planned a girls’ trip to Las Vegas in college just to see him perform. “He was the biggest comedian in the world when I was starting out, so his influence was undeniable,” Glaser says. “There are still so many comics today who remind me of Dane, whether or not people remember him for it. He presented like a dumb frat bro, but he would sprinkle in phrases and new groupings of words that illustrated his point almost poetically. His comedy was almost musical — people would put it on at parties to just hang out to. To this day, I don’t know a comedian my friends listen to like we listened to Dane.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

But even as Cook stood astride show business, his life was secretly being dismantled under his feet. What he didn’t know was that his half-brother, Darryl McCauley — who’d served as Cook’s business manager since before he was famous — had been embezzling from him for years, possibly decades. It all came crashing down in 2008, when Cook got suspicious and started asking questions, and McCauley went on the run before being arrested. When the Massachusetts attorney general’s office finished their forensic audit, they put the total theft around $12 million. And that’s just what they could prove. Cook thinks it might be double that.

Cook avoided talking about it in public for years, for a variety of reasons. He was devastated, he was ashamed, he couldn’t figure out how to make it entertaining. But now he has a documentary — Funny Money, streaming on Netflix starting Nov. 6 — that details the whole sordid tale for the first time. “There was a hope and a concern,” Cook says of the film. “The hope was that this was a true-crime story that’s funny. The concern was that I’m a sad clown. I cried more [doing the film] than I did in therapy. So there’s really some anxiety that you see me like this.” Related Content Dane Cook’s Brother Stole $12 Million, Then Disappeared After Prison Release The Best Tech and Home Audio Gifts From Marshall and Google The Wait Is Over: Parke's NYC Mocknecks & Big Apple Merch Are Finally Here Steel Guitars by the Dozen: A Cultish Concert Pays Tribute to the Most Country Instrument of All

Cook, 56, is sitting in his home office, full of platinum records and framed magazine covers — a shrine to his fiveish-year peak. He’s wearing Earth-tone Nikes and a fitted brown polo, his highlighted hair both thicker and more kempt than it used to be. The shelves behind his desk are filled with fun nerd memorabilia, like an Obi-Wan Kenobi toy and a still-unboxed Wolverine.

As a kid, Cook used to spend hours playing with these toys — Stormtroopers battling G.I. Joes, Chewbacca fighting Doctor Doom. “But it was never ‘evil and bad’ for me,” he says. “It was always ‘misunderstood.’” What was Darth Vader’s trauma? What if Cobra Commander just needed a friend? “I was the only person watching Die Hard like: ‘But what happened to Hans?’”

For the past two decades, he’s been trying to figure out the same things about his brother. “Sometimes I sit and wonder, ‘Who is Darryl?’” he says. He shakes his head. “I don’t know.”

COOK GREW UP IN Arlington, Massachusetts, a working-class suburb of Boston. “I was very much a wallflower introvert,” he says. “A lot of anxiety. Mama’s boy.” He had cystic acne that left deep scars on his face. This is why he always moved around so much onstage — what he calls “the whirling-dervish thing.” “I just didn’t want you to look at me,” he says. “If I don’t stay still, then you won’t key in and go, ‘You’re ugly.’”

Darryl was seven years older — his half-brother from his mom’s first marriage. They were never extremely close on account of the age difference, but they did share a bedroom, and they did hang out — playing R.B.I. Baseball on Nintendo, or raking the leaves while the other held the bag. Darryl was a manager at Burger King and hired Cook to work the drive-thru.

To this day, Cook has never had a drink or done a drug in his life. That’s probably because his dad was a violent alcoholic. The house was “a place of mayhem,” he says: shouting matches, wall-shaking fights, and one harrowing incident when he was 14 involving a kitchen knife that ended with his father being arrested and leaving the house. Cook says he was never a target of the abuse per se, so Darryl didn’t protect him. But just his presence helped Cook feel safe. “I remember so many nights, looking over at him as I was going to sleep,” Cook says. “Just happy he was there.”

Not long after his 18th birthday, Cook started doing standup around Boston. From there it was a long slog to overnight success: six years of living at home, doing shitty gigs at laundromats, Chinese restaurants, and open mics. “I’d spend more on gas driving my mom’s 1978 Lincoln to Maine and back than I’d even make,” he says. “A Tuesday night meant hoping you’d get up at Nick’s Comedy Stop next to the Combat Zone, where maybe I can make a couple prostitutes laugh on the way out.” Eventually he got successful enough to move to New York, and later L.A., where he landed such glamorous jobs as half a season on an ABC sitcom starring Betty White and a Dennis Rodman movie that grossed $292,000 worldwide.

Meanwhile, Darryl — who’d dreamed of being a state trooper but failed the test — was working as a corrections officer at Walpole State Prison (now called MCI-Cedar Junction), a maximum-security facility near Boston. (You might know it from The Town.) “It was a scary place,” Cook says. “I hated that he worked there.” He started plotting how to get Darryl out. “I’m incorporated now,” he recalls thinking. “Maybe at some point I can turn this into a regular around-the-clock job for us.” Then a month later, Darryl was viciously attacked by an inmate. “Some old guy put a can of corn niblets in a pillowcase and boom — cracked Darryl’s head open,” says Cook. “I go see him in the hospital. My mom is terrified. We’re all terrified. That’s when I said, ‘I want you to quit and come work for me.’”

In the beginning, Darryl was more like an assistant: paying the car insurance, boxing up CDs to ship out, selling merch at shows. But as the checks started getting more zeros, the job got bigger. Darryl became Cook’s business manager, handling operations at his company, Great Dane Enterprises, complete with a $150,000 salary. Cook says he had no reservations about giving control of his finances to someone relatively unqualified. “I felt like, he’d believed in me,” he says. “We’d gone through a lot of crazy shit together, we got out of that house, we have some normalcy and an income now. We would sit at dinner and be like, ‘This feels good. Cook-McCauley brothers for life.’

“And there was a certain safety,” he says. “Me already seeing some of the piranhas in this town, and the bad language in the contracts, I’m like: ‘But I’ve got my brother looking out for me.’”

Darryl didn’t show Cook his financial statements. Instead he would create Excel spreadsheets with “summaries” of everything going in and out. Cook says he never questioned them. For one thing, he has “dyscalculia,” the numerical version of dyslexia. (“I see numbers and they just spin around.”) Darryl also kept it low-key. “Same pair of dirty sneakers. No frills,” Cook says. “Anytime I would say to him, ‘Is there anything you want or need?’ he was like, ‘No.’” (In hindsight, that’s probably because he was stealing all Cook’s money.)

And ultimately, Cook says, he never really cared about the money. “I just love the game,” he says. “I can’t tell you how many times I’d leave a gig and they’d call me at home and go, ‘You know you forgot your check?’ So no, I didn’t ask. I believed the statements.”

‘FUNNY MONEY’ TAKES A WHILE to get going, with its first third chronicling Cook’s long rise, but when it finally drops into gear, it’s compelling — especially as it catalogues the breadth and depth of Darryl’s deceit. Cook still isn’t sure when it started, but it grew exponentially. In 2004, Darryl was writing himself checks for $22,000 here, $31,000 there. Two years later — Cook’s commercial zenith — Darryl was making deposits as flagrant as $780,000 and $995,000. As Cook’s (legit, later-hired) business manager says in the film: “There wasn’t even an attempt to hide it.”

By the fall of 2008, Cook decided to transfer all his business dealings to a more established firm. The new business manager kept asking Darryl for his files; Darryl kept ducking him. Soon he stopped returning the manager’s calls. Then he stopped returning Cook’s.

In a joke from his 2003 album, Harmful If Swallowed, a girl tells Cook that all men want is sex. Not true, he says: “Any guy here — if they had the choice — would rather be part of a heist.” The Darryl story also ends with a heist — this one in broad daylight.

In December of 2008, McCauley walked into a Bank of America in downtown Boston with a check from Cook’s company made out to himself for $3 million. It also had Cook’s forged signature. Incredibly, the bank cashed the check, and McCauley stuffed the cash into literal duffel bags, which he loaded into a rented Escalade and drove away. A final $3 million fuck-you.

Increasingly frantic that he couldn’t reach Darryl, Cook went to a bank branch near his house. A sympathetic employee pulled up his accounts. One had $110,000 in it. Another was empty.

“I’ve never been in a plane crash,” Cook says. “But I imagine when everything’s rattling, and you start to hear unusual sounds, and things are tearing apart — that’s kind of how I felt. My legs go out from under me. I’m howling with sadness. Because I know my best friend in the world has done this.”

“It was a shattering unlike I ever imagined,” he continues. “I’ve had a couple of bad panic attacks in my life — like, catatonic. Nothing compared to what I felt that day. I could cry right now thinking of it.”

Cook called the cops, who brought in the FBI. Darryl went on the run — a wild sequence in the doc — and was arrested by Massachusetts State Police a few weeks later. His wife, Erika, was also arrested; when police searched the couple’s home near Boston, they found $800,000 in cash stashed in a wall safe. A separate search of their beach house in Maine turned up hundreds of thousands more: bricks of cash in Tupperware tubs of tomato sauce hidden in the freezer; $90,000 in a box of Bagel Bites; $150,000 buried in the dirt of a potted plant.

Investigators later found that the couple had spent $5 million on real estate and investments and $500,000 on jewelry. There were also vacations in Ireland, a time-share in St. Kitts, and his-and-hers Cadillacs, along with $2.7 million in cashier’s checks that were never accounted for. “I think it’s way more than the $12 million,” Cook says today. “I’m thinking $17 to $22 million is really the number.”

McCauley pled guilty to 27 counts of larceny, three counts of forgery and one count of embezzlement. He was sentenced to six years in Walpole — the very same prison where he’d worked as a guard. Cook, meanwhile, was very fucked. Not only was all his money gone. He also owed the IRS for the taxes Darryl hadn’t paid — a staggering $6 million with interest.

What Cook did next was truly impressive. He still had about $300,000 in stocks that Darryl somehow hadn’t touched. He used the money to book himself an arena tour, renting the venues out of his own pocket. “I take the door, they take the food, I sell my merch,” he says. “If I’m renting a $35,000 dollar arena, there’s nights where I’m walking out with $350,000. I was like, ‘I’m gonna go down maybe. But not because of you.’” He spent the next two years crisscrossing the country, playing a hundred-plus shows, often back to back to back. And by the end, “I’d made everything back that they told me he took.”

That was the financial hole. The emotional hole took much longer.

“The humiliation was way more damaging than the theft,” says Cook. “All my childhood stuff I thought I’d overcome, all the insecurity that was still there but shielded by success, all the self-loathing I felt as a kid — it all came back. I’m on the school playground that I thought I got away from, and everyone’s looking at me going, ‘This fucking idiot. What a moron.’”

He couldn’t write any jokes or get onstage for a year. “I was bad, man. The ruminating was really bad. All through the night. I was trying to find girls to spend time with — just unhealthy. Sex. Trauma dumping. It’s love, and it’s temporary, and then it’s rinse and repeat, another night.”

To make matters worse, this was all going down when Cook was grappling with multiple other catastrophes, both personal and professional. A couple of years earlier, he’d lost both parents to cancer within a span of nine months — a double dose of tragedy that initially brought him and Darryl closer, but ultimately made their estrangement even more painful. Around the same time, Cook was famously (and, in hindsight, unfairly) accused of joke-stealing by a pre-disgraced Louis C.K., leading to a pile-on of haters and internet stand-up police. Not to mention the normal backlash and decline he was already facing from overexposure and his defiantly un-P.C. shtick.

“I’m just spinning,” Cook recalls of this time. “I’m no longer in vogue. Also my parents have passed, and I’m probably ignoring that and not grieving. I’m doing sets at night because it’s alleviating the sadness of the day.”

One of his first shows back was a disastrous, rambling set at the Hollywood Improv, where other comics described him as “spiraling” as he reportedly told “jokes” like: “Go fuck a dirty whore. That’s the best therapy.” Eventually he realized he needed actual therapy. “It was like a year of twice a week,” he says. “Brick by brick. Figuring out again how to move in the world.”

It’s hard not to notice that Cook’s trajectory changed drastically after Darryl’s betrayal. Since 2009, he’s done just two stand-up specials and only a handful of acting gigs (including four episodes of a sitcom that got canceled before it aired). It’s been seven years since he appeared on TV or film at all. From the outside, it looks like his life got derailed and he never got it back on track.

Was it just the natural cycle of fame? The more intellectual turn stand-up took in the 2010s? Or does he blame his brother for that?

“I did blame him for a while,” Cook says. “I knew I was at the end of a run in my career — I’m cooling off. At that point where the pendulum naturally swings and everything slows down, I didn’t have the bandwidth to untangle the knots. But also, being realistic,” he adds, “I wasn’t putting up, like, Sandler $100 million movies. I was hitting doubles.”

For years, Cook struggled with how to tell the story. He wrote a few bad jokes about it. (“My brother was a prison guard. I hired him to protect my money, not help it escape!”) He even tried some material out on his therapist. (“Man. Worst audience. The stonewalling I took on some of my gems…”) For a while he thought about doing a one-man show. But he could never figure out how to get into it all while still delivering for his fans. “They’re there to see me do what I do,” he says. “I wasn’t ready to bum them out.”

Then in 2019, he talked about it on a podcast for the first time, and it unlocked something. Soon after, he got a call from the documentary’s producer offering him a million dollars.

There is, of course, one big, Darryl-sized hole in the film. McCauley turned down multiple requests to be interviewed by the filmmakers. Cook even offered to drop his $12 million restitution claim in exchange for a face-to-face sit-down; Darryl declined. According to Darryl’s LinkedIn page, after his release from prison, he worked for six months at a Home Depot, three years at a grocery store, and five years as a driver for FedEx, before entering “semi-retirement” in 2024. His bio says he “possess[es] strong judgement and decision making skills.” And in the “Skills” section, he lists one: “Finance.”

Cook says he’s never tried to reach out to his brother. He seems to be waiting for Darryl to make the first move. Even 17 years later, he sounds freshly wounded, yet surprisingly open to reconciliation. “Even in this doc, there’s some version of a love letter to my brother,” he says. “Like: ‘You did a lot for me. We did a lot together. Why are you dumb?’”

Cook claims — incredibly  — that if he could go back, he wouldn’t change a thing. “I feel like it’s all brought me to the best of my life,” he insists. “Where I’m at right now is way more interesting than anything that would have happened, had nothing happened.”

“But I do miss my brother sometimes,” he adds. “I miss that guy I game-planned with. That I made those first flyers with back in the day. A million memories of high-fives and bad fast food and driving to gigs. It was cool having an older brother. If I had a time machine, I’d probably go back and throw one more hug on him.”

Just a few months ago, his younger sister Courtney got a DM from Darryl. It was the first time any of them had heard from him in decades. The message, says Cook:

“‘Everybody’s wrong. It was $12.8 million.’ With a money bag emoji.”

LATER THAT NIGHT, COOK rolls into a theater in Santa Monica for the documentary’s premiere — the first time he’s seen it with strangers. Friars Club roastmaster Jeff Ross is in the house; Cook’s pal Dave Chappelle was going to come, too, but he had to bail last-minute. Seated next to Cook is his wife of three years, Kelsi. She’s 26 years his junior — they started dating when she was 18 and he was 42 — but at least Cook jokes about it. (Goes one bit: “People are like, You’re robbing the cradle. I’m like, Relax. She hasn’t slept in a cradle in nine years.”)

The audience is admittedly full of friends and fans, but the movie goes over great. People laugh and gasp in all the right spots. Ross uncorks a few nice heckles. Afterward, Cook is beaming. “Putting up a win with the worst moment of your life is fucking awesome,” he says. “I have regained the narrative that was hijacked from me.”

Earlier, in his office, Cook talked about the future. He hopes the documentary will be a “catalyst” for his career. He’s been inspired by seeing Chappelle and Chris Rock still touring and directing films, and says he’s hungry to get back to that level. “I belong there,” he says. “That’s the class I put myself in.”

He’s been getting in shape — preparing his mind and body. Kelsi is a certified Pilates trainer and fitness instructor, and she has him on a strict 2,000-calorie diet, doing an hour of Pilates and swimming every morning and in bed by 8 every night. He sounds like a prizefighter training for a comeback.

Can he make one? Who’s to say? Flip phones are cool again — why not Dane Cook?

“I have always been rooting for Dane,” says Nikki Glaser. “I’m sure his downfall was schadenfreude for a lot of comedians, but I think the comics at the top now owe him a lot. There’s been a stand-up boom since he showed up on the scene that hasn’t really dropped off. He made it popular, he made it sexy, and he changed the scale at which it could be done. And he’s still got it.”

Lately Cook has been taking meetings, trying to get some momentum back. He says he recently landed a role on a prestige drama from “one of the greatest producers of all time.” He wrote a book about his story and has a new hour of stand-up that he calls the best he’s ever done. His misfortune is already opening doors.

Cook is almost heartbreakingly earnest when he talks about getting back to work. “Permission to speak freely?” he says. “I’d love to work more. I’m so ready. I hope this reminds people, if you have forgotten: I’m a workhorse. I love to show up on time. I love to create an environment for the cast and crew where they go, ‘I want to work with Dane again.’ Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Marty Erlichman, Barbra Streisand’s Manager Since the 1960s, Dead at 97 Martha Stewart ‘Distressed’ by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume

“I didn’t work for a long time,” he says. “I hate being on the bench. I’m OK with whatever it is. I just want to be working.”

In some ways, he sounds like a kid still looking for approval. From an audience, a dad… or maybe a big brother. “When I’m on set and hitting the mark, and I get the arm around me walking out of the studio saying, ‘You brought it today’?” he says. “That’s all I want. I think I’ve got a little bit of that left.”

#3423. ‘The Liberation’ Trailer: Carrie Coon Stars In Guy Nattiv’s Complex Cult Thriller

Bleecker Street on Monday released the first trailer from The Liberation, the dramatic thriller written and directed by Guy Nattiv and starring Carrie Coon in a role that has been garnering award-season buzz since the pic’s world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival.

Coon (The Gilded Age, The White Lotus) plays Rita, a 1980s New Jersey housewife and Holocaust survivor haunted by the weight of her past. She encounters a magnetic spiritual leader (Lily James) and leaves her family to follow her to an all-female commune. When her daughters (played by Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young) arrive to rescue her and become drawn into the group’s world, Rita is forced to choose between the family she left behind and the life she believes can save her. Tracy Letts plays Rita’s husband.

Bleecker Street is setting up a short Oscar-qualifying theatrical run for The Liberation starting Friday in New York and Los Angeles. It is set up for a wider release January 8. Watch on Deadline

At Deadline’s Contenders London, Nattiv recounted the inspiration for the movie came from his own life, when as a boy his family took him to visit his grandmother.

“I was only 8 when my family took me to seminars to see my grandmother and participate with her in those meetings,” he said, later learning it was a cult and that his grandmother had “left his grandfather, left our family.”

Much later, he visited the cult with his camera to seek more answers, saying he entered the process with “a lot of empathy” and found that the cult “tried to free” his grandmother from her trauma of being a Holocaust survivor. “She had the courage to do something very uncommon: To leave your family, say goodbye to your daughters and your husband and go into the unknown and try to save yourself,” he said.

#3422. If You Loved 'East of Eden,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

One of the best things about truly great stories is how they can be endlessly adapted and reinterpreted. John Steinbeck published “East of Eden” in 1952, and each time it’s adapted to a screen, it looks a little different. Netflix’s try at this huge, complex story offers up some searing performances, especially from Florence Pugh as the notorious Cathy Ames. Ames is one of the best characters ever crafted in American literature, but her sociopathic nature has sometimes made her into a simple villain—but the series, and Pugh's performances, adds depth to the charcter. If the limited series has you wanting more complex female characters from classic novels, your next move is obvious: Vanity Fair, starring Reese Witherspoon as Becky Sharp.

First published in the mid-19th century, “Vanity Fair” by William Makepeace Thackeray is an enduring classic of American literature, satirizing the artificial manners and pretensions of Victorian society. At the center of the story is Becky Sharp, whose moral ambiguity and self-serving actions were surprising and unexpected at the time—and have made her a kind of antihero in the modern age. Sharp is a complicated character who, like Cathy Ames, can easily be flattened into a villain, a social climber who uses people.

The 2004 adaptation leans into the more modern take on Sharp’s character, giving her more justification for her actions and humanizing her more than the novel. Sharp is orphaned at a young age, but is almost feral in her determination to secure a position in society—which, at the time, meant securing an advantageous marriage. The story doesn’t have the same sweep as East of Eden, chronicling a relatively short period of time—but that period is the Napoleonic Wars, so there’s a lot going on. This gives the film a similarly epic feel even as it focuses on Sharp’s constant scheming and endless flirtations with people who she thinks can help her out.

In many ways, Sharp is simply playing by the rules imposed on her by men, and if that was scandalous in 1848, it’s almost heroic by today’s standards, and Reese Witherspoon imbues her Sharp with a bit of grace to reflect that. But she’s still someone who does what she must to survive and thrive, and that prickly edge will appeal to fans of Pugh in East of Eden. Rent Vanity Fair on Prime Video.

Need more historical epics with fascinating, complex characters? Luckily, the movies tend to specialize in that—here are a few more movies that fans of East of Eden will love.

If you thought the best thing about East of Eden was Florence Pugh, you’re going to love Lady Macbeth. Pugh plays Katherine, a young woman pushed into an arranged marriage with wealthy landowner Alexander Lester (Paul Hilton) in England in 1865. The marriage is solely intended to produce an heir, and Katherine is initially imprisoned in the house. When Alexander and his father leave Katherine alone for some time, she walks the estate and begins a brazen affair with a worker, setting off a chain of violent events that gets bleaker with each scene. Pugh’s portrayal of another dark, determined woman is mesmerizing. Stream Lady Macbeth on Kanopy or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you want more sprawling family drama in a historical setting, look no further than Legends of the Fall. Set in the early 20th century, it follows Colonel William Ludlow (Anthony Hopkins) and his sons Tristan (Brad Pitt), Alfred (Aidan Quinn), and Samuel (Henry Thomas) as they navigate life choices and deal with the emotional wounds they inflict on each other. From World War I to Prohibition, the Ludlows fall in love (sometimes with each other’s wives), suffer crushing loss, and remain connected to their ranch and the natural beauty of Montana through it all. Anchored by a star turn by Brad Pitt, this movie will scratch the itch left behind by East of Eden. Rent Legends of the Fall on Prime Video.

If you want to see a different take on the novel, check out the 1955 adaptation directed by Elia Kazan (grandfather of Zoe Kazan, who co-wrote and directed the 2026 series). Starring James Dean (who would die a few months after its release), it’s an old-school Hollywood epic that only covers the final third of the book. That makes it a very different narrative experience from the series, which has more room to explore the novel’s complexities—but the film looks amazing, Dean’s performance is terrific, and Kazan directs the heck out of it. Rent East of Eden on Prime Video.

Another choice for epic family drama, Giant was James Dean’s last film, and offers family drama in heaps. Like East of Eden, it follows a family over the course of decades as patriarch Jordan “Bick” Benedict, Jr. (Rock Hudson) tries to maintain his family’s ranching legacy in the face of changing times and a flood of oil money, while his former ranch hand Jett Rink (Dean) pines for Bick’s wife, Leslie (Elizabeth Taylor), and strikes it rich with oil. As money’s corrosive effect takes its toll on Jett, the Benedict family grows and changes, with plenty of drama to spare along the way. Rent Giant on Prime Video.

If East of Eden makes you curious about other adaptations of Steinbeck’s work, your next stop should be John Ford’s 1940 version of The Grapes of Wrath. Set during the Great Depression, it follows Tom Joad (Henry Fonda) after his release from prison for manslaughter. He finds his family has been forced off their land, and joins them in a desperate migration to California in hopes of finding work and security. Along the way, Joad kills again and undergoes what can only be described as radicalization, dedicating his life to organizing labor and fighting back against the predations of capitalist society. It’s a remarkable film pulsing with emotional heft and deep family drama, and if its story and setting are very different from East of Eden, the impact will be similar. Stream The Grapes of Wrath on Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Can the Busy Bar bring Flipper Zero-like hacking to your workday?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The right gadget on your desk can make all the difference for the task at hand, and I think I’ve finally found a smart display that’s more helpful than distracting.

Sure, my monitor and computer will always be the main fixtures on my desk, but the smaller accessories I swap in and out of my setup can make a real difference in my day-to-day routine.

For instance, I added a Google Nest Hub Max underneath my ultrawide monitor a few years ago. While it was great for getting answers to quick questions, controlling my smart home, and checking feeds from my security cameras, having videos, music, and media just a voice command away made it easy to drift off task.

Although I eventually swapped out that smart display for a portable monitor to gain extra screen real estate, part of me still missed having a dedicated clock right on my desk. What I didn’t expect, though, was to find a simple desk clock with the smarts of a display and a built-in Pomodoro timer.

To top it off, the Busy Bar I’ve had on my desk for the past few months comes from Flipper — the same company behind the iconic Flipper Zero pentesting tool. Here’s everything you need to know about this unique gadget that works just as well on your desk as it does mounted on your monitor.

If you’re looking to swap out noisy touchscreens for a simple, focus-first desk display, Flipper’s Busy Bar brings a tactile edge to staying on task. Packing dual front-and-back screens, a built-in Pomodoro timer, mechanical switch controls, and automatic macOS meeting sync, it offers a surprisingly fun desk companion. Add in its fold-out monitor feet, open-source API, and 3D-printable design files for custom mounts, and you get a uniquely hackable status light that fits right into any modern workspace setup.

At 6.64 x 2.17 x 1.61 inches, Flipper’s new Busy Bar won’t take up much space on your desk at all. Just like the Flipper Zero, it comes in white with orange accenting, which I found to be just playful enough without being overly distracting.

In the box, you get the Busy Bar alongside a color-matched braided USB-C cable. While the device can run on its battery for around eight hours — or up to two weeks on standby — I found it easiest to leave it plugged into a USB power adapter underneath my desk. (If you use a Mac, you can also connect it directly to your computer, but more on that later.)

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The front of the device features a bright, pixelated dot-matrix display, but the real star of the show sits right on top: tactile physical controls for adjusting settings and running your timers. There’s a selector switch on the left to toggle between different modes, a giant Start/Pause bar in the middle, and a rotary knob on the right to add time or scroll through menus.

Coming from touchscreen devices like the Nest Hub Max and Echo Show 5, these physical controls offered a refreshing change of pace. I particularly like that the main Start/Pause bar uses the same mechanical switch mechanism you'd find in a mechanical keyboard. While the switches and dials aren’t totally silent, the quiet click they produce is soft enough for an office environment while making the whole experience of using the device genuinely fun.

On the bottom of the Busy Bar, there’s a USB-C port for charging or connecting it to your computer, right alongside two fold-out feet that let you mount it on top of your monitor like a webcam. Before trying that out, though, I wanted to see how it performed sitting directly on my desk.

Unlike the Flipper Zero — which has gotten a bit of a bad rap as a "hacking tool" — the Busy Bar is designed to help you hack your workday. Others can clearly see its large pixelated display and know not to bother you when it’s flipped to Busy. Alternatively, you can switch it to "Custom," which by default displays a "Keep Out" message complete with animated yellow warning tape.

Given that I work from home and don’t sit in a crowded office, my favorite thing about the Busy Bar so far has been its built-in Pomodoro timer. When you switch to Busy mode, the timer defaults to a 20-minute focus period followed by a five-minute rest break. The device’s built-in 0.8W speaker emits a clean chime to let you know when your interval is up, leading into a second work period with another short break in between.

What I like about this hardware-first approach is that I don’t have to pull out my phone — which usually ends up distracting me with notifications when I'm supposed to be focused. Plus, physically slamming down on the Start/Pause bar between work and rest intervals is surprisingly satisfying. Using the Busy Bar throughout my workday has genuinely helped me stay on task, especially when plowing through administrative work that would normally leave me bored out of my mind.

It isn’t just a glorified Pomodoro timer, though. Like other smart displays, it also features built-in apps. My favorite is the standard clock, which shows the current time and date. While that was essentially the only first-party app available for most of my testing period, a recent firmware update added a dedicated Weather app that includes a clock interface.

I initially tested the Busy Bar out in my game room sitting on top of my BlueAnt Soundblade soundbar, where it fit into my setup seamlessly. Eventually, I moved it into my office underneath my desk shelf where I’ve been using it ever since. At just over two inches tall, you can tuck it almost anywhere. However, mounting it on top of my monitor is what truly sold me on it as a companion gadget for a busy workspace.

With the feet pulled out, the Busy Bar perches easily on top of a monitor, just like one of the best webcams or a monitor lightbar. If your desk sits in an open workspace rather than facing a wall, people walking by can instantly see whether you’re available or wrapped up in focus time.

My favorite feature, though, is how it handles virtual meetings. When connected to my Mac with Flipper’s macOS app running, the display automatically flips to "On Call" the instant I join a meeting. Once the video call ends, it seamlessly drops back to your clock or timer.

How do you know what the Busy Bar is showing everyone else while it's resting on top of your screen? Flipper thought of that, too.

Unlike the 6.35-inch RGB LED pixel matrix on the front, the back of the Busy Bar features a secondary 1.54-inch monochrome OLED display. It mirrors whatever is showing on the main screen so you always know what people looking at your monitor are seeing. Flipper also used the extra space on either side of the back panel to include helpful quick-start guides — computer connection instructions on the left, and companion app info complete with a QR code on the right.

At the moment, Flipper hasn’t released its Windows companion app yet, though the website notes it's "Coming soon." That wasn't a dealbreaker for me since I regularly jump between operating systems when testing gear, so I downloaded the macOS app on my Mac mini M6 to get started. Just like the mobile app, the desktop software makes tweaking settings and digging into menus much easier, even if it’s a bit less tactile than using the physical dial and knob.

To get that automatic "On Call" status working when you drop into a meeting, you do need the desktop app running with the Busy Bar tethered to your computer over USB. In practice, it worked reliably, and having quick control right from the macOS Menu Bar made making adjustments effortless.

While I didn’t get a chance to test this feature out with my family at home — the school year is in full swing, after all — I could easily see it being a lifesaver during summer break when the kids are home. Plus, because you can also wall-mount the Busy Bar, it feels like a natural fit for podcasters, streamers, or anyone else who needs a clear "do not disturb" indicator while recording.

With most consumer electronics seeing price hikes lately due to the ongoing effects of RAMaggedon, I was still a bit surprised when I saw the Busy Bar’s price tag. At $249, it costs more than both the Echo Show 8 and the Google Nest Hub Max. Fortunately, the Busy Bar has been available for 20% off for the past month or so, and I hope its discounted $200 price becomes permanent.

Even at $200, you’re paying quite a bit for a device with deliberately fewer features — though that’s kind of the point, right? In Flipper’s defense, the Busy Bar is as customizable and hackable (in the best way) as the Flipper Zero.

For instance, you can integrate it with the rest of your smart home devices to turn on lights, lock your door, or pause your music the second you switch your status to "Busy". It’s a remarkably developer-friendly device too, and there’s already a growing collection of custom-made apps for it. Flipper even released a 1:1 model of the Busy Bar so you can 3D print your own custom mounts and accessories.

While its software ecosystem is still in its early stages, I’ve really enjoyed the simplicity of having the Busy Bar on my desk. It’s a great digital clock, a solid Pomodoro timer, and an ambient focus tool that lets me keep an eye on my day without getting bogged down by endless notifications.

Given how open Flipper has made the platform from the outset, the sky is truly the limit. Here’s hoping Busy Bars end up on more people’s desks and that the tinkering community has as much fun with this device as they did with the Flipper Zero — I know I have.

#3420. Sharon Horgan’s ‘Youth’ Renewed For Season 2 At HBO

Sharon Horgan is returning as literary agent Alex after HBO renewed Youth for a second season.

The news comes less than 24 hours after the season one finale.

Youth follows a 50-year-old divorcee’s search for sex and love whilst juggling caring for her ailing parents and parenting her should-be grown up son.

Horgan stars as Alex in the series, which she created and wrote. [SPOILER ALERT] The eight-part season was left open ended after Alex ends it with Patrick, played by Rupert Friend after discovering a list of pros and cons, with the inability to have children as in the latter column. However, after a one-night stand with her nemesis Malcolm, played by Douglas Hodge, she wakes up to find that her boss Sam, played by Sharlene Whyte, has signed Malcolm. All of this while dealing with a UTI and trying to resolve things with her child Ruari, played by Aran Murphy. Robbie Gee also stars as Frank, Sam’s husband.

Youth is produced by Horgan’s Merman and she exec produces alongside Faye Dorn, Jim Kleverweis, and Dawn Shadforth, who also directs. Watch on Deadline

Youth comes seven years after Horgan’s last HBO show, Divorce, ended after three seasons. Catastrophe co-creator Horgan is also behind Apple black comedy Bad Sisters, Starz’s Courteney Cox-fronted Shining Vale and BBC comedy Motherland.

“I’m so happy to get another opportunity to live out my emotional and biological crises on HBO. I can’t think of a better platform to air my UTI problems on. The response to Youth has been beyond what I could have hoped for. I’m so grateful for the response and the chance to work with this incredible cast and creative team once more,” Horgan said.

Amy Gravitt, EVP, HBO Programming, Head of HBO & HBO Max Comedy Series, added, “In a way that only she can, Sharon has created a show that makes us howl with laughter and with tears – often in the same moment. Each performance in Youth is more delightful than the next. Along with our partners at Merman, we are so thrilled to have this brilliant ensemble back for another season.”

#3419. Watch Hotel Workers Prep for Mariah Carey’s Arrival As Part of New Gucci Holiday Campaign

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

Mariah Carey season is officially underway as the Queen of Christmas makes her first holiday appearance of 2026 with a new Gucci campaign.

The “All I Want for Christmas Is You” singer stars in Gucci’s new holiday video, showing off her new “Butterfly” collection, inspired by her 1997 album of the same name, and designed in collaboration with the Italian fashion house. Directed by Harmony Korine, the clip finds hotel workers and guests scurrying about as they prepare a party in Carey’s honor. Christmas trees are dressed, lights are strung, and candles are lit, just in time for the singer’s arrival (to the sounds of “All I Want for Christmas,” natch).

Gucci says the campaign celebrates “[Carey’s] role as a cultural icon and a fixture of the holiday season,” while capturing the “festive excitement of one of the most anticipated moments of the year.”

Of course there are plenty of presents to go around too, with the campaign showing off the Italian fashion house’s collection of luxe handbags, shoes, and accessories for the season, all “offering inspiration for celebrations, winter escapes, and the many moments shared during the holidays,” per a release.

Carey’s Butterfly collection, meantime, includes jackets, dresses, T-shirts, shoes, and jewelry, many of which feature a custom Gucci butterfly print with crystals.

This sequined jersey top features the butterfly print against a lightweight viscose material. Gucci says the glittery piece “illuminates the holidays,” making it a festive piece to throw on for Christmas parties and New Year’s Eve gatherings alike.

This bag features Gucci’s iconic GG canvas monogram with crystal embellishments throughout. The bag comes with a chain strap and a leather strap, along with leather trim in Carey’s signature lavender colorway.

Carey fans and fashion fans alike will also want to pick up this limited-edition pendant necklace, which features a crystal-embellished GG charm, along with a crystal butterfly charm, both set on a palladium-toned chain.Butterflies, of course, have long been associated with the singer, ever since she released her autobiographical song and album of the same name.

Carey officially kicked off the holiday season on Sunday, with her annual “It’s Time” video, marking the transition from Halloween to Christmas. This year’s video, created in collaboration with beauty brand Sol de Janeiro, has already amassed more than 4.5 million views and counting on YouTube.

Carey is also picking up streams online for her seasonal hit: according to Spotify, “All I Want for Christmas Is You” re-entered the charts at no. 37, with more than 1.8 million streams on Nov. 1.

The Queen of Christmas will also be looking to reclaim her throne at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, after Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” replaced “All I Want for Christmas Is You” as the biggest hit in Hot 100 history, with 25 weeks and counting. Carey’s song had spent a cumulative 22 weeks at the top of the charts.

#3418. 10 Fun and Quirky iPhone Duo Apps Worth Checking Out

The launch of the iPhone Duo marks the first time that Apple has fundamentally changed the form factor of the iPhone. This is an exciting development because, among other reasons, it allows app developers to get even more creative. If you have an iPhone Duo, plan to get one, or if you're just interested in creative app interfaces, then you should take a look at these apps.

With Tiny Computers ($4), when you use the Duo half-open, it turns the bottom display into a keyboard, and the screen goes up top. The app features computers inspired by Commodore 64, Windows 95, iMac G3, Macintosh, IBM PC, Amiga 500, ThinkPad, iBook G3, Powerbook G4, and Windows XP. The attention to detail is great, but early App Store reviews mention that the app can be buggy.

I miss the tactile nature of playing music on my cassette player at home, and my old Sony Walkman clone. Deck-Man ($5) is an app that brings the Walkman's interface, complete with all the clicks and clacks, to your iPhone Duo. Each time you play an album, Deck-Man lets you "insert" the cassette in the player before it starts playing. The app links to your Apple Music account and it also supports playing local music files.

Foldissimo (free, $10 to unlock all songs) simulates the sound of airflow in an accordion as you fold and unfold your iPhone Duo. It has some songs pre-loaded, and you can pay $10 to unlock all songs. Foldissimo also supports a few other instruments (accordion organ, panpipes, and theremin), but you'll need to pay an additional $10 to unlock those.

With Flipcorder ($5), while the viewfinder and the retro interface are visible to you when you have the Duo in tablet mode, your subjects can also see the frame via the outer display. When you fold the Duo, the app saves the clip, and allows you to record up to 30 minutes of video per day, each of which is saved in a virtual "tape."

Orisuji ($5) is a puzzle game where you solve mazes by folding your iPhone Duo. It has 69 levels, and you'll be solving most of these by folding or unfolding the device to shift the position of the maze to make your characters move, unlock doors, or to find keys to get past locked doors.

Toastie ($3) is a game where you, well, make sandwiches: It has 10 recipes for you to master, with a time limit of 15 seconds per step as your in-game customers wait for you to serve them. You fold the phone to "cook" the sandwich; leave it folded for too long and you'll end up with burnt toast.

Marbles Unhinged (Free, $3/each to unlock all levels in a world) is a puzzle game where you guide a marble towards the exit in each level. When you fold your iPhone, it turns the top half of the level into a ramp, and alters the speed of the marble. You can keep the phone at different angles to change the nature of the stage, which will lead you to the solution.

ChompDuo (Free, $1 to unlock all monsters) uses the Duo's folding mechanics to make monsters "chomp" down, and you'll feel each bite via haptic vibrations. When you close the Duo, the monster's eyes stare at you from the outer display. It's a silly app that you or your kids could enjoy playing around with.

Unfold Your City (Free, $5 to unlock all cities) simulates pop-up books to guide you through the highlights of different cities. It reminds me of Robert Sabuda's beautiful pop-up books, especially when you use the app on iPhone Duo. It slowly pops up the artwork for each city as you unfold the device, and displays the cover when you close the "book."

In the Pokémon anime, the Pokédex is an encyclopedia that catalogs information about your friendly neighborhood pocket monsters. Dex Fold (Free, $3 to unlock optional features) simulates the device from the anime, which means that you can only use the app when you unfold the iPhone Duo.

Happy Sunday! Halloween weekend is winding down, and nothing snuffs out the "Sunday Scaries" quite like a cozy night on the couch with a movie to take your mind off things.

Netflix added 30 new movies at the top of the month, including several heart-warming movies to wile away a weekend afternoon. Headlining this Sunday's lineup is a rare Stephen King adaptation that won't scare the crap out of you: Rob Reiner's coming-of-age drama "Stand By Me" for a whopping dose of '80s nostalgia. It's not the only movie on this list that brings the good vibes though. Netflix also got Kristen Wiig's hilarious comedy "Bridesmaids" as well as a Christmas movie led by "Yellowstone's" Dave Annable called "No Sleep 'Til Christmas."

Read on for everything you need to know about the best feel-good films streaming right now on Netflix to end your weekend on a high note.

Rom-coms usually aren't my thing, but "Bridesmaids" is the rare one I'll watch again and again. A big part of its enduring appeal comes down to pitch-perfect performances from Kristen Wiig (who also co-wrote the script), Maya Rudolph and Rose Byrne. More than a decade after seeing it in theaters with the girlies, I'm still quoting it regularly — and laughing just as hard at all the gags.

Paul Feig's breakout comedy dives into the surprisingly cutthroat world of pre-wedding planning. When a well-meaning but increasingly frazzled maid of honor (Wiig) finds herself competing with an effortlessly perfect bridesmaid (Byrne) for the attention of her best friend (Rudolph), things quickly turn ugly. Neither woman is willing to back down, and their petty attempts to one-up each other threaten to derail the entire wedding. Melissa McCarthy, Ellie Kemper and Wendi McLendon-Covey round out an excellent ensemble, each bringing their own unforgettable comedic moments to the mix.

Halloween only just ended, but all the stores have already whipped out Christmas decorations because what is time anyway these days? Netflix added a few yuletide flicks at the top of the month, and while there's no real winners among the bunch, you could do far worse than "No Sleep ’Til Christmas." This romcom stars real-life couple Odette Annable and Dave Annable of "Yellowstone" fame as two strangers who have one very unusual thing in common: neither can fall asleep alone.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Lizzie (Odette Annable) is an engaged wedding planner struggling with insomnia, while Billy (Dave Annable) is a bartender who can't get a decent night's rest without someone beside him. When the two unexpectedly discover that they can sleep peacefully next to each other, they strike up an arrangement to help one another get some shut-eye. Of course, their nightly sleepovers soon have sparks flying, complicating both their love lives just in time for Christmas.

Watch "No Sleep 'Til Christmas" on Netflix now

While it's not a strictly feel-good movie, "Stand By Me" packs enough nostalgia that just seeing the opening is enough to take me back to simpler days. Based on Stephen King's novella "The Body," Rob Reiner's 1986 coming-of-age drama follows four boys growing up in a small Oregon town in the 1950s. Gordie (Wil Wheaton), Chris (River Phoenix), Teddy (Corey Feldman) and Vern (Jerry O'Connell) set out on an adventure through the woods after Vern's iconic line: “You guys wanna go see a dead body?”

As the boys travel together, they run headfirst into one challenge after another, all the while opening up about what's weighing on them. Gordie is grieving the loss of his older brother, Chris is trying to escape his troubled family's reputation, Teddy is dealing with an abusive father, and timid Vern is often picked on by bullies. Through it all, the boys lean on one another and face the difficult realities of growing up head on, the adventure ultimately becoming a bittersweet turning point in their lives.
