#3416. The ‘Ice Where It Happens:’ Watch U.S. Figure Skating Pair’s New ‘Hamilton’-Inspired Routine

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

The Tony-winning Broadway hit, Hamilton, is moving from the Great White Way to the bright white ice.

The official X account for the musical, Hamilton, posted a clip Sunday of U.S. ice dancers Caroline Green and Michael Parsons rehearsing their new rhythm dance to the Broadway show’s hit soundtrack. The two-time U.S. medalists debuted their Hamilton-themed routine at Skate Canada over the weekend, the second stop in figure skating‘s prestigious Grand Prix series of events.

Green and Parsons posted a score of 74.24 points for their Skate Canada rhythm dance (formerly known as the “short dance” or “short program”), on their way to a third-place finish overall. The couple’s two minute and 50 second routine uses three songs from the Hamilton soundtrack: “Ten Duel Commandments,” “Your Obedient Servant,” and “The Room Where It Happens.” All three tracks were written by Lin-Manuel Miranda for the original Broadway show.

As Green explained in a backstage interview, “It’s Hamilton versus Burr. It’s taken from the opening, where Burr’s in the red and pretty much the entire cast is in the white and the cream. But it’s sort of like a modern Hamilton meets figure skating, because unfortunately, we can’t wear really long coats and colonial dress.”

Dag! They amaze and astonish.🎥: Caroline Green & Michael Parsons pic.twitter.com/Yzk4WtAjBC

While Skate Canada marked the Hamilton program’s Grand Prix debut, Green and Parsons actually tested it out on audiences at two smaller “Senior B” events earlier this fall: the Denis Ten Memorial Challenge, where the couple finished third, and the CS Nepela Memorial Trophy, where they finished in fifth place.

The figure skating routine comes on the heels of a 10th anniversary box set released in September. Titled Rise Up! Hamilton, the 7-LP set includes the original Broadway cast recording, the 2016 Hamilton Mixtape recording (featuring Kelly Clarkson, Alicia Keys, and others) plus the first-ever vinyl pressing of Hamildrops: The Complete Collection, Miranda’s sequel to the Hamilton Mixtape. The box set also includes previous unreleased songs, plus an 80-page book with behind-the-scenes photos, as well as a poster, custom slipmat, and other collectibles.

Each box is numbered and released in extremely limited-edition, and it’s almost sold out online.You can stream or purchase a physical copy of the original Broadway recording, meantime, here.

The Hamilton soundtrack topped Billboard’s Broadway albums chart and has been certified diamond. It also took home the Grammy for Best Musical Theater Album in 2016.

This isn’t the first time a figure skater has performed to the Hamilton soundtrack – U.S. men’s star Jason Brown skated to “The Room Where It Happens” for his short program in the 2017-2018 season.

#3415. Bruce Springsteen Endorses Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed: “I’m In His Corner 100%”

Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics

On the eve of the bitterly fought 2026 midterms, Bruce Springsteen on Monday came out strong for Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“Dr. El-Sayed is a fighter for our American Constitution, he’s a fighter for our American Democracy, and he’s a fighter against the corrupt, lawless, and anti-American leadership currently in the White House,” the “Born In the USA” singer said on social media. “That’s why I’m in his corner 100%.”

A vocal critic of Trump and his authoritarian policies onstage, in song and with his high profile, Springsteen rarely gets this direct for an office seeker if they aren’t running for President. Still, with all the drama surrounding the potentially crucial and tightening Great Lakes State race between El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, the full-throated endorsement today has the potential to turn up the volume in an already deafening election cycle.

Having stumped for Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in previous general elections with his greatest hits, Jersey boy Springsteen this year put his politics in to new song with tragic origins. In January, he released the poignant “Streets of Minneapolis” over the killing of two Americans, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota by ICE agents. Watch on Deadline

Out on tour with the E Street Band this spring, Springsteen railed against Trump night after night. He also took ‘Streets of Minneapolis’ to the city itself as Trump attacked the Rock Hall of Famer online and on-stage as a “very boring singer” who “looks like a dried up prune who has suffered greatly from the work of a really bad plastic surgeon.”

After calling Trump and his cruel crew a “reckless and treasonous administration” over the spring and summer on tour, the 77-year old Springsteen appeared with sometimes bandmate Tom Morello last month at the protest-packed Power to the People festival in Columbia, MD. The daylong show was broadcast on MS NOW and streamed online.

Springsteen’s support for El-Sayed comes just hours to go before the polls in Michigan and elsewhere open for Election Day. Estimates are that the Democrats will take the House of Representatives and could, if El-Sayed and a few other critical races go blue, gain previously unimagined control of the Senate — effectively kneecapping Trump’s second term if so.

A bombshell of sorts hit Michigan on Sunday, with El-Sayed primary opponent Rep Haley Stevens coming out for Rogers. The bombshell ended up blowing up in the face of Rogers, the GOP and Stevens’ own face after a car crash of a CNN primetime interview with Anderson Cooper went way off the rails. Now tossed out of the Democratic Party in her home state, Stevens on Sunday night abandoned any critique of El-Sayed’s views on Israel, or anything else, to rant about “Why the anger? Why the frustration?”

While Stevens no longer has a political career in either blue or red circles, El-Sayed now has Bruce Springsteen in his corner.

#3414. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

#3413. Living with Mom and trading on margin. The regular investor gets in on Wall Street's record stock borrowing binge

HOUSTON — During a late night at home in May 2021, Hy Luu, a 29-year-old engineering consultant, was researching how to obtain more capital to invest in shares of Tesla.

That's when he discovered margin investing: the act of borrowing money from a broker to buy securities such as stocks, while using existing investments as collateral. Borrowing would give him more buying power, and he could pay it back as the stock appreciated. The main risk would be a margin call, or having to deposit more money into the account, if its value fell.

It was all too good to be true, Luu thought.

Luu — who lives with his mother, Kim Nguyen, in a three-bedroom, two-bathroom house in Houston — decided to get her opinion on the topic, given that she used to work as an accountant and just so happened to still be awake that evening. The 66-year-old retiree found it interesting.

That was the reassurance he needed, and it wasn't long before he started using margin to invest in Tesla for the first time. A year or so later, he had amassed more than $100,000 of margin debt.

"I went really crazy," he told CNBC in an interview. "The stock was going up, and so I was like, 'There's no way I could lose.'"

After five years of margin investing — including a period in 2022 where he worried that further declines in Tesla could trigger a margin call — Luu is working to pay down his largest margin balance ever. In June, he exercised $165,000 on five Tesla call options and bought 500 shares at $330 per share. After accounting for the cash in his account, this drove his borrowing to more than $156,000.

Tesla swung from below $370 a share to more than $430 during that month.

Between his Tesla investments, his company stock and 401(k) — while subtracting his margin debt as well as other debt he's accumulated, such as his car loan and student loans — Luu's net worth has skyrocketed to more than $800,000 from negative territory seven years ago.

"I'm very close to becoming a millionaire," the investor said. He did stress, "What I'm doing is risky. I don't recommend anyone do it."

Yet, Luu has found himself part of a growing trend taking hold in the market.

Retail investors like Luu are borrowing more and more money to invest. Robinhood's margin book grew to a record $21.6 billion in the second quarter, up 127% year over year and a 332% increase from the $5 billion seen in Q2 2024. To margin invest on the platform, eligible users must have a portfolio value of at least $2,000.

"Robinhood has made a really concerted effort to go after customers that are actively using margin because they're the most active traders," said Devin Ryan, head of financial technology research at Citizens.

Brokerage firms can benefit from margin investing by collecting interest on margin loans, while highly active customers can also generate additional trading-related revenue.

"If you look at the offers that Robinhood has had in the market over the past couple of years, it's been targeting those customers with obviously transfer bonuses, but also very low margin rates, very high yields on their cash," Ryan said.

To be sure, other parts of Robinhood's business are also growing, including retirement assets — which have nearly quadrupled in the last two years.

Another factor fueling the rise in margin investing is easier access through smartphones, according to Ryan.

"Having very little friction in investing and having everything at your fingertips, and then having a really seamless mobile experience where it's not clunky, I think, plays a big part of that," he said.

A Robinhood spokesperson told CNBC its products are designed to appeal to a number of customers, saying that "we don't believe it's accurate to characterize" its transfer promotions as specifically targeting "active traders who are trading on margin or may trade on margin." The company said it tries to "meet users where they are," and they "reject any implication" that the company is "encouraging risky trading."

Robinhood's margin debt isn't the only one reaching records. Total margin debt hit an all-time high of around $1.5 trillion in June, per the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, which incorporates data on both institutional investors such as hedge funds and retail investors.

Not all of that debt is driven by fresh borrowing due to new borrowing decisions. For example, as equities rise in value, an investor may need to cover a short position that's been marked to market, or valued at its current price.

Nonetheless, Sam Huszczo, chief investment officer at SGH Wealth Management, thinks the market's bull run — which has seen multiple record highs this year alone — is feeding a shift in investor psychology, and margin debt is one sign.

"That's greed," the founder said, adding that it's "not everywhere" in the market, but it's "certainly creeping into pockets."

"Margin, that's only the tip of the iceberg of what we can see," he continued. "Fear of missing out is just the emotion of jealousy with a brokerage account."

Huszczo considers the market to actually be "way healthier" than people think. Though he recognizes that increasing margin debt and the rise of risky assets such as leveraged ETFs inject more fragility in the system.

"People need to differentiate between what's a legitimate momentum growth investment and what's reckless chasing," Huszczo also said.

Huszczo shares the commonly held belief among financial advisors that investors' portfolios shouldn't be overly concentrated in one stock or even one sector.

Yet Luu has been zeroed in on Tesla ever since he bought his first share in late 2019. Earlier that year, he had started his current job — a time when he knew nothing about investing, he said. It wasn't until a co-worker told him to download Robinhood months later that he began looking into stocks and other assets.

"I started making money, and I quickly learned, 'Now I'm making money, what do I do with it?'" he said. "I started investing in index funds and even in crypto, and then I did the math. I looked at the returns, and I was like, 'This is very slow returns. I'm never gonna reach retirement, financial independence until like 65.'"

Little did he know that a decision he had made that summer would become his guiding light.

"I was choosing between a Honda Civic and a Tesla Model 3, and my friend, he scheduled a test drive for me to drive the Model 3," Luu said. "My plan was only to go into it just to test drive it. I wasn't going to buy anything. I wasn't going to put in any reservation. Long story short, after the test drive, I put in my reservation the same day, and I got the car like two weeks later."

Seeing the value the car provides in his life, Luu said he can envision a future where electric and autonomous vehicles are commonplace. Because of how much he believes in that future, he considers Tesla the "easiest" investment he's made, and over the course of seven years of investing in the company, he has generally held his shares.

However, things got a bit more difficult with his strategy when Tesla shares began falling in 2022, putting him in the vulnerable position of potentially receiving a margin call. 2022 was Tesla's worst year on record, with the stock finishing off the year at $123.18 after a roughly 65% decline.

In search of more capital, Luu made a serious financial decision with his mother's approval.

"I refinanced the house to get access to an extra $30,000 of capital, and I used that to pay down my margin debt," he said.

Luu understands the level of risk that accompanies trading with margin. Because he's been using margin for most of the nearly seven years he's been investing in Tesla, he has deemed his investing strategy "gambling with an asterisk."

For now, it has paid off. In the last five years, Tesla shares have risen more than 43% to $375. However, the volatile stock is about 25% off of its all-time high near $499.

"It's very easy to see it as gambling, because obviously all your money is in one stock, and that's inherently risky," he said. "But the reason why I say there's nuance to it is because it's a matter of investing temperament, financial discipline and time horizon."

With a time horizon of "many decades," a temperament he labels as "very calm and collected" and a "very high" conviction in Tesla, Luu believes he's "at no risk of panic selling," even when the market tanks.

Still, the situation points out another danger: Missing an opportunity to make an investment when an equity is undervalued. When Luu was scrambling to raise funds to meet his margin obligation, it reduced his flexibility to purchase more Tesla shares at the lower price.

Margin levels this high have been followed by risk-off periods in equities.

Whenever monthly margin debt has grown above 45% year over year since 1960, there were declines in the stock market five out of six times, data from Fundstrat Global Advisors shows. June's margin debt record came in at 49%, but the S&P 500 has still added more than 13% in 2026. A swing into the red by year-end in accordance with this historic pattern would be a dramatic move — one that would be considered highly unusual for the stock market.

The firm also found that the median performance for S&P 500 forward returns following a breakout of 40% year-over-year margin debt growth has been worse off 12 months later as opposed to one month after it. To be exact, the S&P 500's median 12-month forward return is a 4.2% decline, while the median one-month return is a drop of 2.2%.

In essence, the more rapidly margin debt rises, the worse it is for S&P 500 returns over 12 months.

While margin debt doesn't necessarily cause S&P 500 declines, it can exacerbate existing moves to the downside if there's a significant amount of leverage in the market, said Hardika Singh, economic strategist at Fundstrat.

"The premise of gains beget gains, it turns into losses beget losses, and that's what's troublesome," Singh said. "You have these losses, they keep piling up, and then the stock gets sold, and everyone's starting to close out their position, and it becomes this huge train wreck that's very hard to stop, and it adds a lot of volatility to the market."

Then again, Singh sees why investors like Luu are leaning into such a risky strategy. "No one ever got rich by diversifying," she said.

Luu, who said he's been a "hobbyist" from an early age, has folded in investing as one of his many hobbies, which include activities like climbing and playing guitar. It's become such a hobby that he's created his own social media account detailing his investing journey.

Even if Luu reaches his financial goals, he "wouldn't ever stop investing," he said. Instead, he said he "would probably start investing in SpaceX."

It's not just Luu who views trading as a hobby.

Fundstrat's Singh explained that American traders, particularly younger ones, feel they have to take bigger risks to get ahead. She said it's part of a broader trend dubbed financial nihilism, in which young investors grappling with a tough job market and high inflation turn to less-stable investing tools.

"It makes a lot of sense why individuals, specifically retail investors, keep gravitating towards this margin debt," the economic strategist added. "This is like a drug, and I think people just can't get enough of it in this economy."

Kevin Davis, a 59-year-old retail investor who made a living as a rapper in the 1980s and '90s before becoming a stock broker, believes the risks with leveraged trading outweigh the rewards.

"It's gambling. You're borrowing money you don't have, and so if it goes the other way, now you have a clock on your money, and it's ticking," said Davis, who owns an investing technology platform. "The market's not going to save you. It never does."

"Don't play the margin game," the Florida resident warned.

Luu became an engineering consultant because his father, who died of lung cancer in 2012, exposed him to computing. His mother said that between her two sons, Luu most resembles his father not only in terms of his features but also his character.

Reflecting on what her late husband might have thought about Luu's investing pursuits, Nguyen paused for a moment, holding a slight smile.

She then said, "He would've said he's proud of him."

— CNBC's Charlotte Morabito and Deena Zaidi contributed to this report.

#3410. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

Apple revenue beat Wall Street forecasts rising 12% for the fiscal fourth quarter ended in September, led by strong iPhone sales. Mac sales boomed. The giant services sector, home of Apple TV, was a hair soft and numbers for iPads and Wearables were below estimates.

Earnings per share were boosted by a hefty tariff refund.

“Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue … with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever,” said John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO. “We’re closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season.” Watch on Deadline

Apple’s iPhone sales hit $57.58 billion, up 17%. Wall Street – as always – is laser focused on those numbers. Q4 included eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales. Apple’s buzzy, foldable flagship iPhone Duo didn’t hit stores until after the quarter was over.

The company also raised prices on iPhones by $100.

Services, the company’s second-largest segment, came in a $31.57 billion in revenue, up 9.8%. Apple TV had a record Emmy haul this year (28 wins) and in late September claimed its biggest weekly viewership ever with Mayday, Ted Lasso and post-Emmys bumps for Pluribus and Widow’s Bay.

The numbers are falling into a noisy quarter with AI-focused tech stocks (not Apple) emerging Monday from a weeklong bloodbath on spending jitters. Apple is seen as a safe haven with so called AI “hyper-scalers” from Alphabet to Microsoft to Amazon to Meta having lost massive market value in the past week on investors’ growing angst over spending.

Apple (shares up 25% year to date) has in fact been touching the $5 trillion market cap on and off, a feat achieved only by one other company, Nvidia.

The company doesn’t “need to spend [as much] on capex but will let everyone else spend, on frontier models and compute. And we will all use our iPhones to get to it,” Gil Luria from D.A. Davidson. told Bloomberg TV. “Siri will be our personal assistant. And the companies behind Siri — we don’t care.”

Apple is impacted, however, by global shortages of memory and flash storage that’s a complicated byproduct of the AI boom.

“In our view, the September numbers are the appetizer, and the December quarter numbers are the main course as it covers the first full period of iPhone 18 demand and the iPhone Duo launch (Oct. 23),” said tech analyst Dan Ives, ahead of the numbers. The stock will trade on how Ternus frames supply, memory costs and the holiday quarter. Just as important is how he frames himself: this is the Street’s first chance to hear Ternus set priorities on AI, product cadence and capital allocation, and we expect him to lean into the product roadmap as the core of the Apple story.”

There have been some reports that the Duo can crack with normal use. Apple acknowledged the issue last month, saying it affected a small number of devices. Even still, it’s been very hard to match supply to robust demand for the new phone.

Ternus CEO will take questions on his first quarterly analysts call set for 5 pm PT.

#3407. Picard Is the Ultimate Leader. Our Elected Officials Should Take Note

The death of Patrick Stewart last week generated an outpouring of grief for one of the greatest actors of our time.

Amid the mourning, there has been another lamentation, for Stewart’s most famous character, Captain Jean-Luc Picard, the commander of the U.S.S. Enterprise on the television series Star Trek: The Next Generation.

TNG, which aired from 1987 to 1994, offered a vision of sincere optimism and hope that today is often met with outright hostility. Picard is an avatar of classic liberalism. He is a champion of egalitarianism, tolerance, and (dare one say it?) diversity.

It was Stewart’s portrayal of Picard that imprinted a vision of enlightened leadership on generations of fans around the world — an ideal that is disappearing from American political life.

Compare Picard with the grubby politicians of our time, with their venal passions, petty tyrannies, and endless narcissism. Contrast the captain who never mistook violence for strength nor diplomacy for weakness with the bloodthirsty xenophobes who lead us today. Consider a cultured man of endless humility against the anti-intellectual poseurs and swaggering demagogues who dominate contemporary discourse.

Does America today offer leaders who compare favorably with the ideal manifested in Picard?

In “The Drumhead,” an episode of TNG that aired in 1991, an apparent act of sabotage aboard the Enterprise prompts an investigation. As suspicions of a traitor among the crew run rampant, an innocent officer whose racial ancestry singles him out becomes chief suspect. He is persecuted by investigators who use extraordinary powers to turn their inquiry into a paranoid witch hunt.

Picard is alert to the danger from the start. Rather than indulging investigators or capitalizing on the crisis for career advancement, he risks his professional reputation and freedom to stand against prosecutorial overreach, outraged at the idea that individual liberty must be sacrificed on the altar of national security. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

“With the first link, the chain is forged. The first speech censured, the first thought forbidden, the first freedom denied — chains us all irrevocably,” he tells the chief investigator.

Patrick Stewart the actor did not create the lead character of Star Trek: The Next Generation, who is the brainchild of the series creator, Gene Roddenberry. Dozens of writers and producers labored for years to craft Picard into an icon.

Roddenberry’s earlier creation, Captain James T. Kirk, is the embodiment of Kennedy-era astronautical derring-do. The first Star Trek had the swashbuckling sensibility of midcentury adventure novels and 1950s Westerns, and Kirk is Gunsmoke’s Marshal Matt Dillon and C.S. Forester’s Horatio Hornblower, as much as he is John Glenn or Neil Armstrong.

But Picard is different. Although conceived in the 1980s, he isn’t a simple product of the Reagan-era late Cold War. He is a timeless Renaissance man cut from an eternal mold, an epic commander and statesman.

The idea of Picard is ridiculous: a valiant 24th-century Frenchman possessing a taste for Earl Grey tea, the sonorous accent and manners of a perfect English gentleman, and the can-do pragmatism of a Yankee engineer. All at once, he possesses the self-assuredness of De Gaulle, the rhetorical flair of Churchill, and the administrative skill of Eisenhower — free of the historical baggage and pedestrian political compromises that defined each in reality. Related Content Patrick Stewart Knew There Was a Scrooge in All of Us. His Work Was the Cure See Sir Patrick Stewart Become ‘Cowboy Pat’ in Cheeky Country Infomercial Ian McKellen Honors Close Friend Patrick Stewart: ‘A Man to Rely On, to Admire and In My Case, Love’ Kevin Feige, Hugh Jackman, Seth MacFarlane Remember Patrick Stewart: ‘This One Hurts’

Picard is the embodiment of Enlightenment ideals, a Transatlantic hero so noble and fantastical that such a man can only exist on paper.

Patrick Stewart made Jean-Luc Picard real.

Somehow he pulled this great captain out of the ether, as if plucking a star from the firmament of heaven and bringing it to life, to live amongst us earthbound. Who else could summon such a creation into being through sheer art? It is the performance that makes Picard.

The Star Trek universe has always been enthralled by Shakespeare, and it was the Shakespearean actor Stewart who returned the favor, bringing the Bard’s works to life throughout the series he led. Plays-within-plays lay scattered across The Next Generation’s seven-year run, and one never knew when they’d encounter Prince Hal or Prospero on the Enterprise’s holodeck — let alone Sherlock Holmes or Mark Twain.

Stewart made it convincing for a military technocrat to recite long passages of literature from memory, whether Shakespeare’s sonnets, the “Epic of Gilgamesh,” or Moby-Dick. Picard was interested in archaeology and history, in art and music. He could play a flute as adeptly as wield a phaser. The literature and the learning were central to the character — and to his leadership.

The captain of the Enterprise is a warrior poet. He is a statesman, a scientist, and a practical philosopher of formidable intellect and fierce passion. Picard commands men in battle with courage, defends their rights with acuity, and pacifies them with reason. He is a man of physical courage and boundless curiosity, of infinite compassion and deep learning — and he will never back down from a fight when it matters.

Moral conundrums are as central to TNG’s plots as any prosthetic-foreheaded aliens, action sequences, or space battles. Most episodes feature an intractable dilemma that requires much rhetorical debate before the protagonists arrive, some 40 minutes later, at a satisfactory conclusion.

That a broadcast television space opera was often formulaic is immaterial. It wasn’t the action or the special effects, but the ethical and moral debates that set the show apart, the running trial of high ideas and principles. And in that trial, Picard would take the role of prosecution or defense, as warranted. But win or lose, he was ever the Platonic philosopher-king, seeking virtue and justice for the betterment of all.

To Picard, duty and principle outweigh personal interests. Authority carries with it obligations. While it is noble to commit oneself to larger-than-life institutions and the greater good, sometimes bureaucracy gets it wrong and hierarchies must be challenged. Picard scorns tyrants. While rank and discipline matter, the chain of command never trumps right action. And always must the individual be protected from arbitrary abuses of power.

Because on Picard’s ship, everyone matters — or no one does.

In an interview in 1991, after the fall of the Berlin Wall and shortly before the collapse of the Soviet Union, Roddenberry described what was distinct about Picard over the earlier Kirk. Picard was the product of a civilization that had matured not just technologically, but morally, Roddenberry said. He was intended to be the paragon of what humanity could become.

Stewart’s accomplishment was making that paragon human. His acting was the reason Americans sat, week after week, watching a series of morality plays featuring a bald, middle-aged, cerebral European in a space opera.

If one considers the grim and bloody chapter of the 20th century that was drawing to a close in the late 1980s through the early Nineties when TNG aired, it isn’t surprising that a show espousing optimism, and a character defined by enlightened leadership, became such a sensation.

My grandparents, who grew up in Depression-era Dust Bowl Kansas, loved Star Trek: The Next Generation, watching each new episode as it was broadcast on Sunday night. They died around the same time the show completed its original run, long before I ever considered questioning them about it.

But it’s easy to imagine the show’s steady idealism resonated, that they saw in Picard a reflection of their own values. There was a time in America when people aspired to be like Stewart’s character: intelligent, cultured, and self-reliant; a time when Americans thought public servants should be restrained, considerate, and wise.

At the end of the Cold War, it was easy to believe that humanity had overcome some of its greatest challenges, that history is an endless upward trajectory of progress and improvement.

TNG’s United Federation of Planets is Pax Americana, a noble alliance of willing participants all shouldering their share of the burden in a quest for greater prosperity and a better life. Starfleet is collective security in space, a disparate group of alien peoples all bound together by shared values, willing to stand firm against threats to peace and liberty.

It’s become quite difficult to believe in such things now.

Perhaps all of it was always an illusion. Perhaps the post-World War II order the United States helped build is, and always was, no more real than the imagined universe of a science-fiction show. No more real than the words enshrined in America’s founding documents: “All men are created equal.”

Many argue that all high-minded ideals are a utopian pipe-dream, that in the real world, might makes right and power is acquired through blood and conquest.

TNG, for all that it was often just a silly sci-fi show, was a dream of a brighter future. It was a fantasy of humanity living its most meaningful existence.

If you want to tear it down, you must reckon with Captain Picard, a fictional character who lives on in the minds of millions because of Patrick Stewart.

In one of TNG’s most powerful episodes, “Darmok,” an alien captain sacrifices his life fighting alongside Picard against a great beast, trying to establish understanding despite his race speaking only in unintelligible allegories. As his counterpart lays dying, Picard relates to him the ancient Sumerian tale of Enkidu’s death, quoting King Gilgamesh as he mourns his friend’s passing.

“He who was my companion, through adventure and hardship, is gone forever.” Trending Stories Michael Douglas Gives Update on Jack Nicholson: He's 'Well' But Has 'Disappeared' Yes, Matt Damon and David Letterman Were Background Actors on ‘The Gilded Age’ Season Premiere Marty Erlichman, Barbra Streisand’s Manager Since the 1960s, Dead at 97 Martha Stewart ‘Distressed’ by Backlash to Her Homeless Halloween Costume

Captain Picard may be gone, but his legacy remains. Among the many heartfelt tributes being shared in the wake of Stewart’s passing, one fan summed it up simply.

“If ever you don’t know what the right thing to do is, just do what Captain Picard would do.”

#3406. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3405. Grail Names ‘Skateland’ Director Anthony Burns As In-House Creative Producer

EXCLUSIVE: Writer, director and producer Anthony Burns has joined U.S. production and rep company Grail as in-house creative producer to develop and package original film and TV projects.

Burns made his feature directorial debut with Skateland, which he co-wrote and produced. The coming of-age drama premiered at Sundance in 2010, screened at SXSW and starred Shiloh Fernandez and Ashley Greene. He subsequently directed and produced Home Sweet Hell, starring Patrick Wilson, Katherine Heigl and Jordana Brewster.

His producing credits include Monica, starring Trace Lysette and Patricia Clarkson; the Jimi Hendrix biopic Jimi: All Is by My Side, starring André Benjamin; and Green Is Gold. He recently served as showrunner on José vs. Mourinho, Grail’s collaboration with Coca-Cola and Goal for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and collaborated with Bianca on the original project A Song To Raise The Dead. #3403. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3402. Josh Hartnett, Emma Thompson, Sally Hawkins, Danny Huston, Robert Aramayo & Chloe Pirrie Join Elle Fanning & Julianne Moore In Rebecca Miller’s ‘Moonsong: A Life In Seven Verses’ – AFM

EXCLUSIVE: Rebecca Miller’s biopic Moonsong: A Life In Seven Verses, starring Elle Fanning as ‘Goodnight Moon’ and ‘The Runaway Bunny’ children’s author Margaret Wise Brown, has added a roster of A-listers to its ensemble cast as The Veterans prepares to launch international sales at the AFM.

Josh Hartnett (Verity), Academy Award winner Emma Thompson (Sense and Sensibility), Academy Award nominee Sally Hawkins (The Shape Of Water), Golden Globe nominee Danny Huston (Diamond), Bafta Award winner Robert Aramayo (I Swear) and Chloe Pirrie (Emma) are set to join Academy Award nominee Fanning and her previously announced co-star Academy Award winner Julianne Moore. Related Stories News Thriller 'Games We Play', With 'Riverdale' Star Casey Cott, Heads To AFM & Gets North American Release News Hockey's Hollywood Moment Hits AFM As Liam Neeson Will Play Legendary Coach In 'Believe 13' About Bond With Injured High School Star

The Veterans will launch sales at the AFM with a sizzle reel and screenplay, handling international sales outside the U.S., while CAA Media Finance will represent U.S. rights. Watch on Deadline

Set in 1930s New York, the film follows Wise Brown as she discovers her gift for writing children’s stories and pioneers a new, sensory approach to children’s literature alongside a community of brilliant artists and educators.

At once innocent and brazen, she leads a complex life marked by passionate love affairs with the socialite “Big Bill” Gaston and the poet Michael Strange, whose mesmerizing yet destructive influence shapes her journey towards forging her own artistic voice and the children’s masterpieces which since have sold more than 300 million copies in more than 25 languages.

Fanning, who has just hit the big screen in The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping and is soon to be seen in The Nightingale after a high-profile 2025-26 awards season with Oscar winner Sentimental Value, co-stars opposite Moore as Michael Strange and Hartnett as “Big Bill” Gaston.

DGA and Emmy Award winner Miller directs and wrote the screenplay based on Leonard S. Marcus’s biography Margaret Wise Brown: Awakened by the Moon.

Moonsong: A Life In Seven Verses is Miller’s ninth film with her filmography including Angela (1995), Personal Velocity (2002); The Ballad of Jack and Rose (2005), The Private Lives of Pippa Lee (2009), Maggie’s Plan (2015), Arthur Miller: Writer (2017), an Emmy-nominated HBO documentary; and She Came To Me (2023).

Most recently, she directed Mr. Scorsese (2025), a five-part documentary portrait about Martin Scorsese for Apple TV+, which won the Emmy Award for Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Series, the DGA Award for Outstanding Directorial Achievement in Documentary Series / News, and two Critics Choice Documentary Awards for Best Biographical Documentary and Best Limited Documentary Series.

“Margaret Wise Brown is one of the most fascinating characters I have ever encountered. She never lost her child-like view of the world, yet also became a phenomenon within her business, publishing over a hundred books, including Goodnight Moon, Little Fur Family, The Runaway Bunny, books which have become a part of the fabric of our culture,” said Miller, who also wrote the screenplay.

“At once innocent and feral, often feeling out of place in the human world, yet an arch-communicator, sexually liberated yet prey to complex and painful love affairs, the sole guardian of her own creative flame—Margaret feels profoundly modern to me, and I believe, played by Elle Fanning, she will be a totem for young people who are looking for a way to live without compromising the multiplicity of their true selves.”

The creative team also includes Oscar-nominated cinematographer Jarin Blatchke (The Lighthouse, Nosferatu); Academy Award-winning veteran special effects artist Neal Scanlan (Project Hail Mary, Star Wars Sequel trilogy), who is renowned for his work in creature effects, animatronics and puppetry. Academy Award nominee Malgosia Turzanska (Hamnet) will serve as costume designer, while Kim Jennings will oversee production design.

The film will be produced by Round Films (Damon Cardasis and Rebecca Miller). The book was brought to Round Films by Amanda Goodwin, Keri Selig and Sasha Alexander. Martin Scorsese will serve as executive producer.

Miller is represented by CAA, Entertainment 360, 42 West and George Sheanshang. Fanning is repped by UTA, TFC Management, and Hansen Jacobsen. Moore is repped by WME, Entertainment 360, Apex PR.

Hartnett is repped by CAA, Entertainment 360, David Weber at Sloan, Offer, Weber & Dern, and Patricola Public Relations. Thompson is repped by CAA. Hawkins is repped by CAA. Houston is repped by Julian Belfrage Associates, UTA, Untitled and Narrative PR. Aramayo is repped by CAA, 42 in the UK, MJ Management, and Shelter PR. Pirrie is repped by Julian Belfrage Associates, Entertainment 360, Prosper PR.

The film will start shooting in May 2027.

#3401. Hollywood Unions Wonder Whether Next California Governor Will Share Newsom’s Commitment To Expanding Film Tax Credits

The leaders of the major Hollywood unions are glad to hear outgoing California Governor Gavin Newsom’s proposal Monday to expand the state’s Film & TV Tax Credit program yet again, but they won’t be declaring victory until his successor makes it a cornerstone of their tenure, too.

“We thank the Governor for his commitment to our members and this industry,” the Entertainment Union Coalition — which includes SAG-AFTRA, IATSE, DGA, WGAW, Teamsters, AFM, and LiUNA — said in a statement Monday morning. “The EUC is looking forward to working with the next Governor and the Legislature on a proportionate response that takes into account the size of the workforce and infrastructure in California and also modernizes the various structural elements that limit the program’s competitiveness. What is clear is we all share the desire to see our industry thrive in California.”

Newsom declared on Monday that California needs “at least” $1 billion in annual tax credits allocated for film and television productions, which would boost the state’s incentive program by another $250 million. This comes after the soon-to-be ex Governor Newsom pushed the state Legislature to approve a massive infusion into the fund last year, more than doubling it from $330 million to $750 million. Watch on Deadline

The state has been somewhat successful in luring production back to the state. For example, CBS’ Tracker now films in California as of Season 4, as do Netflix’s The Night Agent, Apple TV’s Stick, and Prime Video’s Mr & Mrs Smith. Other notable productions taking advantage of the state’s incentive program are Big Little Lies, I Love LA, Fallout, and The Pitt, to name a few.

Still, particularly in Los Angeles, production declines continue. The state is competing with international territories as well as other states with more robust incentive structures.

Teamsters Local 399 Secretary-Treasurer and At-Large Vice President told Deadline in a remark of her own that the program “has always and will always be about jobs,” and that Newsom’s proposal does not go far enough to address the urgent need in California.

“And while we have seen it work for our state, without a real commitment to further invest in our program, and make key structural changes, we will continue to lose competitive ground as others continue to poach the economic benefits of our industry,” her statement reads.

Dougherty argues that California’s program needs to be uncapped in order to compete with regions like New York, as well as those abroad — and that is only one part of the solution. She also reiterated the need to continued support for a federal tax incentive, which lawmakers officially introduced to Congress in September.

“While we appreciate the Governors support of our industry, and the important jobs it creates, his comments today come a day late and yet again, some dollars short,” Doughter said in her statement. “Our industry cannot survive on expressions of support alone. We need action, investment, and a real commitment to keeping these jobs in California. Teamsters and the other Hollywood Unions and Guilds are prepared to do the work. The question is whether our next Governor will match that commitment.”

The 65-inch LG Evo C6 OLED TV has dropped to $1,399.99 from $1,599.99, a $200 price cut that brings it to its lowest price ever, according to price trackers—and the savings aren't limited to this particular size either, with discounts extending across the C6 lineup, from the compact 42-inch model to the massive 83-inch version, although the 65-inch screen is particularly appealing if you want a larger OLED without spending more than $1,500. You also get a 90-day free trial of Amazon Music with the purchase and complimentary room-of-choice delivery (which would otherwise cost you an extra $19.99).

Beyond the discount, there's plenty to like about the C6 itself, with PCMag calling it an excellent midrange OLED that is slightly brighter than last year’s Evo C5 while still retaining its color accuracy and sleek design, giving you much of what makes LG’s flagship OLEDs appealing at a considerably lower price. The nearly bezel-free design also keeps the focus on the picture, while its 4K OLED panel delivers bright HDR highlights in Dolby Vision, HDR10, and HLG content. That should work well in most living rooms, although a particularly sunny space may still benefit from a brighter Mini-LED TV.

For streaming, LG’s webOS platform covers most major services, and AirPlay and Google Cast make it easy to share videos or photos directly from your phone. You can also use hands-free voice controls through LG's assistant, Google Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot to search for content or ask questions without reaching for the remote. Gamers will also appreciate the C6’s native 120Hz panel, which supports variable refresh rates up to 165Hz, along with AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync compatibility to help keep fast-moving games smooth and tear-free. It’s also highly responsive, with an input lag of just 4.6 milliseconds at 1080p120 and 12.8 milliseconds at 4K60.

The C6’s main drawback is its Wi-Fi 5 connection, which feels dated for a TV at this price, although it should still handle most 4K streaming without trouble. It also lacks an ATSC 3.0 tuner, meaning you won't get support for newer over-the-air broadcast standards.

The mouse has a 3.1in touchscreen supporting app-specific shortcuts as well as a mini multi-touch trackpad and customizable hardware buttons …

The project is currently live on Kickstarter, with a funding deadline of December 8th. Kickstarter pricing is $199, with retail pricing set to start at $249.

Super Mouse features a 3.1″ touchscreen that gives you a faster way to get things done. Turn your everyday actions into one-touch shortcuts. Launch your favorite apps. Switch tools. Run the commands you use most. All with a simple tap.

And you’re in control of what goes on the screen. Choose the shortcuts you want for each app, arrange them the way you like, and Super Mouse automatically brings up the right ones as you switch between apps […]

Super Mouse comes with customizable physical Hyper Keys that let you trigger your favorite shortcuts and even entire workflows with a single press. Need to open multiple apps, run a series of commands, or repeat the same steps throughout your workday? Set up a Hyper Key to do it all with one press.

Double-tap, and Super Mouse becomes a multi-touch trackpad. Switch to trackpad mode and use familiar finger gestures to scroll, swipe, and zoom.

You can also display some content directly on the mouse screen, and even access a swipe keyboard.

Everything is configured via a companion app, which is available for both macOS and Windows. Once configured, the mouse detects the app you’re using and automatically displays the controls you’ve created for it. You can create different profiles for work, home, and more.

#3397. These Surprisingly Powerful Soundcore Earbuds Are Under $35 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3394. Amazon announced five new Alexa devices, including 16-inch Echo Show

Apple recently launched new HomePod mini speakers and its HomeView smart display, and today it’s Amazon’s turn with five new Alexa devices.

This includes a new Echo speaker with visual intelligence and an Echo Show with a larger 16-inch display and a nanomatte option …

The latest smart device lineup kicks off with a next-generation Echo Dot speaker, which includes a home hub, on-device AI capabilities, and a built-in Wi-Fi extender.

For the first time, it includes a built-in smart home hub, so Alexa connects to thousands of compatible devices such as lights, locks, and thermostats right out of the box—plus a built-in eero Wi-Fi extender adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage to your existing network. At its core is Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon, with a new AI Accelerator for on-device AI that sharpens conversational detection and filters out background noise. Music, audiobooks, and podcasts sound great on the new Echo Dot, with crisp vocals and 50% more bass than its predecessor.

The Dot is available today for $99.99, with special Kids editions for $109.99 that include a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids+.

The Echo Studio is a better speaker that now includes HomePod-like room mapping and a camera that allows a live view of your home as well as Alexa-powered visual intelligence features.

Echo Studio with Home Camera takes Amazon’s best-sounding speaker and gives it a richer understanding of the room around it, making Alexa even more useful. The same powerful audio architecture is still at its core—a high-excursion woofer and Dolby Atmos filling the room with immersive spatial sound, now continuously tuned to your space with Advanced Room Adaptation. What’s new is context: with more awareness of its surroundings, Alexa can help in real time—explaining the rules on a board game box you hold up, recognizing a box of cereal to help you reorder it, or letting you check in on the room from the Alexa app while you’re away.

The original Echo Studio without the camera is $219.99, while the new model is available today at $249.99.

The new Echo Time has a display that gradually brightens to mimic a sunrise as your alarm time approaches, and a sleep sensor provides the option of waking you when you’re in a lighter sleep phase.

Echo Time is purpose-built for the bedside—with a customizable display and camera-free design to make waking up and winding down effortless. Make it yours with hundreds of clock faces to choose from—including everything from analog and modern to playful designs and even your favorite sports teams. Its new sleep sensing technology, powered by Omnisense, can sense when you’re in lighter sleep and wakes you within 10 to 60 minutes of your scheduled alarm, no wearable device required. As your alarm approaches, the display gradually brightens to mimic a natural sunrise and the tone builds gently to help ease you awake.

The standard model is available today for $199.99, with a kids version again at $10 more with a year of Kids+ included.

These devices would be a lot more appealing if Amazon didn't stuff them with ads, and keep updating the software with more ads years after you bought it.

A new photo frame syncs to Amazon Photos to show the latest photos as you take them, with the ability to ask Alexa to find the photos you want to display.

Most of the photos we love never leave our phones. The Alexa Photo Frame changes that—pairing the timeless elegance of a traditional frame with the intelligence of Alexa, so your best memories are always on display. It’s the first photo frame with Alexa built in, and it works effortlessly: connect it to Amazon Photos and your pictures sync automatically, with new ones appearing as they’re taken. Alexa intelligently surfaces the shots worth seeing—the ones where you’re smiling, in the right season—and skips the screenshots and clutter. Just ask to see photos of a favorite person, pet, or trip, or swipe through right on the 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen, where every picture looks crisp and vibrant from any angle.

The Alexa Photo Frame is available today for $199.99 in black or $229 in real birch or walnut.

Finally, the tablet-like Echo Show 15 has been upgraded to offer 10% more viewing area on a 16-inch screen in a thinner device with a nanomatte anti-reflective option. Like Apple’s HomeView, there are options for placing on a countertop via an iMac-like stand or mounting on a wall.

The all-new Echo Show 16 is our most advanced display yet, with 20% more power for interactions that feel fast. The 16-inch high-definition screen is nearly 40% thinner with 10% more viewing area, and a new Nanomatte option cuts glare by more than 90% while keeping detail and color razor-sharp. Screen Styles transform it into whatever your home needs most—a family organizer with color-coded calendars, chores, and meal plans; a digital photo frame; or a smart home dashboard with the new Alexa Home Map, showing every light, lock, thermostat, and camera right where it lives in your home. Plus, it has the full Fire TV experience, built in. Echo Show 16 has our best-ever camera on an Echo Show, featuring the widest field of view, auto-framing that keeps everyone in view, and—for the first time—night vision, so you can check in with Live View day or night.

The Echo Show 16 is available for pre-order today at $499.99 or $569.99 with the nanomatte screen. Availability hasn’t yet been confirmed, with the company simply saying that it will begin shipping “later this year.”
