#3346. Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

His data systems make sure Claude’s answers are accurate

IEEE Senior Member Gurmeet Saran is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind Claude’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

If you’ve ever wondered how Claude and similar AI agents can answer complex questions in seconds and where they get the information, you’re not alone.

Gurmeet Saran works to find that answer every day as an engineer at Anthropic in San Francisco, the AI research company behind Claude. The IEEE senior member is developing an infrastructure to understand the mechanics behind the chatbot’s behavior and to ensure its underlying architecture produces reliable outputs.

Gurmeet Saran Employer Anthropic in San FranciscoTitle Member of technical staffMember grade IEEE senior memberAlma maters University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

University of Kalyani, in India; Birla Institute of Technology and Science, in Pilani, India

Safety is a priority for Anthropic, he says. According to Claude’s mission statement, the company wants the AI agent to be “genuinely helpful to the people it works with or on behalf of, as well as to society, while avoiding actions that are unsafe, unethical, or deceptive.” Crucial to the mission is ensuring that researchers can observe and understand how AI models behave, a challenge that is especially acute for large language models, Saran says.

“We have decent tools to monitor databases and web services,” he says, “but for LLMs, we’re still figuring it out.”

Saran’s interest in computing systems dates back to his childhood in Kolkata, where he logged as much time as he could in the school computer lab.

“I remember the first time I used one of the computers,” he says. “What struck me was that you could write instructions, and the machine would follow them exactly. No ambiguity.

After graduating from high school in 1999, he stayed in India to pursue advanced degrees. He earned a bachelor’s degree in electronics and telecommunication engineering in 2004 at the University of Kalyani. In 2010, he earned a master’s degree in software engineering from the Birla Institute of Technology and Science in Pilani.

While a graduate student, he began his career in 2007 at Yahoo as a technical lead of the data team in Bengaluru, India. While there, he encountered the project that shaped his career trajectory: working on web analytics and business intelligence reporting solutions.

“We kept running into a frustrating problem,” he recalls. “Different teams would calculate the same website metric—something like daily active site users—using slightly different logic, and end up with conflicting answers. It sounds like a small issue, but when leadership is making decisions about resource allocation and product development using that data, not knowing which number is correct becomes a problem.”

The team built a central data repository with defined metrics, essentially serving as a single source of truth. Saran created a model that defined what “daily active site users” means, breaking down which events counted, how to handle edge cases (or when standard code fails), and more.

With the new model, data teams across the company could rely on a standard method to determine the number of daily active users for the projects and sites they were responsible for and obtain comparable results using the same logic.

From there, Saran and his team built Yahoo! Digits, an internal web analytics tool used for all the company’s products.

Saran left Yahoo in 2010 to join Intuit as a staff engineer in Mountain View, Calif. He helped build the analytics infrastructure that unified data across the company’s products, including TurboTax and QuickBooks accounting software. During his tenure, Intuit developed a feature that detected fraudulent tax filings in real time. It required Saran and other engineers to build a system to protect taxpayer data while adhering to strict U.S. Internal Revenue Service policies.

“IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations.”

Saran joined Meta (known as Facebook at the time) in 2016 as a lead software engineer in Menlo Park, Calif. The company was facing controversy over its video metrics: Meta publicly acknowledged an error that caused it to overstate the number of views for posted videos.

“This wasn’t a coding bug; it was an architectural problem,” Saran says. He built a system that worked similarly to what he had developed at Intuit, whereby one single truth was defined to govern all video view metrics across the site.

That system, Metric360, eventually became part of the site’s architecture. By the time he left Meta in 2021, he says, Metric360 was being used across the company to calculate video metrics.

He left the company to become a principal software engineer at Wealthfront, a financial services company in Palo Alto, Calif. He helped build the company’s data infrastructure.

Saran joined Anthropic in 2025 as a member of the technical staff.

To describe the implications of his work, he uses a medical analogy: “Imagine a doctor is monitoring a patient’s vital signs and making treatment decisions based on those numbers. What if one or a few of the medical devices used were slightly miscalibrated? Even if most readings are fine, it’s a serious problem because the difficult decisions happen in the margins.

“It’s the same with AI systems. My job is essentially to make sure the instruments are giving accurate readings—that the data means what it says it means.”

His job comes with high stakes and complex problems to solve.

“AI agents are especially tricky to observe,” he says. “When a system is taking sequences of actions [generating conversational responses with different users], you need a way to capture what it did, what information it was working from, and whether outcomes matched what the end user expected. And you have to do all of that without exposing anyone’s private information—the systems are designed to recognize sensitive data and keep it protected as it flows through. It’s a much more demanding observability problem than anything I’ve worked on before.”

Solving for system reliability while AI is still in its early days of adoption is both Saran’s passion and the problem that keeps him up at night, he says.

“I think making AI systems genuinely auditable and transparent is one of the more important engineering problems of the next decade,” he says, “and it doesn’t get talked about as much as model capabilities do.”

“After more than 20 years of building data infrastructure across organizations like Yahoo, Intuit, Meta, and Wealthfront,” he says, “I wanted to contribute back to the technical community through peer review, publishing, and engaging with the broader engineering research ecosystem.”

He says he believes IEEE can play an essential role in shaping the future of AI through its standards work.

“We have standards for everything, from building codes to software testing,” he says. “AI infrastructure needs something similar, and IEEE has the credibility and the reach to do that.”

Another problem that IEEE can solve for, he says, is access: “IEEE operates in a lot of countries where engineers don’t have easy pathways into the global professional community. That kind of connection matters, especially as AI development spreads beyond a handful of organizations in a few cities.”

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3344. Apple fined $15.5 million as South Korea orders changes to App Store rules

Apple and Google were fined today in South Korea over their app payment practices, with regulators also ordering both companies to change several policies. Here are the details.

South Korea’s Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) announced today a series of fines and corrective orders against Apple and Google over violations of the country’s Telecommunications Business Act.

Specifically for Apple, the KMCC imposed a fine of 20.81 billion won (approximately $15.5 million) and ordered the company to revise its App Store policies regarding payment methods and app review procedures, as well as prevent what it referred to as “discriminatory commission” practices from recurring.

This is the first enforcement case under the 2021 amendment to the Telecommunications Business Act, which introduced prohibited acts for app market operators, such as forcing specific payment methods and unfairly delaying app reviews.

In essence, the decision centers around three violations: forcing specific payment methods, unfairly delaying app reviews, and imposing discriminatory commissions.

On the payment methods front, the KMCC said Apple and Google “effectively forced” developers to use their own in-app payment systems by imposing a 26% commission and additional restrictions on third-party alternatives.

“This constitutes an act in which an app market operator unfairly uses its position in transactions to force mobile content providers and others to use a specific payment method,” the KMCC said.

As a result, Apple and Google must revise their policies to allow external payment methods and address restrictions imposed on developers using alternative payment systems.

As for the app review process, the KMCC found that Apple and Google “delayed app reviews, for example by not providing specific reasons when reviews were delayed or not clearly responding to individual inquiries about the reasons for delays and expected timelines.”

Accordingly, Apple and Google must revise their app review procedures to address these issues.

Finally, on the discriminatory commissions, which applied only to Apple, the KMCC found that between July 2015 and January 2023, the company calculated its 30% commission differently for South Korean and overseas developers. While overseas developers were charged based on prices excluding value-added tax (VAT), South Korean developers were charged based on prices including VAT.

“KMCC determined that this constituted an act of unfairly providing rates, numbers, telecommunications facilities, or other economic benefits for telecommunications services or bundled services in a discriminatory manner compared to other users […].”

The KMCC said Apple will also have to take measures to prevent discriminatory commission practices between South Korean and overseas developers from recurring.

According to Reuters, Apple said it “‌disagreed ⁠with the decision and was evaluating options in accordance with South Korean ​laws.” ​Apple added that “⁠it has worked with outside developers ​to enable innovation ​through ⁠its App Store.”

Today’s decision comes on the heels of similar regulatory pressure in other markets, including Brazil and Japan, where Apple has introduced alternative app distribution and payment options in response to local competition rules.

The company has also faced years of scrutiny in the European Union, where it recently overhauled its App Store fees and business terms to address concerns raised by the European Commission.

To read the KMCC’s full announcement, follow this link.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The redrawn IEEE region map that will become effective in 2028.

Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions.”

The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article.

Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections, governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings.

Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter.

If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org.

#3340. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

#3339. iPhone Duo could capture nearly 30% of foldable market in 2027, per report

In a report released today, TrendForce says that with strong demand for the iPhone Duo out of the gate, Apple is poised to capture nearly 30% of the global foldable smartphone market by 2027. Here are the details.

One day after Apple announced the iPhone Duo last month, TrendForce published a report predicting that the company would ship 5 million units of its first foldable iPhone by the end of 2026, capturing 24.8% of the segment.

At the time, TrendForce expected the overall foldable smartphone market to grow by just 0.5% in 2026, with shipments from Android brands alone falling by more than 20% year over year.

By contrast, TrendForce expected the market to reach 23.5 million shipments in 2027, a 16.3% increase. The firm also suggested that Apple’s entry could help drive future growth through improvements in foldable technology, while new AI use cases could further boost demand.

With the iPhone Duo now shipping for nearly a week, TrendForce published a new report today reiterating its previous projections and forecasting that Apple will capture 29.8% of the foldable smartphone market in 2027.

When has a Samsung or any Android flagship outsold the iPhone...the answer is never. The Duo is already the most popular and most discussed Foldable even with its flaws. Google makes most of their most tracking people and selling ads...Samsung makes most of their money selling memory. Apple makes most of their money selling the iPhone...see the difference. Just facts over feelings

TrendForce notes that Apple’s greatest advantage lies in its ability to integrate chips, operating systems, and its developer ecosystem. As app compatibility and hardware reliability improve, the Duo is expected to further expand the practical value of foldable displays, helping shift competition in the foldable smartphone market from form-factor innovation toward multitasking efficiency.

If TrendForce’s projections pan out, Apple will hold second place in the foldable smartphone market in 2027, behind Samsung, whose share is expected to fall from 35.1% in 2026 to 31.9% next year, and ahead of Huawei, which is projected to drop from 24.8% to 21.3%.

#3338. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3337. Apple and OpenAI trade secrets lawsuit now has an official trial date

Judge Edward Davila today formally established the schedule for Apple’s trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against two former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, including a trial date. Here are the details.

A couple of weeks ago, during an October 14 case management conference, Judge Edward Davila instructed Apple and the defendants to agree on a proposed schedule for the lawsuit, working toward a tentative trial date of July 19, 2027.

The parties were given until October 23 to submit their proposed schedule, which the judge has now formally established.

As we’ve been covering since July, Apple filed this lawsuit accusing the defendants of improperly accessing or using confidential information about its products and technologies to help advance OpenAI’s consumer hardware development efforts.

In recent days, Apple scored two procedural wins in its efforts to obtain expedited discovery, with Judge Davila granting the company access to additional documents and information from the defendants ahead of the normal discovery process.

In a case management order issued today, Davila established July 19, 2027, at 9 a.m. as the official trial date, with additional deadlines for discovery, motions, and pretrial proceedings in the meantime.

Notably, the schedule includes a June 1 deadline for the lead attorneys on both sides to meet and discuss a potential settlement.

To be clear, this is a common procedural step in federal civil lawsuits and does not necessarily indicate that Apple and OpenAI are considering settling the case.

#3335. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3334. Russia now requires Apple to store user communications and hand them over if requested

As Bloomberg reported today, Apple and Microsoft are now subject to Russian regulations requiring companies to store users’ communications and provide them to security agencies if requested. Here are the details.

Apple and Microsoft are now in Russia’s state surveillance registry, joining companies and services such as Google Meet, WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Cloudflare, and Blizzard Entertainment, all of which are required to store users’ messages, audio and video communications, and provide them to Russian security agencies if requested.

According to Bloomberg, Apple and Microsoft were added on October 2 to the “organizers of information dissemination” registry, which is maintained by Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor.

Companies on the list are required under Russian law to store local users’ correspondence, audio and video messages and turn that data over to security services if asked. They must also store in Russia information about users and the transmission of their communications for three years.

Companies that fail to comply can face fines and ultimately have access to their services restricted in Russia. Google and its Google Meet video-calling service were added to the same registry in January.

The move comes as Russia continues to tighten restrictions on foreign messaging services, having already blocked or limited access to platforms such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Signal, and Apple’s FaceTime.

Specific to Apple, the company’s relationship with Russia has become increasingly complicated since the country invaded Ukraine in 2022, prompting Apple to suspend product sales and exports while limiting services such as Apple Pay.

However, Apple continued operating the App Store in Russia, which has led to several disputes with local authorities.

In April, Russian users lost the ability to make new App Store purchases or renew subscriptions without an existing Apple Account balance, following government-imposed payment restrictions.

Apple might get away with it by simply exit Russia's market. It won't impact its economy much, afterall.

But what will happen when China will ask to do the same?

In June, the Kremlin demanded an explanation after Apple removed several apps developed by Russian state-controlled company VK from the App Store. Around the same time, Apple also removed banking apps linked to sanctioned Russian financial institutions.

More recently, in August, Russia’s antitrust regulator opened formal proceedings against Apple over its failure to preinstall the state-backed MAX messaging app and the RuStore app marketplace on its devices.

All of that said, neither Apple nor Microsoft has publicly commented on its inclusion in the registry or indicated whether it intends to comply with the requirements.

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3330. Apple seems to have the right approach to the first touchscreen Mac

Steve Jobs famously dismissed the idea of a touchscreen Mac back in 2010 when he said that it “gives great demo” but turns out to be “ergonomically terrible” in real-life use.

It was inevitable that eyebrows would be raised when the company did a U-turn on this by launching the first touchscreen Mac. But while I have no interest myself, I do think the company’s counterargument some 16 years later makes sense …

We thought about this years ago. We’ve done tons of user testing on this and it turns out it doesn’t work. Touch surfaces don’t want to be vertical. It gives great demo, but after a short period of time you start to fatigue – and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn’t work, it’s ergonomically terrible. Touch surfaces want to be horizontal […] that’s why we’ve perfected our multi-touch trackpads over the years.

Current CEO John Ternus addressed this change of heart directly. Specifically, he said that touch was intended to be a supplementary way of interacting with the machine rather than a primary one.

The Mac is first and foremost an indirect input device, built around the trackpad and keyboard. But I think there’s times when it’s comfortable and handy to have touch.

He suggested that it isn’t the headline feature of the new model.

All of these things, and, oh yeah, it has touch as well.

I’m a Mac guy through and through, right from the original Macintosh back in 1984. I’m also a massive trackpad fan, using the Magic Trackpad on my desk setup rather than a mouse. To me, it’s just the perfect way to control a Mac.

There was a period when I quite frequently used a 12.9-inch iPad with Magic Keyboard as a mobile alternative. Like the new MacBook Pro, that setup offered the choice of using the trackpad built into the keyboard or the touchscreen.

What I noticed about my own usage in this laptop-like configuration is that I almost exclusively used the trackpad. The only time I used the touchscreen was for scrolling, especially when I wanted to scroll a significant way down a page. That absolutely tracks with Ternus’ perspective of trackpad first, touchscreen sometimes.

However, when an M1 MacBook Air replaced my iPad with a Magic Keyboard, I didn’t miss the touchscreen at all.

One of the many things that’s changed over the years, in large part because of Apple’s launch of the iPhone way back in 2007, is that almost an entire generation has grown up with a touch interface. For them, the idea of a laptop without a touchscreen seems somewhat archaic.

However, I do very much suspect that even this generation will still use the trackpad as the primary control mechanism for the very reasons Steve outlined 16 years ago.

I use a 2 in 1 Yoga for years and loved it. So, I’d prefer that the MacBook had a hinge like the Yoga to allow it to fully fold into a “tablet” or “tent” mode. But a touchscreen Mac, even only being allowed to use vertical, is a Giant Leap for mankind! 😄

The nightmare scenario for Mac users was Apple compromising the interface in order to support touch. None of us wanted to lose the high resolution UI elements and see them replaced with giant cartoon-like equivalents. None of us wanted to lose the precise control we get from a trackpad. Thankfully, that hasn’t happened.

So no, I won’t be buying one personally, but I can see why Apple added the feature, and I do think the company has the right attitude to it.

Do you agree, or have a different view? Please share your own take in the comments.

#3328. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3325. iOS 27.3 release date: Here’s when to expect new iPhone features

Apple released iOS 27.2 this week with new features for Messages, Siri AI, and Photos, plus an Apple Music rebrand and more. But work on iOS 27.3 is already well underway, here’s when to expect the next big iPhone update.

If you follow Apple closely, the company’s software release patterns quickly become clear.

For example, iOS 27.2 launched this week right around the same time as Apple’s previous releases in years past.

The only difference is that normally we would have expected iOS 27.1 in the last week of October rather than 27.2. But due to Apple making iOS 27.1 exclusive to iPhone Duo, all software releases for the iOS 27 cycle will be off by one number—despite following the same timing as ever.

That means iOS 27.3 is up next, and its release should align with historic patterns for x.2 updates.

iOS 27.3 is expected to arrive in beta within the next few days—Monday, November 2 is likely.

As for the public launch, here’s what past years have shown for comparable x.2 updates:

27.3 should automatically hide the iPhone Dua dock like ipadOS. And add a new left left-hand user interface with the dock at the left.

Based on this pattern, iOS 27.3 is expected to release in mid-December.

Apple always tries to ship its last software update of the year with a little buffer before taking a holiday break. That way if any major issues arise, the company can develop a quick fix and push it out before much of the company takes time off.

As for new iPhone features in iOS 27.3, we’ll know a lot more after the beta arrives. So far though, at a minimum we’re expecting the additional Siri AI languages Apple announced this week, plus the return of the all-new Health app.

Will you install the iOS 27.3 beta or wait for the release version? Let us know in the comments.

#3322. The LG UltraGear 25G590B sounds like overkill with its 1,000Hz refresh rate — but after testing it, every other monitor feels sluggish

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the time of writing, the LG UltraGear 25G590B is the world’s first monitor with a native 1,000Hz refresh rate. That’s blazing fast, making the monitor perfect for esports gamers. The monitor itself sports a sleek and practical design, and features an adequate number of ports. The panel is bright (though it’s IPS only), and it boasts strong color coverage and accuracy. However, the FHD resolution might be a dealbreaker for some, and so might the 1ms response time. Oh, and it’s expensive, too.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Few monitors are like the LG UltraGear 25G590B. While most monitors top out at 320Hz, and some at 720Hz, the 25G590B kicks it up a notch to a whopping 1,000Hz, making it one of the best gaming monitors for esports. Strong color coverage and accuracy stuffed into a bright 25-inch panel makes for a winning combination. The monitor itself looks sleek and premium.

But is it perfect? Not really. Its FHD panel (which is the competition standard) doesn’t make the monitor an all-rounder. And while its 1ms response time is fine, many of its competitors perform far better with their 0.03ms or even 0.02ms response times. The monitor isn’t the cheapest either, priced at $999.

So, should you still buy it, despite its flaws? Find out in my full LG UltraGear 25G590B review.

Power, 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x DisplayPort 2.1, 1x USB-C (upstream), 1x 4-pole headphones/mic jack

There’s a lot to love about the LG UltraGear 25G590B, from its excellent gaming performance (bolstered by its 1,000Hz refresh rate) and its strong color coverage, to its sleek and practical design.

Supplied by: MSI | Tom's GuideCPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X | Graphics card: MSI RTX 5070 Ti 16GB Vanguard SOC | Motherboard: MSI B850E Gaming Plus WiFi | RAM: Kingston Fury Renegade DDR5 32GB | Cooler: Noctua NH-U12S | PSU: MSI MEG Ai1300P PCIE5 | Case: MSI MPG GUNGNIR 110R

First things first, let’s talk about the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s headline feature, and that’s its 1,000Hz refresh rate, achievable at 1080p.

That’s one thousand frames every second. Let that sink in.

In comparison, the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B ($994) and the Sony Inzone M10S II ($1,099) hit only 720Hz at 720p. 1,000Hz is overkill for most gamers but if you’re an esports player looking for speed above all else, this is the monitor for you. Also, you’ll need a powerful machine to hit that frame rate — I’m talking RTX 50-series graphics cards, at the very least. You’ll need a GPU that supports the latest Displayport 2.1 standard, too. Our gaming rig couldn’t achieve 1,000fps in any game I played.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Even so, the gaming and visual experience was nothing short of sublime. You get a 1ms response time, which is slower than that of the Sony Inzone M10S II (0.2ms) and the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B (0.2ms), but that’s because the 25G590B features an IPS panel versus the rival OLEDs, which shift pixel color more quickly. Though I didn’t experience much motion blur or ghosting, I have my qualms — but I’ll discuss that later in the “The Downs” section.

Back to the good things for now. In Forza Horizon 5, which is a highly graphic-intensive game, I hit 250fps while racing. This was with the graphics set to Extreme (Ray Tracing enabled and all). Movement was buttery smooth without any choppines, and it had me wondering how I’d go back after using the 25G590B. Counter-Strike 2, on the other hand, ran at 490fps with graphics set to High, and this jumped to a whopping 840fps when I dropped the graphics to Low.

Similar to the Sony Inzone M10S II, the LG UltraGear 25G590B features a range of gaming features designed for esports players. Via the OSD (On-Screen Display) and joystick, you can toggle an on-screen crosshair. The target point is then fixed in the center to enhance shooting accuracy — something I found useful in Counter-Strike 2 where some weapons lack an ADS mode. The on-screen crosshair helped me aim more accurately in both Counter-Strike 2 and Cyberpunk 2077.

There’s also a Black Stabilizer mode which boosts shadows without affecting lighter areas of the screen. You get AI Scene Optimization, too, which automatically adjusts key picture settings, like color temperature and sharpness, to match the content type — whether that’s work-related tasks, gaming, or movies. In my testing, it worked as described.

And of course, there’s NVIDIA G-Sync and AMD FreeSync for minimizing tears and lags. Overall, this is a competent and powerful esports monitor that doesn’t give you too much to complain about.

Alongside its phenomenal gaming performance, the LG UltraGear 25G590B boasts wide color coverage and accuracy, too. To my eyes, colors in Forza Horizon 5 appeared vivid — though not as vibrant or rich as on an OLED panel. Blacks appeared dark in Cyberpunk 2077 but, again, not as inky as on an OLED screen.

As you can see in the table above, the 25G590B covers 135.8% of the sRGB color space and 96.2% of the wider DCI P3 gamut, upstaging the Alienware AW2524H ($829) — also an IPS panel — in both spaces. 100% coverage is ideal, so the 25G590B does more than enough. You also don’t want coverage to reach too high, as that can then make colors appear oversaturated. None of that here, though — the 25G590B delivers a pleasing viewing experience.

I then measured color accuracy which is represented by Delta-E. It scores the difference between the source color and what appears on the monitor. Lower scores mean higher fidelity, with values near zero representing near-perfect accuracy. In my lab tests, the 25G590B achieved a Delta-E score of 0.14, which is excellent. It’s either on par with or better than its IPS as well as OLED rivals.

In addition to its strong color coverage and accuracy, the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s panel is bright, especially in its SDR mode.

In my lab tests, the 25G590B achieved a peak brightness of 387 nits in SDR and 310 nits in HDR (10% window size). Its SDR performance is better than the IPS Alienware AW2524H, and every other OLED competitor, as you can see in the table above. Low brightness is a limitation of OLED and QD-OLED panels, though, so this is expected.

In real-world use, I found the 25G590B plenty bright in both SDR and HDR modes. I wouldn’t recommend playing with the brightness turned all the way up anyway, as it can potentially harm your eyes.

Right before I started writing this review, I was testing the LG UltraGear 52G930B ($1,697), a gigantic 52-inch monitor that I struggled to carry up and down the stairs. The LG UltraGear 25G590B is its antithesis. It feels featherlight in comparison, and I was so relieved when I managed to pick it up with just one hand as it weighs just 11.46lbs (with stand).

As the numbers in its name suggest, the 25G590B is a 25-inch monitor, and it measures 22.5 x 20.1 x 8.2 inches with the stand attached. This makes it perfect for small spaces. It’s a little smaller than the 27-inch Sony Inzone M10S II, its chief rival, but the trade-off is that you’re getting a ridiculous 1,000Hz refresh rate (more on that shortly).

The 25G590B is sleek and practical. Similar to the Sony Inzone M10S II, LG’s offering features a cantilevered stand which channels the weight into the center, keeping everything balanced and resulting in the monitor using a small circular base. This also frees up space on your desk, giving you more room for freely positioning your keyboard. The stand’s height can be adjusted and the screen titled, and it can also swivel where it’s attached to the base.

Unlike productivity-focused monitors, like the BenQ Creative Pro PD2730S ($1,199) or the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q ($2,499), ports are fairly stripped-back on the LG UltraGear 25G590B — but they’re more than sufficient for hooking up your peripherals. Located next to the power port on the monitor’s rear panel, you’ll find dual HDMI 2.1 and a DisplayPort 2.1 ports, as well as a USB-C upstream port and a 4-pole headphone/mic jack.

Surprisingly, though, there aren’t any USB-A ports on the 25G590B. I don’t really have an issue with that, though, as I keep my keyboard and mouse plugged into our gaming rig’s motherboard. Hey, at least the 25G590B has a modern Type-C port and not an outdated Type-B one, like on the Sony Inzone M10S II.

Though the LG UltraGear 25G590B is powerful, it isn’t without its flaws. It features an IPS FHD panel, and its response time tops out at 1ms only. Oh, and it’s expensive!

This is a complaint similar to the one I had about the LG UltraGear 52G930B. Frustratingly, the LG UltraGear 25G590B doesn’t feature an OLED panel, and its IPS panel’s resolution tops out at 1920 x 1080 Full HD (FHD). Its IPS panel has a 1,000:1 contrast ratio which means that blacks don’t appear inky, while OLED panels typically deliver pitch-black dark scenes.

It’s also important to note that the 25G590B has a 1920 x 1080 FHD resolution. While this is the competition standard and is great for fast gaming, it falls short for everything else. If you’re looking for a monitor that can do everything — gaming and work — the 25G590B won’t be ideal. A monitor that has an FHD competition crop, like the Sony M10S II, will be more suited to at-home gamers, or aspiring esports players.

That, very nicely, brings me to my next point: the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s 1ms response time. Though that should suffice in casual gaming, high-speed camera pans and rapid movements can produce pixel trails or subtle blur. The monitor has a Motion Blur Reduction feature, yes, but it doesn’t make much of a difference aside from reducing the monitor’s brightness.

On the other hand, 0.03ms or 0.02ms response times on OLED panels offer dramatically sharper response. Combine that with better resolutions, better visuals, and better overall performance, and you’ve got yourself a winner. Again, for that reason, the LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B and the Sony Inzone M10S II make for better investments. Even the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 ($949) with its 360Hz refresh rate would be my port of call over the 25G590B.

Finally, let’s talk about the LG UltraGear 25G590B’s price. Retailing for $999 at Adorama U.S. / £899 at Currys U.K., the 25G590B costs a lot for an IPS FHD monitor. Sure, you get a 1,000Hz refresh rate and that won’t come cheap in any world, but it’s also an IPS panel. For just $100 more, you could pick up the Sony M10S II ($1,199) which features an OLED panel and offers a 24.5-inch competition crop as well as an FHD mode.

But of course, if it’s sheer speed you’re after and you want the fastest monitor possible, $999 feels like a fair price to pay. Would you? Let me know in the comments below!

None other monitor does what the LG UltraGear 25G590B can — at the time of writing, at least. It packs a blazing fast 1,000Hz refresh rate, making it a phenomenal monitor for esports players and competitive gamers. It sports a lovely, sleek design that doesn’t take up too much space, and color coverage and brightness doesn’t give you much to complain about.

But things you can complain about? The 25G590B features an IPS FHD panel, and I really wish it was OLED and 4K — something many of its competitors offer for the same price. Also, it’s got a 1ms response time only which is fine for most gamers, but its OLED rivals offer faster 0.03ms (and sometimes even 0.02ms) response times.

If that doesn’t bother you (or you can afford it), and you really, really want to run Counter-Strike at over 800fps, then there’s no better monitor than the 25G590B.

#3319. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3317. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.

#3316. Apple says it’s ‘only getting started’ updating macOS for touchscreens

Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (pre-order here) includes a variety of software optimizations for touch input. But Apple says it’s “only getting started” making macOS more touch-friendly.

The new touchscreen-equipped MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR will ship with macOS 27.2, software that includes a variety of touch-centric optimizations that only impact PROLED XDR users.

Early feedback from hands-on testers, including our own Chance Miller, appears very positive.

Bloomberg’s Chris Welch reassuringly says that Apple is “taking a measured approach as it introduces touch capabilities.” This echoes comments from John Gruber, who says his concerns about touch “adversely affecting the Mac UI” have all been allayed.

But it sounds like Apple plans to roll out even more macOS optimizations for touch in the future.

An Apple employee answering press questions at Wednesday’s event said the company is only getting started optimizing macOS for a touch screen. I’d expect a slew of refinements to arrive alongside macOS 28 next year, much in the way the iPhone Duo’s user experience will inevitably evolve with iOS 28.

Overall, this isn’t necessarily reason for alarm if you’re worried about touch having a negative impact on macOS.

How about, spitballing here, a tablet device that takes advantage of MacOS’s new found touch capabilities? 🙄

Even though Apple has prepared an initial set of macOS changes to support touch input, it’s only natural for the company to continue refining the touch experience in response to early adopter feedback and usage patterns. My assumption is that the same “measured approach” we’re seeing right now will continue guiding these future macOS enhancements.

You can pre-order MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR on Amazon for day-one delivery.

What do you think of Apple’s efforts at adding touch to macOS? Let us know in the comments.
